_comment: Extra example sentences per entry id, shown after the Magoosh flashcard sentence. src "ebook": from the Magoosh GRE Vocabulary eBook. src "gen": written for this app (checked by a second pass). Replace "gen" ones when real Magoosh sentences become available.

aberrant.text: Most of the seedlings grew straight toward the lamp, but a few aberrant specimens curled away from the light, prompting the botanist to test them for a genetic mutation.
The auditors flagged the account not because its totals were large but because its pattern of late-night transfers was so aberrant compared with every other client's routine activity.
Critics who expected another conventional sonnet sequence were startled by the poet's aberrant new volume, which abandoned rhyme, meter and even punctuation.

aberration.text: The manager insisted that the quarter's losses were a temporary aberration rather than a trend, noting that sales had risen steadily for the previous nine years.
For a composer known for cheerful, tuneful pieces, the dissonant and brooding final quartet struck many listeners as an aberration in an otherwise consistent career.
The researchers discarded one reading as an aberration caused by a faulty sensor, since it contradicted hundreds of measurements taken under identical conditions.

abjure.text: Upon entering the monastery, the young nobleman abjured his inheritance and every worldly pleasure, vowing before the abbot to live in poverty.
Under pressure from the inquisitors, the philosopher publicly abjured his heretical doctrines, though his private letters suggest he never ceased to hold them.
The former militant has abjured violence entirely, and he now travels to schools to warn students against the ideology he once embraced.

aboveboard.text: To reassure skeptical investors, the charity made its books public, insisting that every transaction had been aboveboard and fully documented.
Rather than negotiating in secret, the two firms kept the merger talks aboveboard, briefing regulators and employees at every stage.
The auditor suspected the deal was not aboveboard, since it had been arranged through an anonymous intermediary and recorded nowhere in the minutes.

abrogate.text: The new government abrogated the treaty its predecessor had signed, declaring that the agreement had been negotiated under duress.
When the legislature abrogated the old licensing law, small vendors who had been barred from the market for years were suddenly free to trade.
Critics argued that the emergency decree effectively abrogated citizens' right to assemble, since it banned all public gatherings indefinitely.

abstain.text: Although the banquet offered wine at every course, the surgeon abstained, knowing she might be called to the operating room before midnight.
Several committee members chose to abstain from the vote rather than take a side in a dispute that pitted two of their closest colleagues against each other.
During the fasting month, observant families abstain from food and drink from dawn until sunset, breaking the fast together only after dark.

abstruse.text: The philosopher's argument was so abstruse that even specialists in the field needed several readings, and a glossary, before they could follow its central claim.
Far from being abstruse, the physicist's popular lectures made quantum theory accessible to audiences with no mathematics beyond high school algebra.
Because the tax code is written in such abstruse language, many small business owners hire accountants simply to learn which rules apply to them.

abysmal.text: The orchestra's first rehearsal was abysmal: half the players were out of tune, and the brass entered a full bar early.
Despite the restaurant's glowing reputation, the service that evening was abysmal, with diners waiting an hour for food that arrived cold.
Living conditions in the mining camps were abysmal, with workers crowded into unheated shacks and forced to drink contaminated water.

acme.text: Many critics regard the late string quartets as the acme of the composer's art, the summit toward which all his earlier experiments were leading.
At the acme of her career, the architect was designing museums on three continents; a decade later, she could scarcely find a commission.
For ancient rhetoricians, the funeral oration represented the acme of eloquence, a form that only the most accomplished speakers dared attempt.

adamant.text: Despite repeated pleas from her editor to soften the ending, the novelist remained adamant that the protagonist must die in the final chapter.
The union was adamant about its demand for safer equipment; no offer of higher wages could persuade its leaders to drop the issue.
Although his advisers urged a compromise, the governor was adamant in refusing to reopen the negotiations, insisting that the matter was already settled.

adjudicate.text: A panel of three retired judges was appointed to adjudicate the dispute between the neighboring towns over water rights.
Having been asked to adjudicate the regional piano competition, the conservatory professor listened to forty performances before announcing the winners.
International courts often lack the power to adjudicate border conflicts effectively, since sovereign states may simply refuse to accept their rulings.

admonish.text: The librarian admonished the students for talking in the reading room, warning that a second disturbance would cost them their study privileges.
Rather than praising the report, the supervisor admonished its authors to check their figures more carefully before circulating anything to clients.
The judge admonished the jurors not to discuss the case with anyone, cautioning that even a casual conversation could force a mistrial.

admonitory.text: The museum posted admonitory signs beside the fragile tapestries, reminding visitors in stern language that touching the fabric was strictly forbidden.
Her mentor's letter was less congratulatory than admonitory: it praised the promotion briefly and then devoted three pages to the mistakes she must avoid.
With a single admonitory glance over his spectacles, the conductor silenced the violinist who had begun tuning during the pianist's solo.

advocate-n.text: A passionate advocate of public libraries, the author donated her royalties to rural branches and spoke tirelessly about their importance.
The proposal had few advocates on the committee; most members considered it too costly, and only one spoke in its favor.
Early advocates of the germ theory endured ridicule from established physicians before experiments finally confirmed that microorganisms cause disease.

advocate-v.text: The report advocates a gradual approach to reform, arguing that sudden changes would disrupt the very communities they are meant to help.
For decades the physician advocated for stricter limits on tobacco advertising, testifying before legislatures and publishing study after study on its harms.
Though she privately doubted the plan, the consultant was hired to advocate it publicly, and she argued its merits with conviction at every meeting.

aesthete.text: An aesthete to the core, the collector would rearrange a single vase for an hour until the light fell on its glaze exactly as he wished.
Whereas her pragmatic brother judged furniture only by its durability, Clara was an aesthete who could be moved to tears by the grain of a walnut table.
The novel satirizes a self-styled aesthete who claims to swoon at every sunset yet cannot name a single painter whose work he has actually studied.

aesthetic-adj.text: The city council approved the bridge for engineering reasons, but critics complained that no one had considered its aesthetic impact on the historic skyline.
Although the software was functional, its designers paid little attention to aesthetic concerns, and users found its cluttered gray screens unpleasant to look at.
For the gardener, pruning was never merely practical; it was an aesthetic pursuit in which each cut shaped the beauty of the whole hedge.

aesthetic-n.text: The studio's minimalist aesthetic, which favored bare concrete, raw steel and a single accent color, could be recognized in every building it designed.
Rejecting the lush orchestration of his teachers, the young composer developed a spare aesthetic built on silence, repetition and a handful of notes.
Scholars have traced the magazine's cool, ironic aesthetic, visible in everything from its typography to its photography, to a small circle of founding editors.

affable.text: The new ambassador was affable and approachable, chatting easily with junior staff and remembering the names of their children.
Although the professor's writing is dense and forbidding, in office hours he is affable, putting nervous students at ease with a joke and a cup of tea.
Guests who expected the famously stern critic to be cold were surprised to find him affable, laughing readily and inviting questions after his talk.

affluent.text: The suburb grew affluent after the technology firms arrived, and modest bungalows were soon replaced by sprawling houses with private pools.
Charities in affluent neighborhoods often raise more money in a single evening than those in poorer districts collect in a year.
The novelist, born into an affluent family of bankers, never had to worry about money and could spend years on a single manuscript.

afford.text: The residency affords young composers a rare chance to hear their works performed by a professional orchestra before they are published.
Because the archive was only recently opened, it affords historians an unusual glimpse into the private deliberations of the council.
The balcony of the old observatory affords a sweeping prospect of the harbor, which is why painters have long set up their easels there.

alacrity.text: The interns accepted the challenging assignment with alacrity, volunteering to stay late even before the supervisor had finished explaining it.
Expecting resistance to the new policy, the manager was surprised by the alacrity with which the staff embraced it.
She answered the invitation to lecture abroad with such alacrity that her colleagues suspected she had been hoping for it for years.

altruism.text: Biologists have long puzzled over altruism in animals, such as the worker bee that dies defending a hive in which only the queen will reproduce.
Some economists doubt that pure altruism exists, arguing that even anonymous donations provide the giver with a hidden reward of self-esteem.
The nurse's altruism was evident to everyone on the ward: she worked unpaid overtime, gave away her lunches, and never asked for recognition.

amalgam.text: The city's cuisine is an amalgam of the dishes brought by successive waves of immigrants, combining spices, grains and techniques from three continents.
The committee's final proposal was an awkward amalgam of competing plans, stitched together so that every faction could claim some part of it.
Rather than inventing a new character, the novelist created an amalgam of several relatives, borrowing one uncle's temper and another's wit.

ambiguous.text: The contract's wording was ambiguous: 'within thirty days' could refer either to the date of signing or to the date of delivery, and both parties exploited the confusion.
Critics still argue over the painting's ambiguous expression, which some read as a smile of contentment and others as a grimace of quiet despair.
Because the poll's question was ambiguous, respondents who supported the policy and those who opposed it sometimes gave the same answer.

ambivalent.text: The scientist felt ambivalent about the prize: she was proud of the recognition, yet uneasy that it credited her alone for work her whole lab had done.
Many residents are ambivalent about the new stadium, welcoming the jobs it will bring while dreading the traffic and noise it will create.
In his letters the poet seems ambivalent toward his hometown, alternately praising its quiet beauty and cursing its stifling narrowness.

ameliorate.text: The city planted thousands of trees along its busiest avenues, hoping to ameliorate the heat that had made summers nearly unbearable in poorer neighborhoods.
Although the new medication cannot cure the disease, it does ameliorate the worst symptoms, allowing patients to sleep through the night.
Rather than ameliorating tensions between the two departments, the hasty reorganization only deepened their mutual suspicion and made cooperation even harder.

amenable.text: The landlord proved surprisingly amenable to our request; after a brief conversation, he agreed to repaint the apartment at his own expense.
Unlike her stubborn predecessor, the new director is amenable to suggestions from junior staff and has already adopted several of their ideas.
The negotiators hoped that a modest concession on wages would make the union more amenable to a longer contract.

amiable.text: The two rival chefs maintained an amiable relationship, trading recipes and sharing a meal once a month despite competing for the same customers.
Though the negotiations were tense, the delegates' conversations over dinner were amiable, full of laughter and anecdotes about their families.
The guide's amiable manner quickly put the anxious tourists at ease, and by the end of the tour they were treating him like an old friend.

amorphous.text: The protest movement remained amorphous for months, lacking leaders, a platform or even a name, before it finally coalesced around a single demand.
Under the microscope the cells were amorphous blobs, with none of the regular structure the biologists had expected to see.
The consultant's amorphous recommendations, which urged the firm to 'embrace change' without specifying how, left the managers with nothing concrete to do.

amply.text: The theory's predictions have been amply confirmed by experiment, so few physicists now doubt its basic soundness.
The tenants were amply compensated for the disruption, receiving three months of free rent and a generous allowance for moving costs.
The expedition was amply provisioned, carrying enough food and fuel to last twice as long as the planned journey.

amuck.text: When the fire alarm sounded, the crowd ran amuck, trampling the exhibits and shoving toward the exits in a disorderly panic.
The satirist imagines a bureaucracy run amuck, generating forms for their own sake until the agency processes nothing but its own paperwork.
Once the escaped goats ran amuck through the market, stalls toppled, vendors shouted, and it took hours to restore any semblance of order.

anachronism.text: The historical film was riddled with anachronisms: Roman soldiers wore wristwatches, and a medieval peasant casually referred to germs.
In a firm that had long since digitized its records, the elderly clerk's handwritten ledger seemed a charming anachronism.
Critics argue that the hereditary title is an anachronism, a relic of feudal privilege with no place in a modern democracy.

analogous.text: The researcher argued that the spread of rumors is analogous to the spread of infection, since both pass from person to person and grow rapidly in dense populations.
Although the wings of bats and insects are analogous structures, serving the same function of flight, they evolved independently from entirely different tissues.
The position of a museum curator is in some ways analogous to that of an editor: each selects, arranges, and frames material created by others.

anathema.text: To the purist chefs of the old school, frozen ingredients were anathema; they would sooner close the restaurant than serve a thawed fish.
The very idea of borrowing money was anathema to my grandfather, who had watched his own father ruined by debt.
Once celebrated as a reformer, the minister became anathema to his party after he voted with the opposition, and former allies refused even to speak his name.

anemic.text: Despite heavy investment in advertising, the company's sales remained anemic, barely rising above the previous year's disappointing figures.
Critics found the orchestra's anemic rendition of the symphony puzzling, since the same players had performed it with fire only a month before.
Economists blamed the country's anemic recovery on weak consumer confidence, which kept households from spending even as interest rates fell.

animosity.text: The long-standing animosity between the two families erupted at the wedding, where a trivial slight led to shouting and overturned tables.
Despite months of animosity during the campaign, the two rivals shook hands warmly after the result and pledged to work together.
The historian traces the animosity between the neighboring city-states to a disputed boundary river, over which they fought three wars.

anodyne-adj.text: Hoping to offend no one, the committee approved an anodyne mission statement so vague that it could have described almost any organization.
Although the comedian was once known for provocative material, his recent routines have become anodyne, carefully avoiding any subject that might stir controversy.
The press secretary's anodyne remarks about 'continuing dialogue' revealed nothing and ruffled no one, which was precisely their purpose.

anodyne-n.text: For the grieving widow, gardening became an anodyne, a quiet routine that dulled the ache of loss when nothing else could.
Before modern pharmaceuticals, physicians relied on herbal preparations as their chief anodyne, prescribing them for everything from toothaches to broken bones.
The philosopher regarded music as an anodyne for the anxieties of modern life, recommending an hour of Bach to any student tormented by worry.

anomalous.text: The astronomers could not explain the anomalous dimming of the star, which did not match the pattern of any known planet or dust cloud.
In a family of accountants and engineers, her decision to become a sculptor seemed anomalous, yet her parents supported it without hesitation.
Because one patient's reaction was so anomalous, the doctors reviewed her medical history to see what set her apart from the others in the trial.

anomaly.text: A warm day in January is no anomaly in this region, where mild spells regularly interrupt the winter.
The historian noted that the treaty was something of an anomaly: in a century of bitter rivalry, it was the only agreement the two kingdoms ever honored.
Engineers traced the anomaly in the bridge's readings to a loose cable, reassuring the public that the structure itself was sound.

antedated.text: The newly discovered manuscript antedates all previously known copies of the poem by at least a century, making it invaluable to scholars.
Cave paintings in the region antedate the earliest known writing by tens of thousands of years, suggesting that visual art arose long before the alphabet.
The quarrel between the brothers antedated their father's death; they had fought over the farm for years before the will was ever read.

antic.text: The play's antic humor, with actors tumbling over furniture and speaking in absurd rhymes, delighted children but baffled some older critics.
Though the scholar was solemn in his lectures, his letters reveal an antic streak: he signed them with invented titles and doodled ridiculous animals in the margins.
The film's antic energy, all pratfalls and absurd chases, gives way in the final act to an unexpectedly somber meditation on grief.

antipathy.text: The novelist's antipathy toward critics was well known; she refused interviews and once returned a glowing review with an angry note.
Despite their shared politics, the two senators felt a deep antipathy for each other that no amount of party loyalty could conceal.
Her antipathy to cities was so strong that she turned down a prestigious job rather than move away from her quiet valley.

antiquated.text: The hospital's antiquated computer system, installed decades ago and no longer supported by its manufacturer, frequently crashed during busy shifts.
Critics called the dress code antiquated, noting that its rules about hats and gloves reflected the manners of a bygone era.
Although the statute remained on the books, its antiquated penalties (among them the public stocks) had not been enforced in over a century.

antithetical.text: Rote memorization, the reformers argued, is antithetical to genuine inquiry, since it rewards students for repeating answers rather than questioning them.
The director's flashy, crowd-pleasing style seemed antithetical to the spare and meditative novel he had chosen to adapt.
For the monks, the pursuit of wealth was antithetical to their mission; they gave away every gift they received.

apathetic.text: The candidate's speech, though full of passion, failed to stir an apathetic audience that had long since stopped believing politicians could change anything.
Most students were apathetic about the new curriculum, but a small group of passionate parents attended every meeting to fight it.
After years of being ignored by management, the employees grew apathetic, doing the minimum required and no longer offering ideas.

apathy.text: The charity's greatest obstacle was not hostility but apathy: most people agreed the cause was worthy and then simply did nothing.
His apathy toward his studies puzzled his teachers, who remembered him as a boy eager to read every book in the classroom.
Rather than outrage, the scandal produced only public apathy, as citizens shrugged and assumed that every official behaved the same way.

apex.text: The empire reached its apex under the third dynasty, when its territory stretched from the mountains to the sea, and declined steadily thereafter.
Wolves sit at the apex of the food chain in that ecosystem, preying on elk and deer while having no natural predators of their own.
Winning the international competition marked the apex of the young violinist's career, a height she never again approached.

aphorism.text: The essayist condensed her philosophy into a single aphorism, 'A garden reveals the gardener,' which her students still quote decades later.
Rather than building a systematic argument, the moralist wrote in aphorisms, each compressing a lifetime of observation into one memorable line.
The old saying that haste makes waste was an aphorism her grandfather repeated whenever an apprentice rushed a job in his workshop.

aphoristic.text: The philosopher's aphoristic style, in which entire arguments are compressed into a few pointed sentences, makes his books easy to quote but difficult to interpret.
Rather than explaining her decisions at length, the coach offered aphoristic advice such as 'Practice the thing you avoid,' which her players repeated for years.
The novel's dialogue is oddly aphoristic; every character speaks in polished maxims, as if reciting lines from a book of proverbs.
Critics praised the poet's aphoristic closing lines, each of which distills the preceding stanza into a crisp, memorable observation about human nature.

aplomb.text: When the power failed midway through her keynote address, the speaker continued with aplomb, finishing her talk by lamplight as if nothing had happened.
The young pilot handled the engine failure with remarkable aplomb, calmly guiding the aircraft to a safe landing while passengers panicked.
Though the negotiators across the table grew openly hostile, the ambassador responded with aplomb, never raising her voice or losing her train of thought.

apocryphal.text: The tale of the young composer writing an entire symphony in one night is probably apocryphal; no letters or diaries from the period mention it.
Although the quotation appears on countless posters, scholars regard it as apocryphal, since it cannot be found in any of the statesman's writings.
Company legend holds that the founder sketched the first design on a napkin, but longtime employees suspect the story is apocryphal.

apogee.text: The empire reached its apogee under its third ruler; thereafter, costly wars and internal feuds brought about a long decline.
Many critics consider the novel the apogee of the author's career, the point at which her experiments with form finally achieved full mastery.
At the apogee of the speculative frenzy, investors paid absurd sums for shares in companies that had never earned a profit; within months, the market collapsed.

apostate.text: Once the movement's most zealous preacher, he became an apostate after witnessing its leaders' corruption, and he spent his later years writing against them.
The community treated the apostate harshly, refusing to trade with a woman who had publicly renounced the faith of her ancestors.
To the party loyalists, the economist was an apostate: having abandoned the free-market doctrines he once championed, he now advocated sweeping regulation.

apothegm.text: The old sea captain was fond of apothegms, and his favorite, 'a calm sea never made a skilled sailor,' was repeated to every new recruit.
The philosopher's notebooks contain few sustained arguments; instead, they are filled with terse, memorable maxims, each apothegm distilling a lesson on friendship, death, or virtue.
Rather than deliver a lengthy lecture on thrift, my grandmother offered a single apothegm that has guided me ever since: 'Mend today, spare tomorrow.'

apotheosis.text: The ceiling fresco depicts the apotheosis of the slain hero, who rises through the clouds to take his place among the gods.
Many critics regard the cathedral as the apotheosis of Gothic architecture, the culmination of centuries of refinement in vaulting and stained glass.
Within a generation of his death, the general had undergone a kind of apotheosis: statues of him filled every town square, and schoolchildren recited his sayings as if they were scripture.

appease.text: To appease the angry customers, the airline offered free hotel rooms and vouchers, though many travelers remained furious about the cancellation.
The emperor tried to appease the rebellious provinces by lowering their taxes, but the concession only encouraged them to demand independence.
Rather than appeasing the critics by cutting the controversial scene, the director defended it in an open letter.

appreciable.text: The new drug produced no appreciable improvement in patients' symptoms; any differences from the placebo group were too small to measure reliably.
Moving production abroad yielded appreciable savings, enough to lower the product's retail price by nearly a third.
Although the insulation was expensive, it made an appreciable difference to the building's energy use, which fell noticeably within the first winter.

apprehension.text: The villagers watched the rising river with growing apprehension, sandbagging their doorways as forecasters predicted another night of heavy rain.
Despite her apprehension before the surgery, the patient found the procedure far less painful than she had feared.
Investors greeted the new regulations with apprehension, worried that the added costs would erode profits in an already fragile market.

approbatory.text: The committee's approbatory letter commended the young scientist for work that, in its words, had transformed the field.
Although the director had braced himself for scathing reviews, the notices were almost uniformly approbatory, and within a week the theater had extended the play's run.
Her usually stern mentor offered only an approbatory nod, but from him even that small gesture felt like lavish praise.

appropriate-v1.text: The occupying army appropriated the farmers' grain and livestock without compensation, leaving the villages to face the winter with nothing.
Critics accused the regime of having appropriated church lands under the pretext of reform, seizing property that had been held for centuries.
The lawsuit arose when the larger firm appropriated the startup's patented design without permission and began selling it as its own.

appropriate-v2.text: Each year the legislature appropriates a portion of the state budget for the maintenance of rural roads and bridges.
Because the council had appropriated too little for snow removal, the city ran out of road salt in the middle of January.
The university appropriated a separate fund for graduate fellowships, ensuring that research assistants would be paid even if grant money dried up.

appurtenant.text: The deed conveyed not only the farmhouse but also the barns and water rights appurtenant to it, which the buyers regarded as essential to working the land.
The main hospital performs the surgeries, while the appurtenant clinics supply the follow-up care and rehabilitation that support each patient's recovery.
In the orchestra's plan, the smaller chamber ensembles were appurtenant to the main ensemble, supplementing its season with educational concerts in local schools.

arbitrary.text: Employees resented the arbitrary schedule changes, which seemed to follow no pattern and were announced without explanation.
The judge's decision was hardly arbitrary; she cited three precedents and explained in detail why each applied to the case.
Any cutoff score is somewhat arbitrary, the admissions officer admitted, since a student one point below the line is scarcely different from one just above it.

arcane.text: The lawyer navigated the arcane procedures of maritime law with ease, though most of her colleagues had never even heard of the statutes she cited.
Only a handful of scholars can read the arcane notation used by medieval alchemists, whose symbols were designed to conceal their methods from outsiders.
To the uninitiated, the rules of the ancient board game seemed arcane, but the players had learned them as children and followed them effortlessly.

arch.text: He shrugged off her insults because he knew she was only being arch.
Her arch reply to the pompous critic, delivered with a raised eyebrow and a faint smile, made it clear she was mocking him without ever saying so.
Readers who take the narrator at face value miss the joke, for his tone is arch throughout, and his solemn promises about the ending are made only to be slyly broken.
Though the professor seemed stern, his arch asides during lectures, playful jabs at famous theorists, revealed a mischievous sense of humor.

archaic.text: The legal code is full of archaic terms that even lawyers must look up, relics of statutes drafted centuries ago.
Visitors to the remote island are struck by its archaic customs, such as settling disputes through ritual song contests, practices long vanished from the mainland.
Critics found the translation's diction archaic, since its constant 'thee' and 'thou' made a lively modern play sound like a sermon from a distant age.

arduous.text: Restoring the damaged fresco was an arduous task, requiring the conservators to clean each square inch by hand over the course of four years.
Although the summit trail is short, it is arduous: hikers must climb nearly vertical rock for hours with little shade and no water.
The translator described her work on the epic as arduous, since every line demanded weeks of research into forgotten idioms and allusions.

arrant.text: The reviewer dismissed the supposed memoir as arrant nonsense, pointing out that half of its episodes could not possibly have occurred.
Only an arrant coward would abandon his wounded comrades to save himself, the sergeant declared before the court-martial.
Calling the hastily drafted plan a strategy was arrant flattery; in truth, it was little more than a list of wishes.

arriviste.text: The old aristocratic families sneered at the arriviste, whose fortune from railway shares had bought him a mansion but not their acceptance.
Eager to prove she belonged among the city's elite, the arriviste threw extravagant parties and dropped famous names constantly, which only confirmed the established families' disdain.
The novel satirizes an arriviste who, having recently clawed his way into the cabinet, flaunts his new power with petty displays of authority.

arrogate.text: Without consulting the board, the new director arrogated to herself the power to hire and fire staff, a privilege the bylaws reserved for the trustees.
Historians note that the general gradually arrogated civilian authority, first controlling the press and then dissolving the elected assembly.
The committee chair was accused of arrogating decisions that belonged to the full membership, announcing policies that no one else had approved.

artful-adj1.text: The pianist's artful phrasing turned a simple folk melody into something so refined that the audience sat in stunned silence afterward.
The critic praised the film's artful composition, noting how each frame was arranged with the care of a classical painting.
Far from clumsy, the potter's glazes were artful, layering subtle blues and greens so that each bowl seemed to shimmer like water.

artful-adj2.text: The con man's artful excuses fooled even the skeptical detective, who realized only weeks later how thoroughly he had been manipulated.
With artful evasions, the witness managed to answer every question without ever revealing where she had been that night.
The lobbyist was an artful schemer who flattered legislators in public while quietly arranging for their rivals to fund his causes.

artifice.text: The swindler's artifice was elaborate: forged letters, a rented office, and a staff of actors who posed as satisfied investors.
Wary of diplomatic artifice, the negotiator insisted that every promise be written into the treaty rather than trusting the envoy's charming assurances.
Far from being spontaneous, the executive's tearful apology was pure artifice, rehearsed for days with a team of public relations consultants.

artless.text: The child's artless questions exposed contradictions that the adults had tactfully ignored for years, precisely because she had no idea that such things were not supposed to be asked.
Unlike the polished testimony of the other witnesses, the farmer's account was artless and plainly sincere, which is why the jury believed him.
Some readers mistake the poet's artless voice for naivete, but her utter lack of pretense is precisely what gives the poems their honesty.

artlessness.text: The novelist captures the artlessness of her young heroine, who says exactly what she thinks and cannot imagine that anyone would lie to her.
Voters found the candidate's artlessness refreshing; unlike his rehearsed rivals, he admitted mistakes openly and never seemed to calculate his answers.
What the court mistook for cunning was in fact artlessness: the defendant had simply signed whatever papers his trusted accountant placed before him.

ascendancy.text: By the end of the century the merchant guilds had gained ascendancy over the old aristocracy, controlling both the city council and its treasury.
During the decade of the general's ascendancy, no policy could be adopted without his approval, and rival officers were sidelined or exiled.
The spread of streaming services has ended the long ascendancy of broadcast networks, which once dictated what nearly every household watched each evening.

ascetic-adj.text: The philosopher led an ascetic existence, sleeping on a wooden plank, eating one plain meal a day and owning nothing but a few books.
Though heir to a vast fortune, she adopted an ascetic routine, giving away her jewels and refusing even small comforts such as heated rooms.
The monastery's ascetic rules forbade meat, conversation after sunset and any possessions beyond a robe and a bowl.

ascetic-n.text: The hermit was a true ascetic, living for decades in a cave on a diet of bread and water and refusing every gift offered by pilgrims.
Unlike his lavish brother, the younger prince became an ascetic, renouncing his inheritance to live in a bare cell among the monks.
Visitors expected the famous ascetic to be gloomy, yet the man who had forsaken all comforts greeted them with cheerful warmth.

ascribe.text: Doctors once ascribed the fever to foul air rising from swamps, not realizing that mosquitoes breeding in the water carried the disease.
The painting was long ascribed to a master of the Florentine school, but recent analysis suggests it came from the workshop of a minor follower.
She ascribed her success not to talent but to discipline, crediting the years she spent practicing scales every morning before dawn.

askance.text: The veteran editors looked askance at the intern's proposal to abolish the print edition, doubting that a newcomer understood the paper's finances.
Traditional physicians initially viewed the new therapy askance, suspecting that its dramatic results were too good to be true.
When the stranger offered to buy the entire orchard for cash, the farmer eyed him askance and asked to see his credentials first.

asperity.text: The judge rebuked the lawyer with such asperity that the courtroom fell silent and the attorney's face turned crimson.
Although her letters to friends were warm, the critic wrote about untalented playwrights with an asperity that made her reviews feared throughout the theater world.
The mediator's gentle manner stood in sharp contrast to the asperity of the two parties, who addressed each other only in curt, cutting phrases.

assail.text: Critics assailed the new museum in column after column, denouncing its design as a cold and arrogant intrusion on the historic square.
In his pamphlet, the economist assailed the central bank's policies, accusing its governors of recklessness and demanding their resignation.
The theory, once widely accepted, was assailed in a series of scathing reviews that exposed its reliance on flawed data.

assiduously.text: The graduate student assiduously checked every citation in her dissertation, spending weeks in the library to ensure that no source was misquoted.
Having assiduously cultivated relationships with local farmers over many years, the chef could obtain produce that no competitor could match.
Though the restorers worked assiduously, removing centuries of grime one square inch at a time, the project took more than a decade to complete.

assuage.text: The airline tried to assuage the anger of stranded passengers by offering free hotel rooms and vouchers for future flights.
Nothing the doctor said could assuage the family's grief, though her patient explanations helped them understand what had happened.
To assuage fears about the new vaccine, health officials published the full trial data and invited independent scientists to review it.

atavism.text: The sociologist described the revival of blood feuds in the remote province as an atavism, a return to customs the region had seemed to abandon generations ago.
Occasionally a foal is born with small extra toes, an atavism that recalls the horse's distant ancestors, which walked on several digits.
Critics dismissed the heavy stone library as an atavism: in an age of glass and steel, its architect had given it turrets and arrow slits as though the city still feared siege.

attenuate.text: The stick is attenuated at one end to allow the villagers to forage for ants.
As the river spreads across the delta, its current gradually attenuates, until it becomes little more than a sluggish seep through the reeds.
A second layer of insulation attenuated the roar of the highway so effectively that residents could finally sleep through the night.
The drug's side effects usually attenuate after the first few weeks, so doctors urge patients not to abandon treatment during the initial discomfort.

audacious.text: The general's audacious plan called for marching the entire army across the frozen lake at night, a risk no commander before him had dared to take.
Critics called the young architect's design audacious, since it balanced a heavy concert hall on a single slender column.
It was an audacious move for a first-year associate to challenge the senior partner's argument in front of the client, but her boldness won the case.

audacity.text: The intern had the audacity to correct the chairman in the middle of his speech, a breach of etiquette that left the room silent.
Few journalists would have shown the audacity to question the dictator directly, yet she asked him about the missing prisoners on live television.
The committee was shocked by the audacity of the applicant, who demanded a salary higher than the director's before he had even been interviewed.

augment.text: The museum augmented its modest collection of prints with a bequest of several hundred works, making it one of the largest in the region.
Many teachers augment their salaries by tutoring on weekends, since their regular pay barely covers living costs in the city.
Rather than replacing the aging reservoir, engineers chose to augment its capacity by raising the dam wall several meters.

auspicious.text: The clear skies on launch day seemed auspicious, and the engineers began the countdown confident that the mission would succeed.
The album's launch was hardly auspicious: on the day of its release the lead single was pulled from radio, and the opening concert of the tour was canceled for lack of ticket sales.
A strong first quarter provided an auspicious start for the new chief executive, who had promised investors a rapid recovery.

austere-adj1.text: After years of lavish spending, the heiress adopted an austere way of life, forgoing servants, rich food and every luxury she had once enjoyed.
The monks' austere discipline included long fasts, cold baths and nights spent kneeling on stone floors in silent prayer.
Though he could afford comfort, the scholar remained austere in his habits, allowing himself nothing beyond bread, tea and his books.

austere-adj2.text: The chapel's austere interior, with whitewashed walls and plain wooden benches, contrasted sharply with the gilded cathedral across the square.
The designer favored an austere layout for the book, with wide margins, a single typeface and not one decorative flourish.
Visitors expecting ornate furnishings were surprised by the austere rooms of the palace, which held little more than a table and a few chairs.

austere-adj3.text: The headmaster's austere manner, with his cold stare and clipped commands, frightened even the most rebellious pupils into silence.
Colleagues found the judge austere and forbidding, yet her clerks insisted that she was warm once one got past her severe demeanor.
Unlike his genial predecessor, the new abbot was austere, rebuking the novices sharply for the slightest lapse.

autocratic-adj1.text: Under the autocratic system of the old empire, the emperor alone could make law, and no council or court could overrule his decrees.
The constitution was designed to prevent a return to autocratic rule, dividing power among three branches that could check one another.
Although it held elections, the state remained essentially autocratic, since the president could dissolve parliament and govern by decree whenever he wished.

autocratic-adj2.text: The orchestra's autocratic conductor made every decision himself, dismissing musicians who dared to suggest a different tempo.
Employees chafed under the autocratic new department head, who overruled her team's plans without explanation and demanded obedience rather than input.
Though he held no official rank in the family business, the eldest son behaved in an autocratic manner, issuing orders to cousins who were technically his superiors.

autonomously.text: The rover was designed to operate autonomously, choosing its own path across the terrain, since signals from Earth take too long to allow real-time control.
After the reforms, each province managed its affairs autonomously, setting its own taxes and school curricula without seeking approval from the capital.
Senior researchers in the lab work autonomously, pursuing their own projects with little supervision, while junior members follow a prescribed program.

avarice.text: The merchant's avarice was legendary: he hoarded gold he would never spend and refused his servants even a crust of bread.
Moralists of the period blamed the financial collapse on avarice, arguing that bankers' insatiable appetite for profit had blinded them to obvious risks.
In the fable, the king's avarice undoes him: forever craving more treasure, he gambles away the kingdom he already had.

avaricious.text: The avaricious landlord raised the rent every year, even as the building's plumbing failed and its tenants struggled to pay.
In the fable, an avaricious merchant hoards so much gold that he starves in his vault rather than spend a single coin on bread.
Critics accused the firm's executives of being avaricious, noting that they awarded themselves record bonuses while laying off thousands of workers.

avert-v1.text: Embarrassed by the lavish praise, the young author averted her gaze and stared at the floor until the applause died down.
Squeamish at the sight of the needle, the patient averted his eyes and fixed them on a poster across the room.
Passersby averted their faces from the man pleading for spare change, pretending not to see him as they hurried along the crowded street.

avert-v2.text: Quick action by the air traffic controller averted a collision between the two aircraft, which had been assigned the same altitude by mistake.
Last-minute negotiations averted a strike that would have shut down the city's transit system during the holiday season.
Economists argue that the central bank's timely intervention averted a far deeper recession, although critics say it merely postponed the crisis.

avid.text: An avid collector of old maps, the retired judge spent his weekends combing through auctions and dusty bookshops for rare specimens.
The book club's most avid reader finished three novels a week and was always pressing new titles on the other members.
Although she had been an avid gardener for decades, arthritis eventually forced her to give up the hobby she had pursued with such zeal.

badger.text: The journalist badgered the minister's office with daily phone calls until an aide finally agreed to schedule an interview.
The children in the back seat badgered their parents for hours about stopping for ice cream, repeating the request at every exit.
Rather than badger reluctant donors with a stream of letters, the charity sent a single well-crafted appeal and respected their decision.

baleful.text: The villagers took the circling vultures as a baleful sign, and many refused to begin the harvest until the birds had gone.
In the painting, a baleful red moon hangs over the sleeping army, foreshadowing the defeat that the next panel depicts.
Economists issued baleful warnings about the housing bubble, predicting widespread foreclosures that, unfortunately, soon came to pass.

balk.text: The board initially approved the expansion but balked when it learned that the project would require borrowing nearly twice the original estimate.
Many patients balk at the cost of the new treatment, choosing older therapies that are less effective but far cheaper.
The horse had cleared every earlier fence with ease, so the crowd gasped when it balked at the final jump and its rider had to circle back for another attempt.

banal.text: The novel's plot was banal, recycling the same tired story of a small-town girl who moves to the city and finds love.
Hoping for insight, the students were disappointed by the speaker's banal advice to 'follow your passion' and 'never give up.'
What begins as a banal detective story is transformed in its final chapters into a strikingly original meditation on memory.

banality.text: The graduation speech was a string of banalities, each one as predictable as the last, and the audience soon stopped listening.
The diplomat's statement contained nothing but the usual banality that 'both sides must work toward peace,' offering no concrete proposal.
Although the letter seemed to contain only banalities about the weather, the historian read it as a coded report on troop movements.

banish.text: After the failed coup, the plotters were banished from the kingdom and forbidden, on pain of death, ever to return.
The new principal banished mobile phones from the classrooms, requiring students to leave them in lockers until the end of the day.
A brisk walk usually banished the composer's gloom, driving away the melancholy that settled on him after long hours at the piano.

base.text: The prosecutor argued that only base greed could explain the embezzlement, since the defendant had stolen from a fund for orphaned children.
Although the courtier professed noble ideals, his conduct revealed base motives: he betrayed his patron the moment a richer lord offered him a bribe.
The novelist refuses to portray her villain as merely base; even his cruelest acts spring from a wounded and recognizably human pride.

bastardization.text: Purists condemned the pop arrangement as a bastardization of the folk song, since it stripped away the haunting modal melody and replaced it with a generic beat.
The translator complained that the publisher's heavy edits amounted to a bastardization of the original, cutting whole chapters and softening its political critique.
Scholars view the watered-down curriculum as a bastardization of the philosopher's teachings, reducing a rigorous ethical system to a list of slogans.

beatific.text: Marred by the ravages of time, the idols were hardly beautiful, yet each seemed to emanate a beatific aura that not even 500 years could diminish.
The saint in the altarpiece wears a beatific expression, her eyes raised toward heaven as if she were already enjoying paradise.
As she held her first grandchild, the old woman's face took on a beatific glow that none of her family had seen in years.
After finishing the marathon, the runners lay on the grass with beatific smiles, utterly exhausted yet perfectly content.

becoming.text: The actor's modesty after his victory was becoming; rather than boasting, he praised his rivals and thanked the crew.
The historian adopted a sober, measured tone, which was becoming in a report on a national tragedy; sensational language would have seemed disrespectful to the victims' families.
Such petty sniping at a colleague's retirement dinner was hardly becoming in a senior diplomat, and several guests left the room in disgust.

beg.text: The pamphlet merely begs the question, since it argues that the ancient chronicle must be reliable on the grounds that the chronicle itself claims to be accurate.
Critics noted that the study begged the question by measuring intelligence with a test designed on the assumption that the favored group was already more intelligent.
The witness begged the question by asserting that the document was genuine because it bore a genuine signature, which was exactly what the court had asked him to establish.

begrudge-v1.text: Though she had lost the prize to her former student, the sculptor did not begrudge him his success; she was the first to congratulate him.
Neighbors who had struggled through the drought begrudged the rancher his lush pastures, suspecting that he had diverted more than his share of the river.
It is hard not to begrudge a colleague the grants she seems to win without effort, even when one knows that such resentment is unworthy.

begrudge-v2.text: The stingy landlord begrudged every penny spent on repairs, patching leaks with tape rather than paying a plumber.
The overworked surgeon begrudged the hours each week she was required to spend on paperwork, time she would rather have given to her patients.
Though the legislature did fund the museum, it begrudged the money, approving only the bare minimum after months of haggling.

behooves.text: It behooves any researcher who handles public funds to publish her results openly, since taxpayers have a right to see what their money produced.
Given the scale of the risk, it would behoove the city council to consult independent engineers before approving the new tower.
It behooves a translator to respect the author's intentions, even when a looser rendering would sound more elegant.

belie.text: Her surface calm belied her roiling emotions.
The effortless fluidity with which the pianist's fingers moved belied the countless hours he had practiced.
Her upbeat attitude during the group project belied her inherent pessimism towards any collective endeavor.
The calm voice of the pilot belied the gravity of the situation, for the plane had lost an engine and was losing altitude fast.
The modest facade of the house belies its enormous interior, which extends far back into the hillside.
Her cheerful public statements belied the company's real financial state, which was far worse than investors had been told.

belittle.text: Rather than acknowledging his assistant's discovery, the professor belittled it as a lucky accident that any undergraduate could have stumbled upon.
Some reviewers belittle genre fiction as mere entertainment, yet many detective novels explore moral questions with remarkable subtlety.
The coach was careful never to belittle a struggling player in front of the team, knowing how public humiliation could destroy an athlete's confidence.

bellicose.text: The dictator's bellicose speeches, full of threats against neighboring states, alarmed diplomats who feared that an invasion was imminent.
Normally mild, the scholar turned bellicose whenever his theory was questioned, challenging critics to public debates and denouncing them in print.
Anthropologists once portrayed the tribe as bellicose, but later research showed that its members resolved most disputes through elaborate negotiation rather than raids.

belligerent.text: After losing the argument, the delegate grew belligerent, shouting at the chair and threatening to walk out of the conference.
The ambassador's belligerent rhetoric alarmed the neighboring states, which feared that his words foreshadowed an actual invasion.
Though usually mild-mannered, the professor became belligerent whenever anyone questioned his theory, challenging critics to public debates.

bemoan.text: Veteran journalists often bemoan the decline of long-form reporting, lamenting that editors now prefer quick stories that attract clicks.
Rather than spend months bemoaning the loss of their grant, as some colleagues did, the researchers redesigned the study around their existing equipment.
In his final essays, the aging critic bemoaned the passing of an era when poetry was read aloud in every household, a loss he considered tragic.

benighted.text: The reformers regarded the villagers as benighted, yet the villagers' traditional farming methods proved better suited to the arid soil than the experts' modern techniques.
The pamphlet argued that censorship had left the population benighted, cut off from the scientific discoveries that were transforming neighboring countries.
Enlightenment writers often portrayed the preceding centuries as a benighted age of superstition, a caricature that later historians have challenged.

benign-adj1.text: The villagers remembered the old doctor as a benign presence, always ready with a gentle word and never charging those who could not pay.
Far from the tyrant his enemies described, the ruler was benign toward his subjects, lowering taxes after bad harvests and pardoning petty offenders.
The headmistress regarded her pupils with a benign smile, forgiving their small mischiefs as the natural high spirits of youth.

benign-adj2.text: The biopsy showed that the lump was benign, so the surgeon removed it for the patient's comfort rather than out of any concern that it would spread.
Although most skin moles are benign, dermatologists recommend monitoring any that change in size, shape, or color, since these can signal cancer.
The child's heart murmur turned out to be benign, a quirk of blood flow that required no treatment and posed no threat to her health.

bereft-adj1.text: Bereft after her father's sudden death, the young historian set aside her dissertation for a year and spent long afternoons sorting through the letters he had left behind.
The opera's second act finds the heroine bereft, mourning at the tomb of the brother who fell defending the city and refusing every attempt to console her.
The villagers rallied around the bereft parents after the fever claimed their only son, bringing meals to the house and sitting with them through the long nights of mourning.

bereft-adj2.text: When the flood destroyed the library that had been his life's work, the old scholar was bereft, wandering among the ruined shelves in silence.
Bereft after the closing of the factory that had employed three generations of their families, the townspeople struggled to imagine any future for their community.
The orchestra seemed bereft after its concert hall burned down, and several musicians said that playing in a borrowed gymnasium only reminded them of everything they had lost.

besiege.text: After the lottery win was announced, the family was besieged by distant relatives and strangers, all requesting loans or donations.
Following the controversial ruling, the court's press office was besieged with inquiries from reporters demanding an explanation.
Besieged by doubts about her decision to leave the firm, she spent sleepless nights rehearsing every argument for and against it.

besmirch.text: The anonymous letters besmirched the reputation of a scientist whose integrity had never before been questioned, and her funding was suspended pending an inquiry.
Rather than debating her proposals, her opponents sought to besmirch her character with insinuations about her finances.
The plagiarism scandal besmirched the proud name of the old publishing house, and authors who had long been loyal began seeking other publishers.

besotted-adj1.text: The critic was so besotted with the young novelist's debut that his review read less like an assessment than a love letter.
Besotted with his new bride, the prince neglected affairs of state, spending whole days composing poems in her honor.
Though her parents warned that the suitor was a fortune hunter, the heiress was too besotted to heed them, and she married him within a month.

besotted-adj2.text: By midnight the sailors were thoroughly besotted, staggering along the docks and singing after emptying the tavern's last barrel of rum.
The coachman arrived besotted, reeking of gin and barely able to hold the reins, so the travelers refused to board.
The novel's feckless squire is rarely sober; he spends each evening besotted after a bottle of cheap brandy and each morning nursing the consequences.

betray.text: As we age, our political leanings tend to become less pronounced; the once dyed-in-the-wool conservative can betray liberal leanings, and the staunch progressive may suddenly embrace conservative policies.
Although she claimed to be indifferent to the verdict, her trembling hands betrayed how anxious she really was.
The spy's slight accent betrayed his foreign origins, despite years of training to speak like a native.
The poet's careful revisions betray a deep insecurity, for she rewrote even her most celebrated lines dozens of times.

bilious.text: The critic's bilious reviews, which found fault with nearly every production he saw, made him feared by actors and ignored by audiences.
Plagued by chronic pain, the old admiral grew increasingly bilious, snapping at his servants and quarreling with every visitor.
Although the columnist was genial in person, her prose was bilious, and readers learned to expect that politicians, neighbors, and even her own subscribers would feel the sting of her pen.

blatant.text: The essay was a blatant case of plagiarism: entire paragraphs had been copied word for word from a well-known textbook.
The referee's call was so blatant a mistake that even the home crowd booed the decision.
Rather than hiding their favoritism, the officials showed blatant partiality, awarding every contract to firms owned by their relatives.

bleak.text: With no rain forecast for months and the reservoirs nearly empty, the outlook for the region's farmers is bleak.
The novel's bleak vision of the future, in which cities have crumbled and hope has vanished, left many readers shaken.
Although the company's prospects looked bleak after three losing quarters, a surprise licensing deal transformed its fortunes almost overnight.

blinkered.text: The committee's blinkered focus on short-term profits led it to ignore warnings that the mine would poison the town's water supply.
Critics called the historian's account blinkered, since it examined only the diplomats' correspondence and ignored the soldiers and civilians who bore the war's costs.
Raised in a sheltered community that forbade outside books, she had a blinkered view of the world until she left for university.

bolster.text: The new fossil discovery bolstered the theory that birds evolved from dinosaurs, adding yet another piece of supporting evidence.
Hoping to bolster morale after the layoffs, the company organized team retreats and announced modest raises for those who remained.
The city bolstered the old seawall with steel and concrete, strengthening it against the storms that had grown more frequent.

boon-adj.text: The two poets were boon companions for decades, sharing long dinners, lively conversation, and a lifelong habit of reading each other's drafts.
At the harbor tavern the old sailor found his boon companions from the voyage, and they spent the night toasting one another and swapping stories.
Though they sparred ferociously in print, the two critics were boon companions in private, dining together every week and laughing over each other's reviews.

boon-n.text: The new highway proved a boon to local restaurants, which saw their business double as travelers stopped to eat on the way to the coast.
For scholars of medieval history, the digitization of the monastery's archive has been an enormous boon, sparing them long and costly journeys.
Mild winters are a boon for the region's farmers but a hazard for its ski resorts, which depend on reliable snowfall.

boorish.text: The guest's boorish behavior (talking loudly through the toast and helping himself from other diners' plates) embarrassed his hosts.
The diplomat was reprimanded for boorish remarks at the banquet, where he mocked his hosts' cuisine and repeatedly interrupted the foreign minister.
Though the novelist cultivated a boorish persona in public, swearing and sneering at interviewers, his friends insisted he was gracious in private.

bowdlerize.text: The publisher bowdlerized the old ballads for a children's anthology, removing the coarse verses and softening the violence.
Scholars were dismayed to discover that the only surviving edition of the diary had been bowdlerized by the author's prudish nephew, who excised every indelicate passage.
Rather than bowdlerize the playwright's profane dialogue for the school production, the director chose a different play entirely.

brazen.text: In a brazen breach of protocol, the junior diplomat interrupted the treaty signing to announce his own objections to the press.
The thieves were so brazen that they robbed the gallery in broad daylight, walking out with the painting while visitors watched.
Her brazen defiance of the dress code, arriving at the formal gala in hiking boots, delighted some guests and scandalized others.

bridle-v1.text: The new regulations were intended to bridle the banks' appetite for risk, capping the amount they could lend against speculative assets.
The diplomat learned to bridle her impatience during long negotiations, knowing that any show of irritation would only strengthen the other side.
Constitutional term limits were designed to bridle presidential ambition, preventing any one leader from entrenching himself in office.

bridle-v2.text: The veteran surgeon bridled at the suggestion that a young resident should review her technique, and she left the meeting in a huff.
Proud of their town's history, the council members bridled when the visiting consultant described it as a place with no identity.
Accustomed to deference, the professor bridled at his student's blunt correction, his face flushing as he insisted the error was merely a slip.

bristle.text: The novelist bristled when an interviewer suggested that her books were merely autobiography, and she curtly ended the conversation.
Local farmers bristled at the new regulations, which they regarded as an insult from officials who had never worked the land.
Although he tried to appear calm, the mayor visibly bristled at the reporter's implication that he had accepted bribes from developers.

broadside.text: In a scathing broadside published in the morning paper, the retired general accused the ministry of squandering soldiers' lives through incompetence.
The biologist's broadside against the journal's editors, delivered in a public letter, charged them with suppressing research that contradicted their own theories.
Although the review began politely, it soon became a broadside, and by the final paragraph the critic was questioning not only the book but also the author's integrity.

bromide.text: The commencement speaker offered little beyond bromides such as 'follow your dreams' and 'never give up,' which the graduates had heard countless times.
Rather than address the committee's specific concerns, the executive retreated into a familiar bromide about teamwork being the key to success.
The novelist's characters rarely speak in bromides; even in casual conversation, they say things that are surprising and precise.

brook.text: The editor would brook no errors in the magazine's fact-checking, and a single misspelled name was enough to cost a researcher her job.
The general, who brooked no dissent, dismissed any officer who questioned his strategy, even those whose objections later proved correct.
Accustomed to unquestioned authority, the founder refused to brook interference from the new board of directors, and he resigned rather than share control.

browbeat.text: The prosecutor tried to browbeat the elderly witness, shouting questions and sneering at her answers, until the judge ordered him to show some respect.
Rather than persuading the committee with evidence, the chairman browbeat its members into approving the plan by threatening to cut their budgets.
Employees who had been browbeaten for years by a tyrannical manager were at first suspicious of their new supervisor's genuine requests for their opinions.

brusquely.text: The clerk brusquely waved the applicants away, telling them to come back tomorrow without bothering to explain which documents they lacked.
Rather than softening the bad news, the consultant delivered it brusquely, announcing the layoffs in two sentences and leaving the room.
Although she answered reporters brusquely, cutting off any question she considered irrelevant, her colleagues knew her as patient and warm.

buck.text: The young composer bucked the conventions of her conservatory, writing atonal pieces at a time when her teachers prized traditional harmony.
Few legislators were willing to buck the party leadership openly, knowing that dissenters would lose their committee assignments.
Villagers who bucked the chief's authority were rare, since defiance usually meant exclusion from the communal harvest.

bucolic.text: Tired of the noise and traffic of the city, the couple moved to a bucolic village surrounded by orchards, meadows and grazing sheep.
The painter's bucolic landscapes, full of shepherds and gentle streams, offered viewers a nostalgic escape from the industrial cities of his time.
Although the region looks bucolic in tourist brochures, its farms have in fact been largely replaced by factories and warehouses.

bumbling.text: The bumbling apprentice dropped three porcelain cups in a single morning, and the potter finally assigned him to sweeping the floor.
In the comedy, a bumbling inspector knocks over lamps and trips on rugs, yet somehow solves the case by accident.
Though bumbling in the kitchen, where he burned and spilled nearly everything, the chemist was remarkably precise in his laboratory.

burgeon.text: As interest in local history burgeoned, the tiny archive expanded into a museum that now draws thousands of visitors each year.
The software industry burgeoned in the valley, transforming a quiet farming region into one of the country's busiest economic centers.
Scholars expected the movement to fade quickly; instead, it burgeoned, attracting new members in dozens of countries within a few years.

buttress.text: The lawyer buttressed her argument with dozens of precedents, leaving opposing counsel little room to challenge it.
New archaeological finds have buttressed the theory that the city was abandoned because of drought rather than invasion.
To buttress its shaky finances, the orchestra launched an endowment campaign and secured long-term pledges from several foundations.

byzantine.text: The tax code has grown so byzantine, with exemptions layered upon exemptions, that even professional accountants struggle to interpret it.
The novel's plot is byzantine: dozens of characters, several interlocking conspiracies, and a narrator who reveals crucial information only in footnotes.
Newcomers to the ministry quickly learned that its byzantine chain of approvals meant that even ordering paper required signatures from four departments.

cadaverous.text: After months of illness, the poet was cadaverous, his cheekbones jutting sharply beneath skin stretched thin over his skull.
The actor starved himself for the role of the prisoner, and by the final scenes his cadaverous frame and hollow eyes were almost painful to watch.
The painter's portraits of ascetic monks emphasize their cadaverous features: sunken cheeks, bony hands, and eyes set deep in shadowed sockets.

callow.text: The callow lieutenant, fresh from the academy and eager to prove himself, ignored the veteran sergeant's advice and led his men into an ambush.
Reading her first published poems years later, the poet winced at their callow sentimentality, so different from the hard-won restraint of her mature work.
Investors were reluctant to entrust millions to such a callow founder, who had never managed a company or even held a full-time job.

calumny.text: The candidate's rivals spread calumny about his finances, falsely claiming that he had embezzled funds from the charity he founded.
The scientist sued the tabloid for calumny after it printed invented accusations that she had fabricated her research data.
Although the rumors were eventually proven false, the calumny had already ruined the merchant's reputation and driven away his customers.

canard.text: Opponents spread the canard that the reformer had embezzled campaign funds, a fabrication that an independent audit later thoroughly disproved.
The rival firm planted a canard in the trade press, falsely claiming that the new product had failed safety tests, in hopes of delaying its release.
Historians have long since debunked the canard, invented by wartime propagandists, that enemy soldiers had poisoned the wells of occupied villages.

candid.text: In a candid memoir, the former minister admits to mistakes that she had denied throughout her career.
The mentor's candid feedback stung at first, but the young writer came to value it far above the polite flattery she received elsewhere.
Asked whether the project would finish on time, the engineer was candid: without more staff, he said, it would be at least six months late.

candidness.text: The committee appreciated the witness's candidness, for unlike previous witnesses, he admitted his own role in the failures without being pressed.
Her candidness in discussing her struggles with anxiety encouraged other students to speak openly about their own mental health.
Some officials valued the envoy's candidness, but others found his blunt assessments of their governments tactless and impolitic.

capitulate.text: After a siege of several months, the starving garrison capitulated, and the victors allowed its soldiers safe passage home in return for the keys to the fortress.
The union had vowed never to accept the pay cuts, but facing mounting debts and dwindling strike funds, its leaders finally capitulated.
Rather than capitulate to the censors' demands, the editor shut down the newspaper, declaring that she would not print a sanitized version of the truth.

capricious.text: The capricious weather of the mountains, which could shift from sunshine to blizzard within an hour, made planning the climb nearly impossible.
Employees never knew what to expect from their capricious manager, who might praise a report one day and reject the same work the next.
The king's decisions were capricious rather than reasoned; he once exiled a minister simply because he disliked the color of his coat.

cardinal.text: The cardinal rule of the laboratory is never to eat or drink near the samples; every other guideline is secondary.
Clarity is the cardinal virtue of scientific writing, since an elegant idea is useless if readers cannot understand it.
Historians disagree about many causes of the war, but most regard the collapse of the grain trade as the cardinal factor, without which the others would not have mattered.

carping.text: The director ignored the carping critics who objected to every small liberty his adaptation took, and audiences embraced the film anyway.
Her carping comments about the seating chart, the menu, and the music soured an evening that everyone else found delightful.
Although the review contained some valid points, its carping tone (it fussed over minor typographical errors for three paragraphs) made the reviewer seem petty.

castigate.text: The editor castigated the reporter for publishing an unverified story, calling it the most careless error the paper had made in decades.
In a scathing review, the critic castigated the orchestra for its sloppy tempo and out-of-tune brass.
Rather than castigating the student in front of the class, the teacher chose to discuss his mistakes privately after the lesson.

cataclysm.text: For the island's farmers, the volcanic eruption was a cataclysm: ash buried their fields, and the harvest that year was entirely lost.
Many economists feared that the collapse of the largest bank would trigger a cataclysm, wiping out savings and throwing millions out of work.
The paleontologist argued that the extinction was not a single sudden cataclysm but a slow decline spread over hundreds of thousands of years.

catalyst.text: The factory's closure proved the catalyst for the town's reinvention, prompting residents to convert the empty buildings into studios and shops.
A chance conversation with a stranger on a train served as the catalyst for the novel, which the author finished within a year.
Enzymes act as catalysts in the body, allowing chemical reactions that would otherwise take years to occur in fractions of a second.

catholic.text: Her tastes in literature were remarkably catholic, ranging from ancient epic poetry to contemporary graphic novels and obscure scientific treatises.
The museum's catholic acquisitions policy, which welcomed everything from folk quilts to abstract sculpture, set it apart from institutions devoted to a single period.
The scholar's catholic curiosity led her to write books on medieval music, deep-sea biology, and the history of mapmaking.

cavalier.text: The manager's cavalier attitude toward safety regulations, which he dismissed as bureaucratic nonsense, eventually led to a serious accident.
Critics faulted the archivist's cavalier treatment of the historical record when she discarded boxes of old letters without consulting anyone.
He spoke in a cavalier way about other people's money, promising investors huge returns while brushing aside their questions about risk.

cede.text: Under the terms of the peace treaty, the defeated kingdom was forced to cede its coastal provinces to its victorious neighbor.
The founder was reluctant to cede control of the company to professional managers, even after it had grown far beyond his ability to run it.
In return for federal funding, the state agreed to cede authority over the river's management to a regional commission.

celerity.text: The firefighters responded with such celerity that the blaze was contained before it could spread beyond the kitchen.
Critics praised the translator's accuracy but not her celerity; the long-awaited edition appeared a full decade after she began the project.
Messages that once took weeks to cross the ocean by ship traveled with astonishing celerity once the telegraph cable was laid.

censor.text: The wartime government censored soldiers' letters, blacking out any mention of troop locations before the mail reached families at home.
Rather than censor the controversial play, the theater added a discussion after each performance so that audiences could debate its themes.
Librarians resisted pressure to censor the collection, insisting that removing books because some patrons found them offensive would betray the library's mission.

censure.text: The senate voted to censure the member for misusing public funds, a formal rebuke that stopped short of expelling him.
The medical board censured the surgeon for operating without consent, though it allowed him to keep his license.
Several scientists censured the journal for publishing the flawed study, arguing in a public letter that its reviewers had failed their duty.

cerebral.text: The chess master's style was cerebral rather than aggressive, built on deep calculation instead of daring sacrifices.
Some listeners find the composer's music too cerebral, admiring its intricate structure while wishing that it stirred their feelings.
Unlike his impulsive partner, who acted on gut feeling, the detective took a cerebral approach, reasoning methodically from each clue to the next.

chagrin-n.text: To the chagrin of the proud host, the souffle collapsed just as he carried it triumphantly into the dining room.
The scientist discovered, much to her chagrin, that the result she had announced at the conference was caused by a contaminated sample.
The visiting official's chagrin was obvious when he mispronounced the name of the town he was addressing, and he apologized repeatedly to the crowd.

chagrin-v.text: The veteran chess master was chagrined to lose to a twelve-year-old in only fifteen moves, and he declined all interviews afterward.
The minister was deeply chagrined when reporters revealed that his celebrated speech had been lifted almost word for word from an old textbook.
It chagrined the proud engineer that his bridge, praised at its opening, had to be closed within a year because it swayed alarmingly in the wind.

champion.text: The legislator championed the rights of migrant workers for decades, sponsoring bill after bill to guarantee them fair wages and safe housing.
Long before the teaching method was fashionable, a few educators championed it, publishing studies and training colleagues in its use.
The critic championed the neglected novelist, writing essays that restored her to the canon after decades of obscurity.

charlatan.text: The traveling doctor was a charlatan who dazzled crowds with jokes and conjuring tricks before selling them bottles of colored water as a cure for every ailment.
Though he presented himself as a renowned psychic, investigators soon exposed him as a charlatan who relied on hidden accomplices to feed him information.
Serious economists dismissed the television guru as a charlatan, since his flamboyant predictions were designed to sell books rather than to withstand scrutiny.

chary.text: Having been cheated by a fraudulent partner once before, the investor was chary of any deal that promised quick returns.
The famously reclusive novelist is chary of interviews, granting perhaps one a decade and even then refusing to discuss her private life.
