Doctors are often chary of prescribing new drugs until long-term studies have confirmed their safety.

chastise.text: The coach chastised his players for their lack of effort, lecturing them sternly in the locker room for nearly an hour.
After the mistake cost the firm a major client, the partner chastised the associate so severely that he considered resigning.
Rather than chastising her son for breaking the vase, the mother calmly asked him to help sweep up the pieces.

chauvinism.text: The historian argued that the war was fueled by chauvinism, as each nation's press insisted on its own people's superiority and mocked the other side.
The critic's dismissal of all foreign films as inferior revealed a cultural chauvinism that his broader writings otherwise concealed.
Physicists and biologists rarely collaborated at the institute, largely because a disciplinary chauvinism led each group to dismiss the other's methods as crude.

chauvinist.text: A committed chauvinist, the historian dismissed every foreign contribution to science and insisted that his own nation had invented nearly everything of value.
The travel writer was accused of being a chauvinist after describing every culture she visited as a pale imitation of her own.
Cultural chauvinists in the academy long ignored non-Western philosophy, assuming that serious thought had flourished only within their own tradition.

check-n.text: Without natural predators to serve as a check on their numbers, the rabbits introduced to the island multiplied until they had devoured most of its vegetation.
A free press acts as a check on official corruption, since corrupt officials know that their misconduct may be exposed on the front page.
Held in check for years by strict import quotas, domestic demand for foreign cars surged as soon as the restrictions were lifted.

check-v.text: Predators such as wolves check the growth of deer populations, which would otherwise overgraze the forest and strip it of saplings.
The new medication can check the spread of the infection, although it cannot reverse the damage already done.
Constitutional courts were designed to check the ambitions of the executive, preventing any single official from accumulating unlimited power.

checkered.text: Despite a checkered past that included two bankruptcies and a fraud investigation, the entrepreneur persuaded investors to fund his newest venture.
The museum was reluctant to acquire the painting because of its checkered history, which involved theft, forged provenance papers, and several disputed sales.
The nominee's checkered record, marred by leaked scandals and an earlier dismissal for misconduct, made his appointment difficult to defend.

chimera.text: For centuries, inventors pursued the chimera of a perpetual motion machine, though physics had long shown such a device to be impossible.
The dream of a single universal language that would end all misunderstanding proved a chimera; each attempt splintered into rival dialects within a generation.
Some philosophers regard perfect objectivity as a chimera, arguing that every observer inevitably brings assumptions that shape what she sees.

chivalrous.text: In an age of casual manners, the elderly gentleman remained chivalrous, rising whenever a woman entered the room and insisting on carrying her parcels.
The medieval romance idealizes its chivalrous hero, who risks his life to rescue a lady and treats even his defeated enemies with courtesy.
Some readers find the novel's chivalrous gestures charming, while others see in the hero's protectiveness a condescending assumption that women are helpless.

choleric.text: The choleric headmaster was known to fly into a rage over a single untucked shirt, and students tiptoed past his office.
Although the composer's music is serene, his contemporaries described him as choleric, prone to smashing chairs when rehearsals went badly.
Diplomats found the envoy's choleric temperament a liability, since his sudden outbursts repeatedly derailed delicate negotiations.

chortle.text: The audience chortled with delight as the clown stumbled through his routine, their laughter growing louder with each pratfall.
Reading his friend's witty letter, the old professor chortled to himself, pausing every few lines to wipe his eyes.
Instead of scowling at the child's prank, the grandfather chortled and asked to hear the joke again, his shoulders still shaking long after the others had stopped.

churlish.text: It seemed churlish to refuse the villagers' hospitality, so the weary travelers accepted the meal despite having already eaten.
The guest's churlish behavior at the banquet, ignoring his hosts and grumbling loudly about the food, embarrassed everyone at the table.
Although the champion had been gracious in victory, her opponent was churlish in defeat, refusing to shake hands and storming off the court.

circumscribe.text: The new regulations circumscribe the agency's authority, limiting its investigations to cases that involve interstate commerce.
Her freedom was sharply circumscribed during the illness; she could not leave her room and could receive visitors only for an hour each day.
Because the scholar drew only on the archives of one provincial town, critics argued that his sources circumscribed his conclusions far more than his sweeping title implied.

circumvent.text: The company circumvented the export ban by routing its shipments through a third country, a practice regulators later deemed illegal.
Rather than confronting the bureaucracy directly, the activists found a clever way to circumvent it, delivering aid through local churches.
Some students try to circumvent the school's plagiarism software by paraphrasing entire articles, but the teachers usually catch them anyway.

clemency.text: The governor granted clemency to the elderly prisoner, commuting his sentence on the grounds that he had shown genuine remorse and posed no danger.
Despite pleas for clemency from the defendant's family, the judge imposed the maximum sentence, citing the severity of the crime.
The emperor was famed for his clemency, often pardoning rebels who surrendered rather than executing them as his predecessors had done.

coalesce.text: Over millions of years, dust and gas in the early solar system coalesced into planets, drawn together by their mutual gravity.
Scattered local protests gradually coalesced into a national movement with a single leadership and a shared list of demands.
Only in the final chapter do the novel's separate storylines coalesce, revealing that the three narrators have been describing the same night.

cogent.text: The student's essay was so cogent that even the skeptical examiner, who disagreed with its thesis, conceded that the argument was difficult to refute.
Although the proposal was cogent, its lucid reasoning failed to persuade a committee that had already made up its mind.
The defense offered no cogent explanation for the missing funds, only a series of vague and contradictory excuses.

cohesive.text: The new manager turned a group of feuding specialists into a cohesive team that shared information freely and worked toward common goals.
Critics praised the album as unusually cohesive, noting that its songs flowed into one another and developed a single theme.
Although the anthology gathers stories by twenty different writers, it is surprisingly cohesive, since every piece explores the same neighborhood across a single century.

collusion.text: Regulators fined the three airlines for collusion after discovering that their executives had secretly agreed to raise fares on the same day.
The referee was banned for life when investigators uncovered his collusion with gamblers, who had paid him to influence the outcome of matches.
The auction appeared competitive, but the bidders were acting in collusion, having agreed beforehand which of them would win each lot.

colossal.text: The colossal statue towered over the harbor, dwarfing the ships that passed beneath it and awing every visitor who arrived by sea.
The merger proved a colossal mistake, wiping out billions in shareholder value and leading to the dismissal of the entire executive team.
Building the cathedral required a colossal effort, spanning several generations of masons and consuming the resources of an entire region.

commendable.text: The student's decision to report a grading error in her own favor was commendable, since it cost her several points on the exam.
While the charity's goals are commendable, its management has been so inefficient that little of the money reaches those in need.
The rescue crew showed commendable composure, working calmly through the night despite freezing temperatures and the constant risk of another collapse.

commensurate.text: The engineers argued that their salaries should be commensurate with their responsibilities, which had doubled after the merger.
The punishment seemed far from commensurate with the offense: the student was expelled for a minor clerical error.
Investors expect returns commensurate with the risks they take, so a speculative venture must promise far greater gains than a government bond.

complacent.text: Having led the market for a decade, the company grew complacent, ignoring the smaller rivals whose innovations would eventually overtake it.
Public health officials warned the public not to grow complacent as the outbreak waned, since a single lapse in vigilance could allow it to return.
Although her early novels were daring, critics felt that success had made the author complacent, since each new book simply repeated the formula of the last.

complaisant.text: The complaisant innkeeper cheerfully rearranged rooms, cooked late meals, and fetched a doctor for his guests, never once grumbling about the extra work.
Unlike her demanding predecessor, the new assistant was complaisant, happily agreeing to run errands that fell well outside her official duties.
The minister's complaisant attitude toward foreign envoys, whose every request he was eager to grant, alarmed advisers who feared he was being exploited.

complementary.text: The two researchers had complementary skills: she excelled at designing experiments, while he was gifted at interpreting the resulting data.
Painters often place complementary colors side by side, since a patch of red makes a nearby green appear more vivid, and vice versa.
The museum's new wing is complementary to the original building, its sleek glass walls highlighting the ornate stonework of the older facade.

complicit.text: Although the accountant had not personally stolen any money, the court found her complicit in the fraud, since she had knowingly falsified the ledgers to conceal it.
Historians debate whether the townspeople were complicit in the deportations or simply too frightened to protest.
By remaining silent about the safety violations he had witnessed, the inspector became complicit in the disaster that followed.

compound.text: The company's initial error was compounded by its attempt to conceal it, which turned a minor recall into a national scandal.
Drought compounded the region's difficulties, adding widespread crop failures to an economic crisis that was already severe.
Rather than easing tensions, the ambassador's clumsy apology compounded the offense, since it seemed to blame the injured party.

concede-v1.text: After a long night of counting ballots showed him trailing by thousands of votes, the candidate finally conceded and congratulated his opponent.
With only his king left on the board, the grandmaster conceded the game rather than prolong the inevitable.
The defending champion refused to concede even when she trailed by two sets, and her persistence carried her to an improbable comeback.

concede-v2.text: Confronted with the emails, the executive conceded that he had misled investors about the company's debts.
The senator eventually conceded to having accepted improper gifts, though he denied that they had influenced his votes.
Although he long insisted on his innocence, the clerk finally conceded that he had altered the records to hide the missing funds.

concede-v3.text: Under the terms of the treaty, the defeated kingdom was forced to concede its northern provinces to the victors.
The family conceded control of the estate to the bank after failing to repay the mortgage for several years.
Unwilling to concede the fortress to the besieging army, the garrison held out for months on dwindling supplies.

conciliate.text: Hoping to conciliate the angry farmers, the governor promised emergency relief and personally visited the flooded districts.
The new manager tried to conciliate the rival factions within the department by giving each a voice in planning the budget.
Rather than conciliate his critics, the author published a furious rebuttal that only deepened the feud.

concomitant.text: The rapid growth of the city brought concomitant problems: traffic congestion, rising rents, and overcrowded schools all arrived along with the new residents.
Doctors warned that the medication's benefits came with concomitant risks, including dizziness and insomnia, that patients should weigh carefully.
The spread of literacy in the period, and the concomitant rise of cheap printed pamphlets, transformed how ordinary people encountered political ideas.

conducive.text: The open-plan office, meant to encourage collaboration, proved hardly conducive to concentration, since constant chatter made focused work impossible.
A warm, humid climate is conducive to the growth of mold, so archivists keep rare manuscripts in cool, dry rooms.
The mediator arranged the chairs in a circle, believing that a setting without a head of the table would be more conducive to open discussion.

conflagration.text: A carelessly discarded match sparked a conflagration that swept through the dry forest, consuming thousands of acres before the rains arrived.
The old wooden theater was destroyed in a conflagration so intense that firefighters could only keep it from spreading to neighboring buildings.
City planners rebuilt the district in brick and stone, determined that no future conflagration would ever again reduce whole streets to ashes.

conflate.text: Critics complained that the documentary conflated two distinct historical figures who shared a name, attributing one man's achievements to the other.
Many people conflate weather and climate, yet a single cold winter reveals little about long-term trends in global temperature.
The architect conflates classical columns, industrial steel, and traditional Japanese joinery, producing buildings that belong to no single tradition.

confound-v1.text: The results confounded the researchers, who had predicted the opposite outcome and could find no flaw in their experiment.
The riddle confounded every guest at the dinner party; no one could explain how the answer fit the clues.
Economists were confounded by the market's behavior, which rose sharply even as every indicator pointed toward a recession.

confound-v2.text: Beginning students often confound correlation with causation, assuming that because two things occur together, one must cause the other.
The two sisters looked so alike that even their teachers confounded them, calling each by the other's name.
Critics who confound the narrator with the author miss the irony of the novel, whose speaker holds views the writer clearly rejects.

conniving.text: The treasurer was accused of conniving with contractors to inflate invoices, splitting the excess payments among the conspirators.
Historians have long suspected that the queen's own ministers were conniving against her, secretly corresponding with a rival claimant to the throne.
Two clerks connived to alter the ledger, hoping that the auditors would never notice the small sums they had siphoned away each month.

consecrate.text: Before the ruined chapel could host services again, the bishop had to consecrate its new altar, formally setting the space apart from ordinary use.
The veterans' committee chose to consecrate the former battlefield as a memorial ground, dedicating it permanently to the memory of those who had fallen there.
She did not merely study music; she consecrated her entire life to it, forgoing marriage, travel and comfort so that nothing could distract from that single devotion.

conspicuous.text: In a room full of dark suits, the guest in a bright yellow coat was conspicuous, and every photographer turned toward him.
The editor's name was conspicuous by its absence from the acknowledgments, a pointed omission that many readers noticed.
The new tower, far taller than anything around it, is conspicuous from every part of the city.

constituent-n1.text: The representative held town meetings every month, listening to her constituents' concerns about schools, roads and taxes.
After thousands of letters from angry constituents, the senator reversed his position and voted against the bill.
A legislator who ignores the needs of his constituents may find that the voters of his district replace him at the next election.

constituent-n2.text: Trust, the sociologist argued, is an essential constituent of any functioning community, as vital as shared laws or institutions.
Irony is such an essential constituent of the novelist's style that her books lose much of their charm in translations that flatten it.
Rhythm, melody and harmony are the basic constituents of most Western music, though some modern composers have discarded one or more of them.

constraint.text: The architect's most severe constraint was the narrow lot, which limited the building to a width of barely six meters and forced every room into a vertical arrangement.
Far from stifling the poet, the strict meter of the sonnet proved a productive constraint, compelling her to find precise words she might otherwise never have sought.
Because the grant covered only a single year of fieldwork, the researchers had to design their study around that constraint, abandoning several long-term measurements they had hoped to include.

construe.text: The diplomat's silence was construed as agreement, though he later insisted that he had simply been waiting for instructions.
Judges must construe ambiguous statutes in light of the legislature's intent, reading the text alongside the debates that produced it.
She construed his brief reply as a rejection, but he had merely been too busy to write more.

consummate-adj.text: A consummate diplomat, the envoy could soothe furious delegates, extract concessions from rivals and leave both sides believing they had won.
Although the novel's plot is thin, its prose reveals a consummate stylist whose every sentence seems carefully weighed and polished.
The restorer's consummate skill was evident only on close inspection: the repaired sections of the fresco were indistinguishable from the original brushwork.

consummate-v.text: The merger was not consummated until regulators approved the final terms, at which point the two firms at last became a single, fully integrated company.
For decades the composer sketched fragments of the symphony, but only in his final year did he consummate the work, supplying the missing finale that made it whole.
The treaty signed in the spring merely outlined a truce; the alliance was consummated months later, when both parliaments ratified every clause and completed the arrangement.

contemptuous.text: The established painters were openly contemptuous of the young impressionists, dismissing their loose brushwork as the careless daubing of amateurs.
Rather than engaging with her critics' arguments, the philosopher adopted a contemptuous tone, implying that their objections were beneath serious consideration.
Although he claimed to respect the local craftsmen, the visiting designer's contemptuous glance at their furniture betrayed how little he thought of their work.

contentious.text: She became increasingly contentious, misconstruing even an innocuous statement as a hostile one.
As soon as the discussion turns to politics, Uncle Hank becomes highly contentious, vehemently disagreeing with those who endorse the same positions.
The contentious board member objected to nearly every proposal, often prolonging meetings for hours over matters that others considered trivial.
Known as the most contentious scholar in the department, he seemed to relish disputes and would challenge a colleague's claim merely to provoke a debate.
Although the twins were close as adults, they had been contentious children, quarreling constantly over toys, chores, and even who got the last word.

contingent-adj.text: The loan is contingent on the company's passing an independent audit; if the auditors find irregularities, the bank will withdraw its offer.
His acceptance to the program was contingent upon his completing a final course in statistics during the summer.
Historians stress that the war's outcome was contingent rather than inevitable, depending on a few chance decisions made in its opening weeks.

contingent-n.text: A small contingent of scientists from the university attended the conference, representing their department in the international debate.
The largest contingent at the parade came from the veterans' association, whose members marched in uniform behind a brass band.
Each member nation sent a contingent of peacekeepers, so that the mission included soldiers from a dozen countries.

contrite.text: Far from defiant, the scientist was contrite after the flawed data came to light, publicly apologizing to her colleagues and retracting the paper herself.
The editor expected a defensive reply, but the columnist's letter was surprisingly contrite, acknowledging each error and expressing genuine regret for the harm done.
Only when he saw how deeply his careless remark had wounded his brother did Paul become contrite, spending the evening trying to make amends.

contrition.text: The defendant's apparent contrition, including his tearful apology to the victims, persuaded the judge to reduce his sentence.
Far from showing contrition, the executive blamed his subordinates and insisted that the company had done nothing wrong.
In a letter full of contrition, the student admitted to cheating and asked the professor for a chance to redeem himself.

contrive.text: The prisoners contrived to escape by digging a tunnel beneath the kitchen, concealing the dirt in their mattresses for months.
Although the invitation list was closed, the reporter contrived to get into the gala by posing as a caterer.
The clever steward contrived a meeting between the feuding cousins, arranging for both to arrive at the same inn on the same night.

conundrum.text: The museum faced a genuine conundrum: displaying the fragile manuscript would expose it to damaging light, yet keeping it hidden would defeat the purpose of acquiring it.
For generations of physicists, reconciling gravity with quantum theory has remained a conundrum that resists even the most ingenious attempts at solution.
Urban planners confront a familiar conundrum when a neighborhood improves, since the very amenities that attract new residents also drive up rents and push longtime tenants out.

convivial.text: Unlike the stiff formal banquets of previous years, this year's reunion was convivial, full of laughter, toasts and old friends lingering late at crowded tables.
The historian argues that coffeehouses thrived not merely because of the coffee but because of their convivial atmosphere, where strangers chatted freely and debates ran late into the night.
Although the conference sessions were dry and technical, the evenings were convivial, with researchers from rival labs sharing meals, stories and music.

convoluted.text: The tax code has grown so convoluted that even specialists must consult several cross-referenced provisions to answer what seems like a simple question.
Critics praised the film's performances but found its plot convoluted, with so many flashbacks and double crosses that audiences struggled to follow it.
Instead of stating her objection plainly, the committee chair offered a convoluted explanation that looped through three hypotheticals before reaching any point at all.

copious.text: The researcher took copious notes during each interview, filling several notebooks with details that she later organized into her book.
Despite copious rainfall in the spring, the reservoir remained low because of the previous year's drought.
The feast featured copious amounts of food, far more than the guests could possibly eat.

cornucopia.text: For the botanist, the unexplored valley was a cornucopia: nearly every trail revealed orchids, ferns and mosses she had seen only in illustrated guides.
The newly opened archive proved a cornucopia for historians, yielding letters, diaries and ledgers in such abundance that cataloging them will take years.
Rather than the meager offerings they had expected, the travelers found a cornucopia at the village market, its stalls overflowing with fruit, spices and fresh bread.

corollary.text: Higher tuition has had an unfortunate corollary: students graduate with heavier debts and are therefore less willing to take low-paying public service jobs.
Cheaper air travel produced a natural corollary in the coastal towns, where hotels multiplied to accommodate the new crowds of visitors.
If the theory is correct, then a corollary follows: the same plants should flower earlier wherever winters are warmer.

corroborate.text: The detective refused to rely on the witness's account alone and waited until fingerprints and phone records could corroborate her story.
Although the hypothesis was intriguing, reviewers insisted that independent laboratories must corroborate the results before the journal would publish them.
Newly deciphered tax records corroborate the chronicler's claim that the city was prosperous, supporting what many scholars had dismissed as mere civic boasting.

cosmopolitan.text: The port city had long been cosmopolitan, its streets alive with merchants, sailors and scholars speaking dozens of languages and trading ideas along with goods.
Unlike her provincial contemporaries, who wrote only of their native villages, the novelist had a cosmopolitan outlook shaped by years spent in capitals across three continents.
The restaurant's menu is thoroughly cosmopolitan, drawing on Ethiopian, Korean and Peruvian traditions rather than confining itself to any single national cuisine.

cosseted.text: The heir had been cosseted since infancy, attended by servants who anticipated his every wish, so he was ill prepared for life on his own.
Critics argue that protective tariffs cosset domestic manufacturers, sparing them the competition that would otherwise force them to innovate.
Rather than cosseting her students with easy praise, the piano teacher insisted on relentless drills and blunt criticism.

coterminous.text: The parish's boundaries were coterminous with those of the old manor, so the same families had worshipped and worked within the same lines for centuries.
The chairman's influence proved coterminous with his term of office; once he stepped down, his proposals were quickly abandoned.
In this region, the watershed and the county are coterminous: every stream within the county's borders drains into the same lake, and no stream beyond them does.

countermand.text: The general countermanded the order to retreat, instructing his troops to hold their positions until reinforcements could arrive.
Shortly after the manager announced the office closure, the chief executive countermanded the decision, and the staff were told to report to work as usual.
The captain countermanded the first officer's order to change course, insisting that the original heading was safer despite the approaching storm.

cow.text: The dictator's secret police cowed the population so effectively that even private conversations among friends avoided any mention of politics.
Refusing to be cowed by the powerful landowner's threats, the young lawyer filed suit on behalf of the evicted tenants.
The committee members, cowed by the chairman's reputation for vindictiveness, approved his proposal without raising a single question.

craven.text: The king's craven retreat, abandoning his troops to flee the battle, cost him the respect of his entire army.
Fearing the minister's anger, the manager made the craven decision to blame his assistant for a mistake he himself had made rather than face the consequences.
Unlike her craven colleagues, who stayed silent to protect their positions, the young auditor reported the fraud despite the risk.

credence.text: Because the letter surfaced decades after the events it described and bore no signature, historians gave little credence to its account of the treaty negotiations.
The discovery of similar fossils on two distant continents lent credence to the long ridiculed theory that the landmasses had once been joined.
Investors placed no credence in the startup's projections, which promised profits far beyond anything its modest sales could plausibly support.

creditable.text: The debut novel is a creditable effort, carefully plotted and cleanly written, though nothing in it suggests the arrival of a major new voice.
Given the limited budget and an inexperienced cast, the community theater staged a creditable production: hardly dazzling, but solid and worthy of respect.
Although the team finished far from first, its creditable showing in the tournament earned polite praise from coaches who had expected it to collapse.

credulity.text: The swindler relied on the credulity of his investors, who accepted every glowing report without once asking to see the company's accounts.
Medieval bestiaries, with their unicorns and fire-dwelling salamanders, reveal less about zoology than about the credulity of readers who accepted whatever travelers reported.
A good scientist must balance openness with skepticism, since too much credulity toward striking results can lead an entire field astray.

crestfallen.text: The young scientist was crestfallen when the journal rejected her paper, having spent three years on the research it described.
The crowd, so jubilant at halftime, filed out of the stadium crestfallen after the home team surrendered its lead in the final minutes.
Expecting praise for his first novel, the author was crestfallen to find that his mentor had written only a single, lukewarm line in the margin.

cryptic.text: The poet's cryptic final lines have puzzled readers for generations, since they seem to hint at a secret without ever naming it.
When asked about his plans, the director gave only a cryptic reply, saying that 'the answer lies in the question.'
The spy left a cryptic message on the cafe table, a string of numbers and symbols that only her handler could decode.

crystallize.text: Only after reading the survey data did the team's vague concerns about the product crystallize into a clear list of design flaws.
The philosopher's scattered early notes gradually crystallized into a coherent theory of justice, which she published a decade later.
Years of diffuse discontent crystallized into a movement when the government raised bread prices, giving protesters a single, concrete grievance.

culminate.text: The months of negotiations culminated in a historic treaty, signed with great ceremony in the capital.
Her long career culminated in a lifetime achievement award, the highest honor her profession offers and a fitting end to decades of work.
The festival culminates in a grand fireworks display over the harbor on its final night.

culpability.text: The investigation established the airline's culpability for the crash, finding that it had ignored repeated warnings about the faulty engine.
Although the driver denied culpability, the security footage clearly showed him running the red light.
The committee sought to determine the degree of each official's culpability, distinguishing those who approved the scheme from those merely unaware of it.

cumbersome.text: Early portable computers were so cumbersome that business travelers dreaded hauling them through airports, often wishing they had simply brought paper files.
The expedition left the cumbersome brass telescope behind, since its weight and awkward length made it nearly impossible to carry up the narrow mountain trail.
The old diving suit, with its copper helmet and lead-weighted boots, was so cumbersome on land that divers had to be helped to the ladder before each descent.

cupidity.text: The merchant's cupidity was legendary; he charged interest even on loans to his own brother and hoarded coins while his employees went unpaid.
The novel traces how cupidity corrupts a once honorable family, as each generation sacrifices loyalty and love for a larger share of the inheritance.
Regulators blamed the financial crisis less on ignorance than on cupidity, noting that bankers had knowingly sold worthless securities to enrich themselves.

curmudgeon.text: The neighborhood curmudgeon complained about everything, from children playing in the street to the color of the new mailboxes.
Though the old critic cultivated a reputation as a curmudgeon, grumbling at every premiere, his private letters reveal a surprisingly tender heart.
Even the office curmudgeon, who rarely had a kind word for anyone, grudgingly admitted that the new intern's report was excellent.

dearth.text: The region's dearth of rainfall has forced farmers to abandon thirsty crops like rice in favor of hardier grains that tolerate drought.
Despite the abundance of commentary on the poet's life, there is a surprising dearth of careful analysis of the poems themselves.
Historians of the period face a dearth of reliable sources, since most records were destroyed in a fire and only fragments survive.

debase.text: Critics complained that the studio had debased a subtle literary classic, reducing its moral complexity to a string of chase scenes and explosions.
When the emperor mixed ever more copper into the silver coinage, he debased the currency, and merchants soon demanded more coins for the same goods.
The senator warned that personal insults would only debase public discourse, turning serious disagreements over policy into a contest of cheap ridicule.

debonair.text: The debonair diplomat, impeccably tailored and effortlessly witty, charmed even the hostile delegates at the tense summit.
Though he had grown up in a cramped farmhouse, the actor projected a debonair elegance on screen that made audiences assume he was born to wealth.
Guests at the gala were captivated by their debonair host, who greeted each of them by name and moved through the crowded ballroom with easy grace.

debunk.text: In a witty and devastating essay, the physicist set out to debunk the claims of perpetual motion inventors, and by the final page not one of their supposed machines still seemed credible.
Although the myth that we use only a tenth of our brains persists, neuroscientists have repeatedly debunked it by showing activity across virtually every region.
The historian delighted in debunking cherished legends about the town's founding, mocking the tale of a heroic ancestor that turned out to have no documentary basis.

decimation.text: The decimation of the bison herds in the nineteenth century left the plains nations without the animal on which their food and shelter had depended.
Ecologists fear that the fungal disease could cause the decimation of amphibian populations, since in several regions it has already left ponds that once teemed with frogs almost silent.
Although the town's buildings survived the plague largely intact, the decimation of its inhabitants left entire streets empty and fields untended for a generation.

decorous.text: The ceremony was a decorous affair, with guests speaking in hushed tones and bowing politely to the elders.
Although the debate was heated, the candidates remained decorous, avoiding personal insults and addressing each other with courtesy.
The children, usually rowdy, were unexpectedly decorous during the visit to their grandmother, sitting still and thanking her for every treat.

decorum.text: The chairman reminded the committee members to observe decorum, since shouting and personal attacks had no place in the hearing.
Despite the tense atmosphere, the diplomat maintained perfect decorum, never raising his voice or showing irritation.
The student's loud outburst during the solemn memorial ceremony was a shocking breach of decorum that embarrassed his entire family.

decry.text: Environmental groups decried the decision to open the protected wetlands to drilling, calling it a betrayal of future generations.
Although many critics decried the novel as immoral when it was first published, it is now taught in schools as a classic.
The medical association decried the proliferation of unproven remedies, warning that patients were abandoning effective treatments in favor of them.

deferential.text: The junior associates were deferential toward the senior partner, never interrupting him and always waiting for his opinion before offering their own.
Visitors to the temple adopted a deferential posture, bowing their heads and speaking only in whispers.
Although the young scientist was deferential to her mentor in public, she privately disagreed with many of his conclusions.

defray.text: A grant from the historical society helped defray the cost of restoring the chapel's fragile frescoes, though the parish still had to raise the remainder.
To defray the expenses of her research trip, the graduate student taught evening classes and sold several of her photographs.
Conference organizers offered small stipends to defray travel costs for scholars from underfunded universities, though the sums rarely covered the full fare.

degrade.text: The manager had a habit of degrading junior staff in meetings, belittling their suggestions so harshly that most stopped offering ideas at all.
Rather than debate her arguments, the opposing columnist sought to degrade her, describing her work as the scribbling of an unqualified amateur.
Advocates argued that the textbook's crude caricatures degraded the very communities they claimed to depict, presenting them as ignorant and unworthy of respect.

deign.text: The celebrated conductor did not deign to acknowledge the student musicians who had waited hours to meet him, sweeping past them to his car.
The aristocrat rarely deigned to speak with shopkeepers, instead sending servants to conduct any business she considered beneath her.
When the famous author finally deigned to answer the young critic's letter, his reply consisted of a single dismissive sentence.

delegate.text: Overwhelmed by paperwork, the new principal learned to delegate scheduling and budgeting to her assistants so she could focus on the quality of teaching.
A founder who refuses to delegate any responsibility soon becomes a bottleneck, since every decision, however trivial, must wait for her approval.
The director delegated the lighting design to a young technician, trusting him with a task she had always insisted on handling herself.

deleterious.text: Prolonged exposure to loud noise can have deleterious effects on hearing, causing damage that is often permanent.
The pesticide was banned after studies showed that it was deleterious to bees, whose populations had collapsed in treated areas.
Rather than helping the fish, the chemical proved deleterious, killing thousands of them within weeks of its release.

deliberate.text: Because the testimony of the two key witnesses was flatly contradictory, the jury deliberated for three days before finally reaching a unanimous verdict.
Rather than accept the first offer, Elena deliberated over the two positions for weeks, listing the advantages and drawbacks of each.
The board spent the afternoon deliberating whether to expand overseas, with members weighing the potential profits against the considerable risks.

delineate.text: In her opening chapter, the historian delineates the causes of the famine one by one, devoting several pages to drought, trade policy and war.
The contract carefully delineated each party's responsibilities, specifying who would pay for materials, labor and any delays.
Rather than offering vague promises, the candidate delineated her plan, walking voters through exactly how each program would be funded and which agency would run it.

demean.text: The coach refused to demean his players after a loss, insisting that public humiliation only erodes the confidence a team needs to improve.
Some critics felt that the actor demeaned himself by appearing in a string of crude commercials, squandering the dignity he had earned on the stage.
Although she disagreed sharply with the intern's analysis, the editor took care not to demean him, criticizing the argument while respecting the person.

demonstrative.text: Unlike her reserved husband, who rarely showed any emotion, she was demonstrative, embracing guests at the door and weeping openly at weddings.
Her cousins were far more demonstrative than the stoic family she had married into, greeting her with kisses, tears, and loud declarations of affection.
Though the coach was not demonstrative by nature, he leapt from the bench and hugged each player when the team clinched the championship.

demur.text: When asked if she wanted to visit the war-torn region without a translator by her side, the journalist demurred.
When the committee asked him to chair the new project, the professor demurred, explaining that his research already consumed all of his time.
Most members approved the merger enthusiastically, but a few demurred, voicing doubts about the partner company's finances.
She usually accepted invitations eagerly, yet she demurred at the offer to speak at the ceremony, preferring to remain in the audience.

demure.text: In the portrait, the young woman appears demure, eyes lowered and hands folded, though her letters reveal a far bolder personality.
Unlike her flamboyant sister, who dominated every gathering, Clara remained demure, speaking softly and rarely drawing attention to herself.
Critics expected the famously outspoken actress to dominate the interview, yet she remained demure throughout, answering briefly with lowered eyes and deflecting every compliment.

denigrate.text: Rather than engaging with his rival's arguments, the candidate tried to denigrate her character, spreading insinuations about her past.
The tabloid's attempt to denigrate the scientist backfired when her colleagues publicly defended both her integrity and her research.
Jealous of his success, the older composer denigrated the young man's work in every interview, dismissing it as noisy and shallow.

denote.text: On the map, a small blue triangle denotes a campsite, while a red circle marks a ranger station.
In musical notation, a dot above a note denotes that it should be played short and detached.
The term 'renaissance' originally denoted a rebirth of classical learning, though it is now used far more loosely.

denouement.text: In the novel's denouement, the long-lost heir is revealed, the feuding families are reconciled, and every mystery introduced in the first chapter is finally explained.
The protracted legal battle reached its denouement when the appeals court ruled in the tenants' favor, ending a dispute that had dragged on for fifteen years.
Critics admired the play's first two acts but found its denouement rushed, as if the playwright had grown tired of untangling the plot threads he had so carefully woven.

derelict-adj.text: The inspector was found derelict in his duties, having approved the bridge as safe without ever visiting the site.
Parents accused the school board of being derelict, since it had ignored complaints about bullying for years without taking any action.
A night watchman who sleeps through his shift is plainly derelict, however loyal he may otherwise be to his employer.

derelict-n.text: After the canneries closed, a row of derelict warehouses lined the harbor, their windows smashed and their doors left open to the wind and the gulls.
Urban explorers are drawn to the derelict asylum, whose empty wards and collapsing roof have stood untouched since the last patients left decades ago.
Rather than let it crumble further, the council voted to convert the derelict railway station, boarded up and unused for thirty years, into a public library.

deride.text: Early critics derided the novel as sentimental trash, though later generations recognized it as a subtle exploration of class.
Many engineers derided the proposal for a suspension bridge across the wide strait, calling it a fantasy, until the completed span silenced them.
Rather than engage respectfully with rival theories, the professor derided them in lectures, mocking their proponents as naive and uninformed.

derisive.text: When the candidate claimed to have single-handedly balanced the budget, the audience responded with derisive laughter that drowned out the rest of his speech.
The reviewer's derisive dismissal of the exhibition, which he called a collection of expensive doodles, provoked angry letters from the artists.
Although the scientist expected skepticism, she was unprepared for the derisive comments of colleagues who openly mocked her hypothesis at the conference.

derivative.text: Although the band's first album was praised for its originality, its second was derivative, borrowing heavily from the groups it had once mocked.
The critic dismissed the novel as derivative, noting that its plot, characters and even its setting closely echoed a famous nineteenth-century work.
Far from being derivative, the painter's style owed nothing to her teachers; she invented her techniques entirely on her own.

derive-v1.text: The name of the town derives from an old word for 'ford,' reflecting its origin as a crossing point on the river.
Much of the family's wealth derived from a single shipping company founded by a great-grandfather.
Many modern breeds of dog are derived from a small number of ancestral lines that humans domesticated thousands of years ago.

derive-v2.text: From the pattern of cracks in the plaster, the engineer derived the direction in which the foundation had shifted.
Working only from a few observations of the planet's orbit, the astronomer derived its mass with remarkable accuracy.
Students in the logic course must derive each conclusion step by step from the stated premises, justifying every move.

derogative.text: Historians note that the term was originally derogative, coined by critics to belittle the movement, before its members proudly adopted it.
Although the report aimed to be neutral, its derogative descriptions of rural schools as backward and worthless offended many teachers.
The editor removed several derogative adjectives from the review, reasoning that criticism should assess the work rather than simply disparage it.

desecrate.text: The felon had desecrated the holy site, and was on the church's Top 10 Anathema list.
Vandals desecrated the ancient burial ground, overturning headstones and scrawling graffiti across a site the community had revered for centuries.
Villagers regarded the proposed mine as an attempt to desecrate their sacred mountain, a place where ceremonies had been held for generations.
Soldiers who looted the cathedral were accused of desecrating it, since they stabled horses in the nave and melted down the holy vessels from the altar.

desiccated.text: The composer's late works struck critics as desiccated, technically flawless but devoid of the passion that had animated his youthful symphonies.
Students found the textbook's desiccated prose so lifeless that they turned instead to the lively lectures of a popular historian.
Once a spirited forum for debate, the society had become a desiccated institution by the century's end, its meetings reduced to reading the minutes aloud.

desideratum.text: For the new laboratory, a stable supply of electricity was the chief desideratum, since even a brief outage could ruin months of experiments.
Affordable housing near the city center remains a desideratum for young families, yet few developers have found a way to provide it profitably.
In choosing a site for the observatory, the astronomers listed dark skies as their foremost desideratum, followed closely by dry weather and high altitude.

despot.text: The despot silenced every critic, imprisoning journalists and confiscating the property of anyone suspected of disloyalty.
Though he came to power promising democratic reforms, the general soon revealed himself as a despot, dissolving the legislature and ruling through terror.
Historians debate whether the emperor was an enlightened reformer or merely a despot whose harsh decrees occasionally happened to benefit his subjects.

destitute-adj1.text: The economic collapse left thousands of families destitute, dependent on soup kitchens and charity for their daily meals.
Although the painter now commands high prices, he spent his early years destitute, sleeping in shelters and relying on friends for food.
The charity focuses on elderly widows left destitute by the death of a spouse, providing housing and a small stipend to those with no other means of support.

destitute-adj2.text: The committee's report was long and polished yet destitute of original ideas, merely restating recommendations that had been ignored for a decade.
Critics found the sequel destitute of the wit that had made the original so charming, its jokes stale and its dialogue flat.
After years of drought, the valley was destitute of vegetation, its once green hillsides reduced to bare rock and dust.

deter-v1.text: Her advisor tried to deter her from switching to philosophy, arguing at length that the academic job market was bleak, but she would not be dissuaded.
Friends attempted to deter Marco from buying the crumbling farmhouse, pointing out the costly repairs, yet their warnings only strengthened his resolve.
No amount of reasoning from her parents could deter Anna from her plan to sail alone across the ocean; she had a ready answer to each of their objections.

deter-v2.text: The city installed brighter streetlights in the park, hoping to deter the vandalism that had flourished under cover of darkness.
Steep fines for late filing are meant to deter carelessness, though critics argue they mainly punish those who cannot afford an accountant.
Thorny spines deter grazing animals, allowing the cactus to conserve the precious water stored in its fleshy stems.

detrimental.text: Although the pesticide boosted crop yields, it proved detrimental to bee populations, which in turn threatened the pollination the farms relied on.
Researchers found that chronic sleep deprivation is detrimental to memory, impairing the brain's ability to consolidate what was learned during the day.
Far from helping the company, the aggressive cost cutting was detrimental in the long run, since it drove away the experienced engineers who kept its products reliable.

devolve-v1.text: The new constitution devolved authority over schools and hospitals to regional governments, leaving the capital responsible mainly for defense and trade.
When the founder retired, the task of managing daily operations devolved to her deputy, who had quietly prepared for the role for years.
Rather than making every decision herself, the director devolved budgetary control to department heads, trusting them to allocate funds wisely.

devolve-v2.text: What began as a civil exchange about zoning rules soon devolved into a shouting match, with neighbors hurling personal accusations across the hall.
Without a clear leader, the reform movement devolved into rival factions that spent more energy attacking one another than pursuing their shared goals.
Critics lamented that the once thoughtful talk show had devolved into a spectacle of staged quarrels and cheap sensationalism.

diabolical.text: In the novel, the villain devises a diabolical scheme to poison the city's wells, relishing in advance the suffering it will cause.
Although the tyrant presented himself as a benevolent father to his people, historians describe his methods of surveillance and punishment as diabolical.
The conspirators' plan was diabolical in its cruelty: they intended to frame an innocent clerk for the fire and watch him be condemned for their crime.

diatribe.text: The retired professor's letter to the editor was a diatribe against the university administration, accusing it of betraying every principle of scholarship.
Instead of a reasoned critique, the pamphlet offered a lengthy diatribe against modern architecture, condemning glass towers as monuments to greed.
Audience members expected a gracious acceptance speech, but the novelist launched into a diatribe against the publishers who had rejected her early work.

dictatorial.text: The editor's dictatorial management style, in which every decision required his personal approval, drove several talented writers to quit.
Although the committee was supposed to reach decisions collectively, its chairman behaved in a dictatorial manner, ignoring every objection.
The country slid into dictatorial rule as the president dissolved the legislature and silenced the press.

didactic.text: The children's book is so didactic that its story disappears beneath a constant stream of lessons about sharing and honesty.
Unlike his earlier plays, which preached moral lessons, the playwright's late work is not didactic; it presents dilemmas without resolving them.
The curators insisted that every exhibit leave visitors with a lesson about the region's history, so the galleries felt didactic and offered little room for simple wonder.

differentiate-v1.text: What differentiates the architect's buildings from those of her contemporaries is the use of unfinished timber, which gives even her largest projects a rustic warmth.
A subtle bitterness in the aftertaste differentiates this regional cheese from its more famous cousin, which is otherwise nearly identical in texture.
Economists argue that in a crowded market, reliable customer service may be the only feature that differentiates one airline from another.

differentiate-v2.text: Isolated on separate islands for millennia, the finch populations gradually differentiated, each developing a beak suited to the seeds available in its own habitat.
Once a mountain range separated the two groups of salamanders, they began to differentiate, eventually becoming distinct species that can no longer interbreed.
Bacteria living in scalding hot springs and their relatives in the cooler surrounding soil have slowly come to differentiate, each lineage evolving enzymes suited to its own temperature.

diffident.text: The diffident young scholar rarely spoke at seminars, though her papers revealed that she understood the material better than anyone.
Although diffident in social gatherings, where he hardly said a word, the pianist became commanding the moment he sat at the keyboard.
Her diffident manner, which led her to preface every opinion with an apology, concealed a sharp and original mind.

dilapidated.text: The once grand theater had become dilapidated, its roof leaking, its seats torn and its ornate plaster ceiling crumbling onto the stage.
Investors saw potential in the dilapidated warehouse, reasoning that its sagging floors and broken windows could be repaired more cheaply than a new building could be erected.
Although the landlord advertised the apartments as charming, tenants found them dilapidated, with peeling paint, rotting window frames and plumbing that barely worked.

dilatory.text: The committee's dilatory approach to the investigation, including months of postponed hearings, allowed crucial evidence to disappear.
Frustrated by the contractor's dilatory pace, the homeowners hired another firm, which finished the renovation in a few weeks.
The student was dilatory about his thesis, spending the year organizing his desk and reading unrelated novels instead of writing.

dilettante.text: Although he spoke confidently about Renaissance painting, the gallery owner soon realized that the collector was a dilettante who had read only a few popular books.
The serious musicians resented the dilettante who joined their ensemble, since he practiced rarely and treated rehearsals as social occasions.
Having dabbled in poetry, pottery and astronomy without mastering any of them, the heiress was dismissed by critics as a mere dilettante.

diligent.text: A diligent archivist, Maria spent months cross-checking every date in the collection, refusing to publish the catalog until each entry had been verified.
Although she was not the most gifted student in the program, her diligent practice, hours every day without fail, eventually made her its finest pianist.
The auditors were diligent, examining each receipt rather than sampling a few, and so uncovered discrepancies that earlier reviews had missed.

diminutive-adj.text: The diminutive gymnast, barely reaching her coach's shoulder, generated astonishing power on the vault.
Despite its diminutive size, the hummingbird defends its territory fiercely, chasing off birds many times larger than itself.
The architect's diminutive cottage, with rooms scarcely large enough to turn around in, was a deliberate rebuke to the sprawling mansions nearby.

diminutive-n.text: In many languages, adding a suffix to a noun creates a diminutive: a word for a little house or a small dog is formed from the ordinary word.
Linguists note that speakers often use a diminutive, such as 'booklet' or 'piglet,' to express affection as well as small size.
Although he was named Juan after his grandfather, the family always called him by the diminutive 'Juanito' to distinguish the boy from the old man.

disabuse.text: A single semester of organic chemistry disabused him of the notion that medical school would be easy.
The tour guide tried to disabuse visitors of the popular belief that the castle was haunted, explaining that the eerie noises came from wind in the chimneys.
Early investors were quickly disabused of their faith in the company when an audit revealed that its reported profits had been invented.

disaffected.text: Disaffected with the party leadership, which had ignored their concerns for years, many younger members left to form a new organization.
The rebellion drew its strength from disaffected soldiers who had not been paid for months.
Teachers worried about the growing number of disaffected students who saw school as irrelevant to their lives and resented its rules.

discord.text: Discord within the coalition, as partners quarreled over nearly every appointment, eventually brought down the government.
The composer deliberately introduced discord into the final movement, letting clashing chords unsettle listeners before resolving into harmony.
Although the siblings had always been close, disputes over their father's estate sowed a discord that lasted for years.

discreet.text: Wary of embarrassing his colleague, the professor made a discreet remark after class rather than correcting her error in front of the students.
The diplomat was famously discreet, never revealing in public what had been said in private negotiations, which made both sides trust him.
Unlike her predecessor, who announced every rumored acquisition to the press, the new chief executive was discreet, disclosing deals only after contracts were signed.

discrete.text: The course is divided into discrete modules, each of which can be completed independently of the others.
What appears to be a continuous line on the screen is actually a row of discrete pixels, as anyone who magnifies the image enough to count them will discover.
The researchers identified three discrete stages in the disease, each with its own distinct symptoms.

discriminate.text: Young infants can discriminate between many speech sounds that their parents' language does not use, an ability that fades as they grow accustomed to their native tongue.
Because the two species of warbler look nearly identical, birders must discriminate between them by listening closely to differences in their songs.
A skilled radiologist can discriminate a harmless shadow from a dangerous one, detecting slight variations in shape that an untrained eye would overlook.

discursive.text: The lecturer's discursive style, which wandered from medieval poetry to modern economics to his own childhood, left students unsure what the lecture was actually about.
Although the memoir is discursive, frequently straying into anecdotes about minor acquaintances, its detours are so charming that few readers mind.
The editor urged the author to trim the discursive middle chapters, which abandoned the main argument for long excursions into family history.

disenfranchise.text: The novel depicts a republic that disenfranchises anyone without property, so that only landowners may cast ballots in its elections.
Reformers argued that the poll tax served chiefly to disenfranchise the poor, who could not afford to pay for the privilege of voting.
When the district's boundaries were redrawn without updating the registry, thousands of residents were effectively disenfranchised, unable to vote anywhere at all.

disheartened.text: Disheartened by a string of rejections, the young novelist nearly abandoned writing, until one editor's encouraging note restored her confidence.
The researchers were disheartened when the trial showed no benefit, since they had devoted a decade to developing the drug.
Although volunteers were initially eager, many grew disheartened as the cleanup dragged on and the river seemed as polluted as ever.

disingenuous.text: It was disingenuous of the company to claim it had no knowledge of the defect, since internal memos showed engineers had warned executives years earlier.
The official's disingenuous show of surprise at the scandal fooled no one, as reporters soon revealed that he had helped to orchestrate it.
Critics called the author's modest disclaimer disingenuous: while claiming to offer 'mere impressions,' she in fact presented a carefully argued indictment.

disinterested.text: To resolve the dispute fairly, both companies agreed to hire a disinterested arbitrator who had no financial ties to either side.
A disinterested observer, with no stake in the outcome, would have seen that both teams had played unfairly.
The scholar's review was disinterested, praising and criticizing the book on its merits even though its author was her longtime rival.

disparate.text: The anthology gathers disparate voices, from medieval mystics to contemporary engineers, whose only common thread is an interest in silence.
Unifying such disparate traditions as Baroque counterpoint and West African drumming, the composer created a sound unlike anything her audience had heard.
Although the two witnesses described the same event, their accounts were so disparate that investigators wondered whether they had seen the same accident.

dispassionate.text: Even while describing the atrocities, the historian maintained a dispassionate tone, letting the documents speak for themselves.
Judges must be dispassionate, setting aside their own sympathies and resentments in order to weigh the evidence impartially.
Unlike her fiery colleague, the negotiator remained dispassionate throughout the crisis, calmly analyzing each option.

dispatch-n.text: The new clerk handled the backlog of requests with remarkable dispatch, clearing in a single afternoon what had languished for weeks.
Because the patient's condition was worsening rapidly, the surgical team acted with dispatch, wasting no time on unnecessary tests.
Far from the slow bureaucracy she had expected, the permit office processed her application with admirable dispatch, returning the approval within a day.

dispatch-v.text: The chess champion dispatched her first three opponents in under twenty moves each, barely pausing to consider their openings.
Eager to reach the more interesting questions, the lecturer dispatched the preliminary definitions in a few brisk minutes.
The seasoned editor could dispatch a stack of routine letters before lunch, answering each one quickly and accurately.

dispensation.text: The athlete received a special dispensation from the league, allowing her to compete despite missing the qualifying deadline because of injury.
Because of the drought, farmers were granted a dispensation from the usual restrictions on drawing water from the river.
The monastery's rule forbade speaking at meals, but the abbot granted a dispensation to the novice who had to translate for visiting guests.

dissemble.text: The spy dissembled so skillfully that her colleagues never suspected she was passing their secrets to a foreign government.
When questioned about the missing funds, the treasurer dissembled, feigning confusion and insisting that the records must have been misfiled.
Rather than dissemble about his reasons for resigning, the minister openly admitted that he could no longer support the government's policy.

disseminate.text: The health agency disseminated information about the vaccine through radio broadcasts, posters and community meetings.
The invention of the printing press allowed scholars to disseminate their ideas far more widely than hand-copied manuscripts ever could.
The activists used social media to disseminate their message, reaching millions of people within days.

dissipate-v1.text: Within five years the heir had dissipated the family fortune on racehorses, gambling, and lavish parties, and the ancestral estate had to be sold.
Rather than dissipate their lottery winnings as so many others had, the couple invested the money and continued to live modestly.
Auditors charged that the ministry had dissipated its entire reconstruction budget on consultants and ceremonies, leaving the damaged bridges unrepaired.

dissipate-v2.text: Although the morning fog lay thick over the harbor, it dissipated within an hour of sunrise, leaving the fishing fleet a clear view of the channel.
The crowd that had gathered outside the courthouse slowly dissipated once the verdict was announced, its members drifting back to offices and cafes across the city.
Engineers designed the heat sink with dozens of thin fins so that warmth from the processor would dissipate into the surrounding air rather than accumulate inside the case.

dissolution.text: The novel traces the young heir's slide into dissolution: nights of gambling, drinking and carousing gradually consumed both his inheritance and his once promising reputation.

Contemporary moralists blamed the city's decline on the dissolution that prevailed among its ruling class, whose lavish banquets and open vices contrasted starkly with the austerity of earlier generations.
Far from living in dissolution, as rumors in the capital suggested, the exiled poet spent his final years in sober routine, rising early and drinking nothing stronger than tea.

docile.text: Unlike their wild ancestors, domesticated sheep are docile, following a shepherd's dog without resistance wherever it steers them.
The regime preferred a docile press, one that printed official statements without question and never challenged those in power.
Although the new recruit was docile during training, obeying every order without complaint, he proved surprisingly independent once he reached the field.

dog.text: Rumors of plagiarism dogged the historian for years, resurfacing with every new book despite repeated investigations that cleared him.
Mechanical failures dogged the expedition from the start, delaying its departure and repeatedly stranding the team in remote villages.
Though she had achieved great success, the composer was dogged by a self-doubt that followed her relentlessly from one premiere to the next.

dogmatic.text: The professor was so dogmatic about his theory that he refused even to read studies that contradicted it.
Unlike his dogmatic predecessor, who insisted that there was only one correct way to run every play, the new coach encouraged players to experiment.
Her dogmatic views on nutrition, which she presented as beyond question, alienated colleagues who valued open debate.

doleful.text: The doleful tolling of the village bell announced to every household that the fishing boat lost in the storm would not be coming home.
Although the children's book ends happily, its middle chapters are so doleful that several parents reported their children weeping at bedtime.
The shelter dog's doleful expression, with drooping ears and downcast eyes, persuaded the visiting family to take him home rather than the livelier puppy beside him.

dolorous.text: The soprano's dolorous final aria, sung as her character mourns a lost child, left much of the audience quietly wiping their eyes.
Rather than celebrating the treaty, the veteran's memoir adopts a dolorous tone, lingering over the friends he buried and the villages he saw reduced to ashes.
Medieval painters often gave the Virgin a dolorous countenance at the foot of the cross, her eyes lowered and her hands clasped in grief.

doughty.text: The doughty explorer pressed on across the ice sheet even after two of her companions turned back, undaunted by the storms that battered their camp nightly.
Though small and outnumbered, the doughty garrison refused to surrender the fortress, repelling three assaults before reinforcements finally arrived.
Critics dismissed the reformer as naive, yet she proved a doughty opponent of entrenched interests, facing down threats and lawsuits without once retreating from her position.

dovetail.text: The historian's findings dovetail neatly with the archaeological record: the documents describe a fire in the granary, and excavators found charred grain precisely where the texts indicated.
Because her research interests dovetailed with the laboratory's ongoing project, Priya was able to contribute meaningful work within her first week.
Planners hoped the new bus routes would dovetail with the train schedule, so that commuters arriving at the station would never wait more than a few minutes for a connection.

dupe-n.text: Believing every advertisement he saw, the gullible collector became an easy dupe for any dealer who claimed to have a rare manuscript for sale.
The spy insisted he had been merely a dupe: his handlers had assured him the sealed envelopes held business contracts, and he never thought to look inside.
Critics argued that the committee had become a dupe of industry lobbyists, since it accepted without question studies whose funding and methods should have aroused suspicion.

dupe-v.text: The forger duped several respected museums, selling them paintings so skillfully aged that even experts accepted them as genuine.
Investors were duped by the fund's glossy brochures, which promised steady returns while concealing that early profits came from new deposits.
The con artist duped the elderly couple into signing over their house by posing as a government inspector.

duplicity.text: The diplomat's duplicity became clear only later: while publicly championing the alliance, he had been secretly negotiating a separate treaty with its rivals.
Voters forgave the candidate's occasional blunders, but they would not forgive duplicity, and the revelation that he had promised opposite things to rival donors ended his campaign.
In the play, the servant's duplicity drives the plot, as he professes loyalty to each of the feuding brothers while quietly working to ruin them both.

duress.text: The court threw out the confession because it had been obtained under duress, after the suspect was threatened and denied sleep.
Treaties signed under duress, the historian argued, rarely last, since the weaker party seeks to overturn them as soon as it can.
The employee claimed that she had approved the payments only under duress, fearing that her supervisor would fire her if she refused.

ebullient.text: Normally reserved, the professor grew almost ebullient when her student's thesis won the prize, laughing, embracing colleagues and toasting everyone in the room.
The composer's ebullient finale, with its rushing strings and triumphant brass, stands in deliberate contrast to the somber movement that precedes it.
Investors were ebullient after the successful launch, though the chief financial officer cautioned that such exuberance might prove premature.

eccentric.text: The eccentric inventor wore a pith helmet to the laboratory each day and insisted on conducting experiments only at night.
Though her neighbors found her habits eccentric, such as keeping dozens of clocks all set to different times, the retired astronomer insisted the arrangement helped her think.
Scholars once dismissed the poet as merely eccentric, noting his odd habits of writing on wallpaper and refusing to wear shoes, but his experiments now seem visionary.

eclectic.text: The restaurant's eclectic menu featured dishes from Japan, Peru and Morocco side by side, often combining two cuisines on a single plate.
The architect's eclectic style combined Gothic arches, modernist glass walls and traditional tile roofs, borrowing freely from every period she admired.
Her library was eclectic, with books on quantum physics shelved beside medieval poetry and cookbooks.

economical.text: The novelist's economical prose, in which not a single word is wasted, conveys more in a paragraph than many writers achieve in a chapter.
The engineers designed an economical heating system that used half the fuel of the old one while keeping the building just as warm.
Rather than hiring a large staff, the startup remained economical, relying on a few versatile employees who handled many tasks.

edifying.text: The lecture was edifying, leaving the audience with a deeper understanding of the moral questions raised by modern medicine.
Although the documentary was billed as edifying, it offered little more than sensational footage with no insight at all.
Victorian parents favored edifying novels for their children, stories meant to improve both the mind and the character.

effacing.text: Despite winning the prize, the self-effacing scientist credited her laboratory assistants and declined to give interviews about her own contributions.
The captain's self-effacing manner surprised reporters, who had expected boasting but heard him attribute the victory entirely to his teammates.
Rather than dominating the conversation, the self-effacing host kept the spotlight on his guests, asking about their work and saying little about his own accomplishments.

effervescent.text: The host's effervescent personality kept the long evening lively; she moved from table to table, sparking conversation and laughter wherever she paused.
Critics praised the young actor's effervescent performance as the heroine's sister, whose bubbling enthusiasm offers relief from the play's darker scenes.
Although the book's subject is grave, its author remained effervescent throughout the promotional tour, greeting each audience with obvious delight and boundless energy.

efficacious.text: The new treatment proved efficacious in the clinical trial, reducing patients' symptoms in nearly every case the researchers studied.
The city's anti-litter campaign was surprisingly efficacious; within months, the streets were noticeably cleaner.
Many folk remedies turn out not to be efficacious: in controlled trials, patients who took them recovered no faster than those who took nothing at all.

effrontery.text: After arriving an hour late to the interview, the applicant had the effrontery to ask whether the company could rearrange its schedule to suit his preferences.
The committee was astonished by the effrontery of the contractor, who, having delivered a flawed bridge design, submitted an invoice demanding a bonus for early completion.
Few junior scholars would presume to correct the eminent historian in public, yet Dana showed the effrontery to interrupt his keynote and dispute his central claim.

egotist.text: An egotist to the core, the conductor claimed full credit for the orchestra's success and never once acknowledged the musicians who performed the music.
Although he presented himself as a humble servant of the public, his memoir reveals an egotist who measured every event by its effect on his own reputation.
Conversations with Victor were exhausting, since the egotist inevitably steered every topic back to his own accomplishments.

egregious.text: The referee's egregious error, awarding a goal that had clearly gone wide, prompted an official investigation.
The report documented egregious violations of safety rules, including locked fire exits and missing alarms.
Among the many mistakes in the translation, the most egregious was rendering 'peace' as 'war' in the treaty's opening line.

eke.text: After the factory closed, many families eked out a living by selling vegetables from their gardens and taking whatever odd jobs they could find.
Through the long drought, the herders eked out their dwindling stores of grain, rationing every handful so that it would last until the rains returned.
Living on a meager stipend as a graduate student, Lena could eke out only the barest subsistence, rarely affording anything beyond rice, beans and used books.

elaborate-adj.text: The wedding featured an elaborate ceremony, with three processions, a full choir and costumes embroidered by hand over several months.
Unlike the plain facades of modernist buildings, the cathedral's front is elaborate, crowded with carved saints, gargoyles and intricate tracery.
The heist in the novel relies on an elaborate plan involving forged blueprints, a fake delivery and precise timing, each step depending on the one before.

elaborate-v.text: When the reviewers asked her to elaborate on her methods, the scientist added a detailed appendix describing each step of the experiment.
The senator declined to elaborate, offering only a brief statement and leaving reporters to speculate about what the vague remark had meant.
In the second chapter, the author elaborates on an idea merely sketched in the introduction, filling it out with historical cases and statistical evidence.

elegiac.text: The documentary's closing scenes are frankly elegiac, lingering over empty factories and shuttered storefronts as the narrator mourns a way of life that has vanished.
Written after the death of her brother, the poet's final collection is elegiac in tone, each poem circling back to memories of their shared childhood.
Instead of a triumphant march, the composer ended the symphony with an elegiac adagio, a quiet lament for the soldiers who never returned.

elicit.text: The comedian's joke elicited only a few scattered laughs, and he quickly moved on to his next routine.
The survey was designed to elicit honest responses, so it guaranteed anonymity to every participant.
The novel's ambiguous ending elicited strong reactions from readers, some of whom wrote delighted letters to the author while others demanded a sequel that explained it.

elucidate.text: The professor used a simple diagram to elucidate the concept, and students who had been confused for weeks finally understood it.
Rather than elucidating the policy, the spokesman's long statement only left reporters more puzzled than before.
The editor added footnotes to elucidate the poet's obscure references to local legends and forgotten politicians.

elude.text: The meaning of the poem's final stanza eludes even seasoned critics, who continue to propose rival interpretations with little agreement.
Although she could perform the calculation flawlessly, the underlying logic of the proof eluded her until a tutor explained it with a diagram.
