Why the ancient builders aligned the monument with that particular star still eludes archaeologists, who have found no inscriptions explaining the choice.

elusive.text: The snow leopard is famously elusive, so wildlife photographers may spend months in the mountains without glimpsing a single one.
The name of the tune remained elusive; Mark could hum its melody perfectly yet could not recall what it was called.
For decades the particle proved elusive, escaping detection in experiment after experiment until more sensitive instruments finally captured its signature.

embellish.text: The monks embellished the manuscript's margins with gold leaf and intricate vines, transforming a plain text into a luminous work of art.
Rather than leave the facade bare, the architect embellished it with colored tiles and carved stone flowers that caught the afternoon light.
The singer liked to embellish the simple folk melody with trills and grace notes, decorating it without obscuring the tune.

embroiled.text: For nearly a decade the two families were embroiled in a bitter dispute over the boundary between their farms, with neither willing to concede an inch.
Hoping to remain neutral, the small nation was nevertheless embroiled in the conflict when both neighboring powers demanded its support.
The professor had hoped to focus on research but instead found herself embroiled in departmental quarrels over hiring and funding.

embryonic.text: Research on the new battery chemistry is still embryonic; the team has produced promising results in the laboratory but has yet to build a working prototype.
Though the city's arts district is only in its embryonic phase, a handful of galleries and studios have already begun to draw visitors to the old warehouses.
Historians trace the embryonic forms of modern banking to medieval merchants, whose crude letters of credit would eventually develop into sophisticated financial instruments.

eminent.text: The conference featured several eminent physicists, including two Nobel laureates and the director of the national laboratory.
Although she later became an eminent historian, respected throughout the field, her first book was rejected by a dozen publishers.
The university invited an eminent judge to deliver the commencement address, a jurist admired for decades of distinguished service on the high court.

empathetic.text: An empathetic nurse, Grace could sense a patient's anxiety before a word was spoken and knew exactly how to ease it.
Readers found the memoir's narrator deeply empathetic, since she portrayed even her harshest critics with a keen understanding of the fears that drove them.
Unlike his brusque predecessor, the new counselor was empathetic, listening patiently and responding to each student's worries as though he felt them himself.

empiricism.text: The philosopher rejected pure speculation in favor of empiricism, insisting that any claim about the natural world must ultimately be tested against observation.
Early physicians often relied on tradition rather than empiricism, so remedies persisted for centuries even when careful observation would have shown them to be useless.
The economist's empiricism set her apart from colleagues who built elegant theoretical models; she trusted only conclusions drawn from carefully gathered data on actual households.

emulate.text: Young painters of the period sought to emulate the old masters, copying their compositions in museums in hopes of one day equaling their skill.
Many developing economies have tried to emulate the export-led growth of successful neighbors, adopting similar policies in hopes of matching their prosperity.
The apprentice watched the master carpenter closely, striving to emulate his precise joinery until her own work could rival his.

enamor.text: The young architect was so enamored of glass towers that she proposed one for every site, even where local planners had requested low brick buildings.
Visitors who arrive expecting to dislike the city often leave enamored of its narrow streets and lively markets, vowing to return the following year.
Though critics had long scorned the genre, the director was openly enamored of old musicals, and his new film lovingly recreates their lavish dance numbers.

encumber.text: The startup's growth was encumbered by debt from its early years, which forced the founders to spend revenue on interest payments rather than new hires.
Hikers are advised not to encumber themselves with heavy gear on the steep ascent, since every extra pound slows progress up the narrow trail.
Reformers argued that layers of outdated regulations encumbered small farmers, who spent more time filling out forms than tending their fields.

endemic.text: Because the tiny frog is endemic to a single mountain forest, conservationists warn that clearing that forest would erase the species from the wild entirely.
The island's long isolation produced many endemic plants, species that grow there naturally and nowhere else on earth.
Although the herb now appears in cuisines worldwide, botanists trace it to a single valley, where it is endemic, and argue that every cultivated variety descends from those wild plants.

enervate.text: Dave found the professor's lecture so enervating that not even a potent cup of joe could keep his eyes from drooping.
The long, humid summer enervated the workers, who by August could barely summon the energy to finish their shifts.
Far from invigorating her, the months of chemotherapy enervated the patient so thoroughly that she slept most of each day.
Endless committee meetings enervate even the most enthusiastic faculty members, leaving them too drained to pursue their research.

engender.text: The new policy engendered widespread resentment among employees, who felt they had not been consulted.
The teacher's patient encouragement engendered in her students a lasting love of reading that many of them carried into adulthood.
Economic inequality, the sociologist argued, tends to engender distrust, since those left behind suspect that the system is rigged.

enjoin.text: The physician enjoined her patient to rest for a full week, warning that returning to work too soon could turn a minor strain into a lasting injury.
The monastic rule enjoins novices to keep silence during meals, and the abbot enforces this command without exception.
In his will, the merchant enjoined his heirs to keep the family library intact, directing that no volume ever be sold or divided among them.

enmity.text: The enmity between the two scholars, rooted in a decades-old dispute over credit for a discovery, was so deep that they refused to attend the same conferences.
Despite centuries of enmity, the neighboring kingdoms eventually signed a treaty, surprising observers who had assumed their hostility was permanent.
Rather than a friendly rivalry, the two firms maintained an abiding enmity, each seizing any opportunity to undermine the other.

enormity.text: Only when the archives were opened did historians grasp the enormity of the regime's crimes, which included the systematic persecution of entire villages.
The novel refuses to soften the enormity of the tyrant's deeds; it records his cruelties toward prisoners in plain, unflinching prose.
Although the official claimed he had merely followed orders, the tribunal insisted that no directive could excuse an enormity as monstrous as the burning of a defenseless town.

enthrall.text: The storyteller enthralled the children so completely that not one of them stirred until the tale ended and the lanterns were lit.
Although the lecture concerned the seemingly dry subject of medieval tax records, the historian's vivid anecdotes enthralled an audience that had expected to doze.
Birdwatchers are often enthralled by the courtship dance of the crane, standing motionless in the cold for hours to watch it unfold.

entice.text: The city tried to entice young professionals to relocate with promises of cheap housing and vibrant nightlife, though the reality proved far less glamorous.
Advertisements for the timeshare enticed buyers with talk of luxurious villas, but the actual units were cramped and far from the beach.
The recruiter enticed the engineer to leave her stable job by describing lavish stock options that, in the end, proved nearly worthless.

entrenched.text: Reformers struggled against the entrenched interests of the old guild, whose members had controlled the trade for centuries.
The belief that women could not do mathematics was so entrenched in the culture that even brilliant girls were discouraged from studying it.
Once a bureaucracy becomes entrenched, it resists every attempt at change, protecting its procedures long after they have outlived their purpose.

enumerate-v1.text: Census takers set out to enumerate the region's population, visiting every household to count its residents.
Because the colony is spread across hundreds of cliffs, biologists use aerial photographs to enumerate the nesting birds, tallying individuals from the images.
Before the grant could be renewed, the museum had to enumerate its holdings, arriving at a precise count of every object in storage.

enumerate-v2.text: In her opening statement, the prosecutor enumerated the defendant's alleged offenses, naming each in turn: fraud, forgery and obstruction of justice.
The treaty enumerates the rights guaranteed to each signatory, listing them article by article so that no party can later claim ambiguity.
Rather than summarize the flaws in general terms, the reviewer enumerated them one after another, citing a specific page for each problem.

ephemeral.text: The artist creates ephemeral sculptures of sand and ice that vanish within hours, preserved only in photographs.
Unlike the ephemeral fame of internet celebrities, the composer's reputation has endured for more than two centuries.
The joy of the victory proved ephemeral; within days, the team was mired in scandal.

epigram.text: Rather than building a sustained argument, the essayist relied on the epigram, compressing each insight into a pithy, witty line that readers could easily quote.
At the retirement dinner, the dean offered a single epigram instead of a long speech, and the guests laughed at how neatly his clever phrase summed up a forty-year career.
The play's dialogue sparkles with epigrams, clever quips that the characters toss off so casually that the audience scarcely has time to laugh before the next one arrives.

epiphany.text: While staring at the tangled data late one night, the chemist had an epiphany: the anomaly was not an error but evidence of an unknown compound.
The novel's turning point is a quiet epiphany on a train, when the heroine suddenly understands that the life she has been building belongs to her parents rather than to herself.
For years the composer struggled with the finale, until a sudden epiphany during a walk in the rain revealed how the opening theme could return transformed.

eponym.text: The clinic's founder became the eponym of the syndrome she first described, and medical students now learn her name alongside its symptoms.
Few residents realize that their town has an eponym: it was named for an eighteenth-century surveyor whose portrait still hangs in the courthouse.
The word 'boycott' preserves the surname of its eponym, a land agent whose tenants refused to deal with him, so that his name became a general term for organized refusal.

equitable.text: The mediator sought an equitable settlement, one that neither the landlord nor the tenants could reasonably claim favored the other side.
Critics argued that the flat tax was not equitable, since it asked a struggling family to sacrifice a far larger share of its necessities than a wealthy one.
To ensure an equitable division of the workload, the manager rotated the least desirable assignments so that no single employee bore them every month.

equivocal.text: Whether we can glean an artist's unconscious urges through his or her art remains equivocal; that we can ever even really tap into another person's hidden motives remains in doubt.
The minister's equivocal answer, which could be read as either support or opposition, satisfied neither side of the debate.
The results of the trial were equivocal: some patients improved, others worsened, and the researchers could not say whether the drug worked.
Rather than giving an equivocal reply, the candidate stated plainly that she opposed the tax increase.

equivocate.text: Pressed by reporters about whether the factory would close, the spokesperson equivocated, offering vague references to 'ongoing reviews' rather than a straight answer.
A witness who equivocates under oath, phrasing each reply so that it can later be read two ways, may damage a case more than one who simply lies.
Unlike her predecessor, who would equivocate whenever a question became uncomfortable, the new director answered directly, even when the truth was unwelcome.

eradicate.text: A decades-long vaccination campaign finally eradicated the disease, which has not been seen anywhere in the world since.
The new manager vowed to eradicate corruption in the department, firing every official involved in the bribery scheme.
Although the gardeners worked tirelessly to eradicate the invasive weed, it returned each spring from roots buried deep underground.

err.text: The historian acknowledged that he had erred in dating the manuscript, having mistaken a later scribe's handwriting for the original author's.
When uncertain about a patient's allergies, doctors choose to err on the side of caution, prescribing a safer alternative drug.
Even the most careful translators occasionally err, and the novel's first English edition contains several passages that misrepresent the original.

errant.text: Unlike the disciplined monks who kept to the cloister, the errant friar roamed from village to village, preaching wherever he happened to stop.
The shepherd spent the evening searching for an errant lamb that had strayed far from the flock into the rocky hills.
The romances of the period celebrated errant knights, yet real lords distrusted such men, preferring vassals who stayed on their own lands rather than riding off wherever adventure called.

erratic.text: The patient's erratic heartbeat, racing one moment and slowing the next, alarmed the physicians, who could find no pattern in its rhythm.
Investors grew nervous about the company's erratic leadership, as the chief executive reversed major decisions without warning or explanation.
Because the old bus ran on an erratic schedule, sometimes early and sometimes an hour late, commuters never knew when to leave home.

ersatz.text: During the wartime shortages, households brewed an ersatz coffee from roasted chicory and acorns, a poor substitute that fooled no one.
The theme park's ersatz Venetian canals, complete with painted skies and chlorinated water, struck the critic as a charmless imitation of the real city.
The memoir's ersatz humility, apparent in passages where the author praises himself while pretending to be modest, irritated reviewers more than open boasting would have.

erudite.text: The erudite professor could quote Greek poetry, discuss Chinese philosophy and explain quantum mechanics with equal ease.
Although the essay was erudite, filled with references to obscure scholars, it was accessible to general readers.
The librarian was surprisingly erudite; she had read nearly every book in the collection and could discuss each one in depth.

eschew.text: The chef eschews processed ingredients, insisting on preparing every sauce and bread from scratch.
Hoping to appeal to ordinary voters, the candidate eschewed technical jargon and spoke in plain, simple language.
The monks eschew all forms of luxury, living in bare cells and wearing only coarse robes.

esoteric.text: The seminar focused on an esoteric branch of mathematics that only a handful of specialists in the world fully understand.
The poet's allusions are so esoteric that even well-read critics need footnotes to understand them.
What began as an esoteric practice among a small circle of mystics eventually spread to millions of ordinary followers.

espouse.text: Although he had once espoused free-market principles, the economist later became a vocal advocate for government regulation.
The organization espouses a philosophy of nonviolence, training its members to resist injustice without ever using force.
Few scientists were willing to espouse the controversial theory publicly, fearing damage to their reputations.

estimable.text: Although she never achieved fame, the librarian led an estimable life, quietly teaching generations of children to read and earning the gratitude of the entire town.
The committee chose the most estimable candidate for the ethics post, a judge whose integrity even her political opponents admired.
The novel has estimable qualities, including careful research and graceful prose, though its sluggish plot may test some readers' patience.

ethereal.text: The choir's ethereal harmonies seemed to float above the congregation, so light and delicate that they hardly seemed produced by human voices.
The designer favored ethereal fabrics such as chiffon and silk gauze, which drifted around the models like mist as they walked.
Unlike the heavy, earthbound figures of his early sculpture, the artist's late work is almost ethereal, with slender forms that appear weightless.

euphoria.text: The euphoria that followed the treaty's signing soon faded, as citizens realized that peace would not immediately restore their ruined economy.
Market analysts cautioned that the euphoria surrounding the new technology was overblown, since few of the companies involved had ever turned a profit.
After years of failed attempts, the team's euphoria at finally detecting the signal was so intense that they celebrated long into the night.

evanescent.text: The painter tried to capture the evanescent colors of dusk, which shifted and faded so quickly that she had only minutes to work each evening.
Much online fame is evanescent: a video that captivates millions on Monday is often forgotten entirely by the end of the week.
Chemists struggled to study the evanescent intermediate compound, since by the time their instruments could register it, it had already broken down into more stable products.

evasive-adj1.text: When the storm shifted course, the captain took evasive action, steering the ship far to the south to avoid the worst of the waves.
The gazelle's evasive zigzagging makes it difficult for a cheetah to close in, since each sudden turn forces the predator to slow down.
Pilots practice evasive maneuvers so that, if another aircraft strays into their path, they can swerve away from danger instantly.

evasive-adj2.text: Asked directly whether the company had known about the defect, the spokesperson gave an evasive answer about ongoing reviews and never said yes or no.
The witness grew evasive under cross-examination, offering vague recollections and conveniently forgetting details she had described clearly the day before.
Frustrated by the minister's evasive replies, reporters pressed him to state plainly whether taxes would rise, but he spoke only of unspecified adjustments.

evenhanded.text: A good mediator must remain evenhanded, giving each party equal time to speak and refusing to signal sympathy for either side.
Although the biographer clearly admired her subject, her treatment of his failures was evenhanded, neither excusing them nor dwelling on them unduly.
Critics accused the referee of favoring the home team, but a review of the footage showed that his calls had been scrupulously evenhanded.

exacerbate.text: The drought was exacerbated by poor water management, which allowed much of the remaining supply to leak away.
Rather than calming the crisis, the government's heavy-handed response exacerbated it, sparking even larger protests.
Chronic stress can exacerbate many physical ailments, so doctors often advise patients with heart disease to reduce the pressures in their lives.

exacting.text: The surgeon's exacting standards meant that her residents rehearsed every procedure until it was flawless.
Restoring antique clocks is exacting work; a single misplaced gear can prevent the entire mechanism from functioning.
The editor was notoriously exacting, returning manuscripts covered in corrections for even the smallest error of grammar or fact.

exalt.text: The poem exalts the humble farmer, portraying him as a hero whose labor sustains the entire nation.
Because the river goddess was believed to bring the floods that fertilized their fields, the villagers exalted her in hymns sung at every harvest festival.
Critics who once exalted the painter as a genius later dismissed his work as derivative and shallow.

exasperate.text: The composer's constant revisions exasperated the orchestra, which had to relearn the score after every rehearsal only days before the premiere.
Nothing exasperated the professor more than students who asked questions she had answered moments earlier; by the third repetition her patience had worn thin.
The software's frequent crashes so exasperated the staff that several began keeping handwritten records rather than risk losing another day's work.

excoriate.text: The review excoriated the new opera, condemning its libretto as incoherent and its score as a clumsy imitation of better composers.
Although the governor had expected mild criticism, the editorial board excoriated her proposal, calling it reckless, cynical and an insult to taxpayers.
The auditor's report excoriates the charity's management in unsparing terms, faulting its leaders for years of careless bookkeeping and misleading statements to donors.

excruciating.text: The fractured ankle caused excruciating pain, so severe that the hiker could not put the slightest weight on it and had to be carried down.
Migraine sufferers describe the attacks as excruciating, with throbbing so intense that even dim light and quiet sounds become unbearable.
Although the dentist promised only mild discomfort, the procedure proved excruciating once the anesthetic wore off halfway through.

execrate.text: Villagers execrated the landlord whose evictions had scattered their families, and his name became a byword for cruelty in local songs.
Though celebrated in his lifetime, the general is now widely execrated, as historians have documented the brutal reprisals he ordered against civilians.
The reformers did more than disagree with child labor; they execrated it from every pulpit and podium, denouncing it as a moral stain on the nation.

exegesis.text: Her exegesis of the poem's final stanza, which traced each image back to classical sources, persuaded many scholars to reconsider its meaning.
Rather than offering a close exegesis of the constitution's text, the judge relied on broad appeals to fairness, a method her colleagues found insufficiently rigorous.
Students in the seminar spend entire sessions on the exegesis of a single paragraph, weighing every word and debating how medieval readers would have understood it.

exemplar.text: The restored town hall is regarded as an exemplar of civic architecture, and designers from neighboring cities study it when planning their own public buildings.
Young scientists were encouraged to model their conduct on the retired chemist, an exemplar of rigor who rechecked every result before publishing.
Teachers often hold up the essay as an exemplar for their students to imitate, pointing to its clear thesis and economical prose.

exemplify-v1.text: The cathedral's soaring arches and stained glass exemplify the Gothic style, displaying nearly every feature that defines the period.
Her patient, meticulous research, conducted over decades without shortcuts, exemplifies the scholarly virtues the prize was created to honor.
With its flat skyline and endless rows of identical houses, the suburb exemplifies the postwar housing boom and its emphasis on affordability over individuality.

exemplify-v2.text: To exemplify the principle of buoyancy, the teacher dropped a block of wood and a stone into a tank of water and asked students to explain the difference.
The author exemplifies her abstract claim about memory with a vivid anecdote from her own childhood, making the theory concrete for readers.
The lecturer exemplified each grammatical rule with a sentence from a famous novel, so that students could see the rule at work.

exhort.text: The coach exhorted her exhausted players to give one final effort, shouting encouragement from the sideline throughout the last minutes.
In his sermons, the preacher exhorted the congregation to care for the poor, urging them again and again to share what they had.
Public health posters exhorted citizens to wash their hands frequently, pressing the message with bold slogans on every bus and train.

exiguity.text: The exiguity of the museum's budget meant that the curators had to borrow display cases and rely on volunteers to guard the galleries.
Historians must work around the exiguity of surviving records from the period; a handful of letters and a single tax roll are nearly all that remain.
Despite the exiguity of their rations, a thin soup and a crust of bread each day, the prisoners organized lectures and concerts to sustain their morale.

exonerate.text: New DNA evidence exonerated the prisoner, who had spent twenty years in jail for a crime he did not commit.
The investigation exonerated the pilot, finding that the crash had been caused by a mechanical failure rather than human error.
Although the committee exonerated the senator of wrongdoing, many voters remained convinced of his guilt.

exorbitant.text: Tenants protested the exorbitant rent increase, which would have doubled their monthly payments despite no improvements to the building.
The critic found the film's running time exorbitant: at nearly four hours, it far exceeded what its slender plot could justify.
Hospitals were accused of charging exorbitant prices for routine supplies, billing patients many times what the items cost wholesale.

expansive.text: Usually taciturn at meetings, the engineer grew expansive at the reunion dinner, chatting freely with old colleagues and telling stories late into the night.
The interviewer's warm manner made the reclusive novelist unexpectedly expansive, and she spoke at length about her childhood, her influences and her doubts.
In his letters the statesman is far more expansive than in his guarded public speeches, sharing opinions and confidences with friends in long, garrulous paragraphs.

expound.text: The professor expounded on his theory for two hours, explaining each assumption and answering every objection in detail.
In her latest book, the philosopher expounds a new approach to ethics, laying out its principles chapter by chapter.
Asked to expound on his brief remark, the witness declined to provide any further details.

expunge.text: The editor expunged every trace of the retracted study from the journal's archive, so that later researchers would not cite its fabricated data.
Although the council voted to expunge the offensive remarks from the official minutes, many residents had already recorded them and shared them widely.
The new regime tried to expunge the deposed king from national memory, removing his portraits, renaming streets and rewriting textbooks.

expurgate.text: The publisher agreed to print the novel only if the author would expurgate the passages that censors had deemed obscene.
Students were surprised to learn that the version of the play they had studied was expurgated, with its bawdy jokes and coarse insults removed for classroom use.
Rather than expurgating the diaries to spare the relatives' feelings, the family published them in full, including every harsh remark the author had made about them.

extant.text: Only three copies of the original manuscript are extant; the rest were destroyed in the fire that consumed the monastery's library.
Although many ancient languages have disappeared, some of their descendants remain extant and are still spoken today.
The oldest extant map of the city dates from the sixteenth century, though earlier maps are mentioned in records.

extenuating.text: The judge reduced the sentence, citing extenuating circumstances: the defendant had stolen the medicine only to treat his gravely ill daughter.
Although late submissions normally receive no credit, the professor accepted Mei's essay, since a family emergency was clearly an extenuating factor.
The committee found nothing extenuating in the official's conduct; his misuse of funds was deliberate and entirely inexcusable.

extrapolate.text: From a few fossilized teeth, paleontologists extrapolated the size and diet of the entire animal, an inference some colleagues considered too bold.
It is risky to extrapolate from a single successful classroom to an entire school district, since conditions that worked for one teacher may not hold elsewhere.
By observing how the glacier retreated over the past decade, the team extrapolated a date by which the valley would be free of ice altogether.

facetious.text: The senator's facetious suggestion that the committee simply flip a coin drew laughs, though some colleagues felt the joke trivialized a serious debate.
Although his essays are often facetious, their jokes conceal a serious argument about the decline of public reading that careless readers tend to miss.
Asked why she had become an economist, she gave the facetious reply that she had been too pessimistic for any other profession.

facile.text: The report offered a facile explanation for the company's decline, blaming a single bad quarter while ignoring years of mismanagement.
Although the debut novel is fluently written, its facile ending, in which every conflict melts away in a final reconciliation, betrays the complexity of the themes it raises.
Serious historians resist facile comparisons between ancient and modern empires, insisting that the differences matter as much as any superficial resemblance.

factious.text: The factious committee could not agree even on an agenda, as rival blocs spent each meeting accusing one another of bad faith.
The founders warned that a factious spirit, in which citizens place loyalty to their party above the common good, could tear the young republic apart.
What had been a unified reform movement grew factious after its leader's death, splintering into competing groups that each claimed to be her true heirs.

factitious.text: The town's prosperity proved factitious, propped up entirely by a single government contract that vanished as soon as the war ended.
Collectors learned that the dealer's antiques were factitious: the patina on the furniture had been produced with chemicals rather than centuries of use.
The advertising campaign created a factitious demand for the gadget, persuading consumers that they needed a product that solved no real problem.

fallacious.text: The argument that a policy must be good because it is popular is fallacious, confusing public approval with actual merit.
The report's conclusions were fallacious, resting on a flawed sample that included only the most successful companies.
Critics exposed the fallacious reasoning behind the advertisement, which implied that correlation proved causation.

fastidious.text: The fastidious editor insisted on checking every comma and footnote, sometimes delaying publication by weeks.
A fastidious dresser, the diplomat never appeared in public without a perfectly pressed suit and polished shoes.
Unlike his fastidious roommate, who alphabetized the spice rack, he left dishes piled in the sink for days.

fawn.text: Courtiers fawned over the young king, praising his every remark as brilliant in hopes of winning titles and estates.
The junior associate's habit of fawning on senior partners, laughing at their weakest jokes and lavishing praise on their briefs, earned him little respect.
Instead of offering honest criticism, the reviewers fawned over the celebrated novelist's latest book, heaping flattery on a work that was plainly weak.

feckless.text: The feckless nephew squandered every opportunity his aunt arranged, skipping interviews, missing deadlines and blaming others for each failure.
Critics described the regulatory agency as feckless, noting that it had issued warnings for years but never once enforced a penalty.
Though her brother was charming, he was also feckless, so the family entrusted the estate to the sister, whose diligence was beyond question.

fecund.text: The decade the physicist spent at the institute was her most fecund; she published a dozen influential papers and trained a generation of students.
The novelist possessed a fecund imagination, producing plots, characters and whole invented languages faster than his editors could review them.
Rather than exhausting the subject, the conference proved remarkably fecund, generating new collaborations and research questions that occupied the participants for years.

fell.text: In the old ballads, the fell sorcerer poisons the kingdom's wells and curses its children, and only a humble shepherd dares to oppose him.
The plague was a fell visitor to the medieval town, sweeping through its crowded streets and sparing neither rich nor poor.
Although the tyrant styled himself a benevolent father to his people, his fell deeds, including the imprisonment of dissenters and the seizure of their lands, told a different story.

ferret.text: The investigative reporter spent months ferreting out the details of the scheme, combing through records and interviewing dozens of former employees.
A patient archivist, she managed to ferret out the missing letter from a box of unrelated papers that had been mislabeled for decades.
Auditors are trained to ferret out hidden losses, since a company in trouble will often bury its worst figures in footnotes and obscure subsidiary accounts.

fete.text: Upon returning from the expedition, the explorers were feted with banquets and parades, though the public soon forgot their achievement.
The village feted its oldest resident on her hundredth birthday, holding a festival in her honor complete with music and speeches.
Although the scientist was feted abroad, receiving honors and lavish receptions, she remained almost unknown in her own country.

fickle.text: Fashion designers must cope with a fickle public whose tastes can shift overnight, making last season's bestselling style suddenly unwanted.
The poet's patrons proved fickle, lavishing support on him one year and abandoning him the next for a more fashionable writer.
Voters in the district are notoriously fickle, switching allegiance so often that no candidate can take their support for granted.

finagle.text: By flattering the clerk and hinting at a nonexistent appointment, Leo managed to finagle a meeting with the director that others had waited weeks to get.
The contractor finagled extra payments from the city by submitting invoices for work that had never actually been done.
Unable to get tickets honestly, the students finagled their way into the sold-out concert by posing as members of the stage crew.

firebrand.text: The young firebrand stirred up the dockworkers with speeches urging them to strike immediately, alarming even the union leaders who shared his goals.
Once a firebrand who delighted in provoking her colleagues, the professor mellowed with age and became a patient mediator in departmental disputes.
The pamphleteer was a born firebrand, writing tracts designed to inflame the public and provoke confrontation with the authorities.

flag.text: By the fourth hour of the negotiation, the delegates' energy had begun to flag, and even the chair struggled to keep her eyes open.
Public interest in the reform flagged once the initial scandal faded from the headlines, and the bill quietly died in committee.
The marathoner's pace never flagged; if anything, she ran the final miles faster than the first ones.

fledgling.text: The fledgling democracy struggled to establish independent courts, since its leaders had no experience governing outside of a dictatorship.
Although the fledgling company had only a handful of employees, its inexperienced founders boldly bid for contracts against established firms.
As a fledgling reporter, Nadia made mistakes that seasoned journalists would have avoided, such as quoting sources without verifying their claims.

fleece.text: The Internet is filled with get-rich-quick schemes that intend only to fleece the Pollyannaish and unsuspecting.
The dishonest mechanic fleeced unsuspecting tourists, charging them for repairs that were never performed on their rental cars.
Investors who trusted the charismatic promoter were fleeced of their savings, discovering the fraud only when the fund suddenly vanished.
Street vendors near the monument were known to fleece visitors, passing off cheap trinkets as rare antiques at extravagant prices.

flippant.text: The minister's flippant reply to questions about the flood, in which he joked that residents needed swimming lessons, provoked outrage across the region.
Although the teacher welcomed humor in class discussion, she objected to flippant remarks during the solemn lesson on wartime refugees.
His tone in the apology was so flippant that the clients concluded he did not take the data breach seriously at all.

flounder.text: Asked an unexpected question about his own data, the graduate student floundered, stammering through half-formed answers until his advisor intervened.
Without clear direction from its new leadership, the once thriving magazine floundered, losing readers and advertisers year after year.
Although Tom excelled at written exams, he floundered in the oral portion, where he struggled to organize his thoughts under pressure.

flummox.text: The puzzle flummoxed even the seasoned mathematicians at the conference, none of whom could explain why the obvious approach failed.
Tourists are often flummoxed by the city's transit map, whose overlapping colored lines seem designed to bewilder rather than guide.
The sudden failure of the experiment flummoxed the researchers, since they had followed the protocol exactly and could find no plausible cause.

flush.text: Flush with profits from a record harvest, the farmers' cooperative invested in new equipment and a larger storage facility.
The newly endowed library was flush with funds, able at last to purchase rare volumes it had long coveted but never afforded.
The region's rivers are flush with salmon every autumn, providing an abundant food source for bears and eagles alike.

flux.text: After the founder's sudden death, the company was in a state of flux, with no clear successor and no agreed strategy.
After the election produced no clear winner, the ministry's economic policy remained in flux for months, as officials hesitated to commit to any plan before learning who would lead them.
Because the rules of the new program are still in flux, applicants cannot be sure which requirements will apply to them.

foible.text: The biography treats its subject with affection, noting his foibles, such as his habit of reading the last page of a novel first, without mocking him.
Every great detective in fiction seems to have some foible, whether a fondness for oddly flavored tea or an insistence on arranging objects symmetrically.
Colleagues tolerated the professor's foibles, including his refusal to use email and his penchant for lecturing in rhyme, because his teaching was superb.

foment.text: Agitators tried to foment unrest among the workers, spreading rumors that the factory would soon close.
The pamphlets were designed to foment rebellion, urging citizens to rise up against the colonial government.
Accused of fomenting discord within the party, the senator insisted that he had merely voiced legitimate concerns.

foolhardy.text: Setting out to climb the peak in winter without a guide or proper gear was foolhardy, and the rescue team was lucky to find the hikers alive.
Although the general admired bold tactics, he considered a frontal assault on the fortified hill foolhardy, likely to waste lives for no gain.
Investing one's entire savings in an untested startup may seem courageous, but most financial advisors would call it foolhardy.

forlorn.text: The forlorn child sat alone at the bus station, having given up hope that anyone would come to collect her.
After the factory closed, the town took on a forlorn appearance, its empty storefronts and silent streets reflecting the residents' despair.
Her letters from the besieged city grew increasingly forlorn, abandoning all talk of rescue and asking only that her family remember her kindly.

forthcoming-adj1.text: The company promised that a full explanation would be forthcoming, but weeks passed without any statement.
Although funding for the project had been approved, the money was slow to be forthcoming, delaying construction for months.
When no help was forthcoming from the government, the villagers organized their own relief efforts.

forthcoming-adj2.text: The witness was unusually forthcoming, volunteering details that the investigators had not even thought to ask about.
Unlike her guarded predecessor, the new spokeswoman was forthcoming with reporters, answering their questions openly and at length.
The biographer found the novelist's family less than forthcoming; they refused to discuss his early life.

forthright.text: Unlike politicians who hedge every statement, the mayor was forthright about the budget crisis, telling residents plainly that services would be cut.
The reviewer's forthright critique was more useful to the author than polite praise, since it told him in the first paragraph that the novel's second half collapses.
Patients appreciate a forthright doctor who explains the diagnosis directly instead of softening it into vague reassurances.

fortuitous.text: The discovery was fortuitous rather than planned: the chemist noticed the new compound only because a contaminated dish happened to be left out over a holiday.
Their meeting was entirely fortuitous: both had missed the same train and ended up sharing a taxi.
A fortuitous change in the weather allowed the climbers to reach the summit just before the storm returned.

fractious.text: The fractious toddler resisted every attempt to calm him, kicking his feet and wailing through the entire flight.
Managing the fractious board was the chairman's hardest task, as its members quarreled constantly and stormed out of meetings in protest.
The horse was so fractious that only the most experienced riders dared mount it, and it threw even them on occasion.

frivolous.text: The judge dismissed the lawsuit as frivolous, noting that it had no legal basis and seemed intended only to harass the defendant.
While his colleagues debated serious policy questions, the young aide made frivolous jokes that irritated everyone in the room.
Although critics dismissed the novel as frivolous, its playful surface concealed a serious meditation on grief.

frugal.text: Though she earned a modest salary, her frugal habits allowed her to save enough to buy a house by the age of thirty.
The frugal family repaired their own furniture, grew their own vegetables and rarely ate at restaurants.
Unlike his extravagant brother, who spent every penny he earned, the younger son was frugal, investing carefully and avoiding debt.

frustrate.text: The senator's allies hoped that a lengthy series of procedural objections would frustrate the bill's passage, delaying the final vote until the session expired.
Repeated equipment failures frustrated the research team's efforts to replicate the experiment, so the promising results remained unconfirmed for another year.
A fragmented permitting process often frustrates architects' plans to build affordable housing quickly, since each additional review adds months of costly delay and some projects never break ground.

furtive.text: Before snatching the fruit, the young monkey cast furtive glances toward the dominant male, as if it hoped to avoid being seen and punished.
Unlike the open deliberations of the council, the negotiations were furtive: envoys met at night in unmarked houses and destroyed their notes before dawn.
Ashamed of his taste in novels, the narrator made furtive trips to the library, always checking that no colleague was nearby before he borrowed a book.

futile.text: The villagers' attempts to hold back the rising river with sandbags proved futile, as the water poured over the barrier within hours.
Recognizing that further negotiation was futile, since neither side would move from its position, the mediator suspended the talks.
Breeders once tried to tame the wild horses for farm work, but the effort was futile; generation after generation remained as unruly as ever.

gaffe.text: At the state dinner, the ambassador committed an embarrassing gaffe, toasting the host country by the name of its historic rival.
The new manager's gaffe of praising the department's former head, who, as everyone else knew, had been dismissed for misconduct, produced an awkward silence.
Etiquette guides for travelers warn of common gaffes, such as refusing food offered by a host or pointing with a single finger, that can offend local customs.

gainsay.text: The data from three independent laboratories were so consistent that even the theory's harshest critics could not gainsay the central finding.
No one at the meeting dared to gainsay the founder, since contradicting her in public had ended more than one promising career at the firm.
Although the historian's conclusions are open to debate, one can hardly gainsay the thoroughness of her research, which draws on hundreds of unpublished letters.

gall-n1.text: After missing every deadline that semester, the student had the gall to ask the professor for an extension on the final paper as well.
Critics were astonished by the gall of the young playwright, who, after one modest success, publicly lectured veteran directors on how to stage his work.
It takes considerable gall for a company recently fined for polluting the river to advertise itself as a champion of environmental stewardship.

gall-n2.text: Decades after the disputed inheritance divided the family, the brothers still felt nothing but gall toward one another, refusing even to attend the same funerals.
The memoir is steeped in gall: never having forgiven the colleagues who took credit for her discovery, the author revisits each slight with undiminished resentment.
Rather than reconciling after the bitter election, the defeated faction nursed its gall for years, obstructing every initiative the victors proposed out of sheer rancor.

galvanize.text: The colonel's speech galvanized the troops, who had all but given up.
The report's stark photographs of the polluted harbor galvanized a previously apathetic public, and within weeks thousands of residents had joined the cleanup effort.
The coach hoped that a rousing halftime speech would galvanize her demoralized players into mounting a comeback in the second half.
Although the scientific community had long neglected the disease, a single outbreak in a major city galvanized researchers, who soon launched dozens of new studies.

gambit.text: Her opening gambit in the negotiation, a generous concession on price, was calculated to make the supplier more flexible on delivery terms.
The lawyer's gambit of calling the defendant's own mother as a witness was risky, but it ultimately won the jury's sympathy.
Sensing that his rival was nervous, the chess player sacrificed a pawn in an audacious gambit, betting that the resulting attack would outweigh the lost material.

garrulous.text: The documentary's garrulous narrator filled every silence with trivial asides about his lunch and the weather, so viewers often lost track of the actual subject.
Whereas her reserved sister rarely spoke at dinner, Elena was garrulous, chattering about neighbors, recipes, and television plots until the dessert was cleared.
Long flights can be exhausting when one is seated beside a garrulous passenger who insists on narrating every minor detail of his vacation photographs.

gauche.text: At the formal embassy dinner, the young attache made the gauche mistake of asking the host about his salary, a lapse that embarrassed everyone at the table.
Though brilliant in the laboratory, the physicist was notoriously gauche at receptions, where he interrupted conversations and forgot to introduce his own guests.
Etiquette manuals of the period warned that it was gauche to mention the price of a gift, since polite society regarded such talk as a mark of poor breeding.

genial.text: The host's genial manner, warm, relaxed and generous with compliments, quickly put the nervous guests at ease.
Grapes flourish in the valley's genial climate, where mild winters and gentle breezes allow them to ripen slowly.
Although the negotiations had been tense, the genial atmosphere of the closing dinner allowed the delegates to relax and even joke together.

genteel.text: The novel satirizes a genteel family that prides itself on elegant manners and fine china while quietly sinking into debt.
The tea room retained a genteel air, with lace tablecloths, silver pots and patrons who spoke in hushed, refined voices.
Raised in a genteel household where table manners were strictly observed, Clara was startled by the boisterous customs of the rural boarding school.

germane.text: The committee chair repeatedly steered the discussion back to the budget, reminding members that anecdotes about past conferences were not germane to the vote.
In a strong essay, every example should be germane to the thesis; a digression, however vivid, only distracts the reader from the argument.
The judge excluded testimony about the defendant's childhood, ruling that events from four decades earlier were not germane to a contract dispute that began last spring.

gerrymander.text: By drawing the district as a narrow, winding strip that captured only friendly neighborhoods, the legislature gerrymandered the map to protect incumbents.
Reformers proposed an independent commission to redraw boundaries, arguing that lawmakers could not be trusted not to gerrymander seats in their own party's favor.
The court struck down the plan because it was clearly gerrymandered: districts snaked across the state to dilute the votes of one party's supporters.

glean.text: From scattered references in merchants' letters, historians have gleaned a surprisingly detailed picture of daily life in the port.
The reporter gleaned the outlines of the deal bit by bit, piecing together remarks from several officials who refused to speak on the record.
Although the manual was poorly written, the technician gleaned enough from its diagrams and footnotes to repair the machine.

glib.text: The candidate's glib answers impressed the audience at first, but his polished phrases seemed hollow once reporters asked about specifics.
Rather than a glib apology crafted by the public relations team, the victims wanted a sincere acknowledgment of the harm done.
The salesman was glib, able to talk smoothly about any product, yet customers sensed he believed none of what he said.

glut-n.text: A glut of new apartments in the city center forced landlords to offer months of free rent, since there were far more units than tenants.
Economists warned that the bumper harvest would create a glut of wheat, driving prices so low that many farmers would lose money on every bushel.
Rather than suffering from a shortage of information, today's researchers face a glut: thousands of papers appear each week, far more than anyone could read.

glut-v.text: Aggressive planting across the region glutted the market with avocados, and by summer growers were leaving fruit to rot on the trees.
When several studios release blockbusters in the same month, they glut the theaters, and even well-reviewed films struggle to find an audience.
Cheap imports threatened to glut the domestic steel market, so the ministry imposed temporary quotas to keep supply in line with demand.

goad.text: Opponents goaded the young boxer with insults, hoping to provoke him into a reckless attack that would leave him exposed.
Tired of her brother's teasing that she would never finish a marathon, Rosa was finally goaded into signing up for one.
The columnist deliberately goaded his readers with provocative jabs, knowing that indignant letters would boost the paper's circulation.

gossamer.text: The designer's gown was made of a gossamer silk so fine that it seemed to float around the model rather than hang from her shoulders.
Early morning light revealed gossamer threads strung between the hedges, each so delicate that a single breath could have broken it.
Critics praised the pianist's gossamer touch in the nocturne, noting that even the fastest passages sounded weightless rather than heavy or forced.

graft.text: The new mayor promised to root out graft in the building department, where inspectors had long accepted cash to overlook safety violations.
Because contracts were awarded to whoever paid the largest kickback, graft rather than merit determined which firms built the city's roads.
The historian argues that graft was so pervasive in the colonial administration that officials viewed bribes as an ordinary supplement to their salaries.

grandiloquent.text: The mayor's grandiloquent speech, full of references to destiny and glory, seemed absurdly inflated for the opening of a municipal parking garage.
Readers found the memoir grandiloquent, as the author described his modest business career in the lofty rhetoric usually reserved for great conquerors.
Unlike her grandiloquent predecessor, who delivered every announcement as though addressing posterity, the new principal spoke plainly and briefly.

gregarious.text: Unlike the solitary leopard, the lion is a gregarious animal, living and hunting in prides that may include more than a dozen members.
Although he was gregarious at parties, moving easily from one circle of guests to the next, the novelist insisted on complete solitude when he wrote.
The firm deliberately hired gregarious salespeople, reasoning that those who enjoyed meeting strangers would thrive in a role built on constant networking.

grovel.text: After the disastrous launch, the executive groveled before the shareholders, apologizing profusely and begging them not to sell their stock.
Trembling before the throne, the courtier groveled at the emperor's feet, pleading for mercy after his plot was discovered.
Rather than grovel for a raise, Nora calmly presented evidence of her contributions and let her record speak for itself.

guffaw.text: When the comedian mimicked the pompous professor, the audience guffawed so loudly that the next line was drowned out entirely.
Unlike his sister, who merely smiled at the joke, Sam guffawed, slapping the table and roaring until tears filled his eyes.
The solemn ceremony was interrupted when a guest guffawed at the officiant's slip of the tongue, his booming laughter echoing through the hall.

guileless.text: The swindler never recruited guileless villagers as accomplices, since their candid faces and inability to tell even a small lie would have betrayed his scheme at once.
Her testimony was so guileless, full of admissions that damaged her own case, that the jury concluded she could not possibly be lying.
The child's guileless answer, offered without any attempt to hide the broken vase, disarmed parents who had braced themselves for an elaborate excuse.

gumption.text: It took real gumption for the young baker to open a shop across the street from the town's most beloved bakery, but her ingenuity and persistence paid off.
Stranded when their bus broke down, the students showed gumption, arranging rides with local farmers and reaching the conference only an hour late.
The founder lacked capital and connections, but she had gumption: she taught herself accounting, pitched to dozens of investors and refused to quit after each rejection.

hackneyed.text: The screenwriter's first draft relied on hackneyed devices, such as the amnesiac hero and the villain who explains his plan, that audiences had seen countless times.
Although the speech was meant to inspire, its hackneyed phrases about thinking outside the box and reaching for the stars left the graduates yawning.
Once fresh and startling, the metaphor of the city as a jungle has become hackneyed through endless repetition in newspaper columns.

hagiographic.text: The authorized biography is frankly hagiographic, omitting every scandal and presenting the industrialist as a flawless benefactor.
Scholars have grown wary of hagiographic accounts of the explorer, which celebrate his courage while ignoring his brutal treatment of the people he encountered.
The documentary avoids a hagiographic tone; although it admires the conductor's genius, it also records his tyrannical treatment of musicians.

hail.text: Critics hailed the young architect's library as a masterpiece, praising its luminous reading rooms and its graceful integration with the surrounding park.
Although the treaty was hailed as a triumph when it was signed, within a decade most historians regarded it as a costly failure.
Researchers hail the new vaccine as a breakthrough, citing trial results far better than any previous candidate had achieved.

halcyon.text: Retirees in the village often reminisce about the halcyon summers of their youth, when the lake was clear and days passed in unhurried calm.
The decade after the civil war proved a halcyon interval for the republic, marked by steady trade, peaceful elections and growing prosperity.
The novel opens in a halcyon setting, a sunlit estate where nothing disturbs the family's tranquility, only to shatter that peace in the second chapter.

hamper.text: Heavy snowfall hampered rescue efforts for days, blocking mountain roads and preventing helicopters from reaching the stranded villagers.
A lack of reliable data has hampered attempts to measure the policy's effects, leaving economists to rely on rough estimates.
Her progress in learning the cello was hampered by an old wrist injury that made long practice sessions painful.

hamstrung.text: Hamstrung by a tiny budget and a shortage of staff, the agency could do little to enforce the environmental rules it was charged with upholding.
The coalition government was hamstrung by internal disagreements, unable to pass even routine legislation for most of its term.
Although the new principal had bold plans, she was hamstrung by district regulations that left her almost no authority to act.

haphazard.text: The museum's early collection was assembled in haphazard fashion, with curators buying whatever happened to be for sale rather than following any coherent plan.
Because the files had been stored in such a haphazard manner, the auditors spent weeks locating receipts that should have taken minutes to find.
Critics argue that the city's haphazard development, with factories beside schools and highways cutting through parks, reflects decades without any zoning.

harangue-n.text: The chairman's harangue lasted nearly an hour, and by the time he finished berating the staff for low sales, several employees had quietly left the room.
Instead of a reasoned rebuttal, the candidate delivered a harangue, shouting accusations at his opponent while the moderator tried in vain to intervene.
The pamphlet reads less like a scholarly analysis than a harangue: page after page denounces modern architecture in increasingly overheated language.

harangue-v.text: Every morning the foreman would harangue the crew for twenty minutes about safety lapses, although most of the workers had heard the same lecture hundreds of times.
Rather than persuading the undecided delegates, the speaker harangued them at such length that many walked out before the vote.
Frustrated by the slow pace of reform, the activist stood on the courthouse steps haranguing passersby about corruption until the police asked him to move.

harried.text: The harried receptionist, fielding a dozen calls while patients lined up with minor complaints, barely had time to glance at her own lunch.
Constantly interrupted by small requests from every department, the harried office manager began to dread the sound of his telephone.
Parents of toddlers often look harried by late afternoon, having spent the day refereeing squabbles, fetching snacks, and cleaning up spills.

haughty.text: The haughty curator refused even to look at the amateur's paintings, remarking that he did not waste his time on people without formal training.
Although she had been raised in great wealth, the heiress was never haughty; she treated the household staff as equals and remembered each of their birthdays.
The diplomat's haughty tone, which implied that the smaller nation's concerns were beneath his notice, doomed the negotiations from the start.

hauteur.text: The duchess received the petitioners with icy hauteur, barely glancing at them and addressing her replies to her secretary instead.
Although the new partner was talented, his hauteur toward junior associates, whom he treated as beneath his notice, soon made him unpopular.
The waiter's hauteur, evident in his disdainful glance at diners who mispronounced the wine list, spoiled an otherwise excellent meal.

hector.text: The coach hectored his players from the sidelines, shouting insults and threats until several of them refused to return for the next season.
Rather than persuade the committee, the lobbyist tried to hector its members, warning that he would ruin the career of anyone who voted against his client.
Witnesses complained that the prosecutor had hectored them during questioning, raising his voice and badgering them until they contradicted themselves.

hedge.text: Asked whether the drug was safe for children, the researcher hedged, noting that the data were limited and that further trials might change the picture.
Good scientific writing avoids overstatement, but some authors hedge so heavily, with 'perhaps' and 'possibly' in every clause, that readers cannot tell what they actually believe.
Instead of giving a clear forecast, the economist hedged her prediction, saying growth could rise or fall depending on factors no one could yet measure.

hegemony.text: For centuries the empire's naval hegemony allowed it to dictate trade terms to its neighbors, none of whom could challenge its fleets.
Some cultural critics worry about the hegemony of a few streaming platforms, which now largely decide what audiences around the world watch.
Although the party had enjoyed decades of unchallenged hegemony in the region, a series of scandals finally allowed rival groups to win power.

heretic.text: In a department devoted to classical economics, the young scholar was regarded as a heretic because she argued that markets rarely correct themselves.
Chefs who once dismissed him as a heretic for serving dessert first now imitate his menus, which have become the new orthodoxy.
The physician was treated as a heretic by his colleagues when he insisted that surgeons wash their hands, an idea that contradicted the accepted medical wisdom of his day.

heyday.text: In its heyday, the resort town drew visitors from across the continent, but its grand hotels now stand mostly empty.
The critic argues that the novelist's heyday came early; after the triumph of her second book, her work never again reached such heights.
During the heyday of the silk trade, the city's markets overflowed with merchants, and its wealth funded palaces that still dominate the skyline.

histrionic.text: The lawyer's histrionic closing argument, complete with tears and a dramatic collapse into his chair, struck the judge as more theater than reasoning.
Although the novel's heroine faces real hardship, her histrionic reactions, fainting at bad news and declaiming her woes to strangers, undercut the reader's sympathy.
Unlike her histrionic co-star, who wept and shouted in every scene, the veteran actress conveyed grief through restrained, almost imperceptible gestures.

hoary.text: The professor dismissed the argument as a hoary cliche, one that had been repeated in textbooks for so many generations that no one questioned it anymore.
At the center of the village stands a hoary oak, so old that local legend claims it sheltered travelers long before the church was built.
The comedian's routine relied on hoary jokes about mothers-in-law and bad cooking that had been old even in his grandfather's day.

hobble.text: Chronic underfunding has hobbled the city's transit system, leaving it unable to replace aging trains or extend service to growing suburbs.
The reform was hobbled from the start by a clause requiring unanimous approval, so that a single objection could block any change.
Investors worried that the lawsuit would hobble the startup's expansion, tying up its funds and distracting its leaders for years.

hodgepodge.text: The museum's early collection was a hodgepodge of fossils, coins, stuffed birds and folk costumes, assembled without any organizing principle.
Critics dismissed the bill as a hodgepodge of unrelated provisions, lumping farm subsidies, tax breaks and highway funding into a single confusing package.
The town's architecture is a hodgepodge, with medieval cottages jostling against glass office towers and a mock Tudor supermarket.

hoodwink.text: The swindler hoodwinked dozens of retirees into investing in a nonexistent gold mine, supplying them with forged reports of rich deposits.
Although the forger's painting hoodwinked several experts, a chemical analysis revealed pigments that had not existed in the artist's lifetime.
Voters resent being hoodwinked, and the candidate's lead vanished once it emerged that his celebrated tax plan contained hidden fees.

hound.text: Creditors hounded the failed merchant for years, sending agents to his door and following him from one city to the next.
Because photographers hounded the actress for months after the trial, she finally left the city and moved to a farm where no stranger could approach unseen.
The inspector hounded the suspect with repeated interviews and constant surveillance, refusing to relent until he confessed.

hubris.text: The engineer's hubris proved disastrous: convinced that his design could not fail, he dismissed the warnings of colleagues who had spotted a flaw in the supports.
In Greek tragedy, a hero's hubris typically invites ruin, as when a mortal presumes to rival the gods and is punished for his arrogance.
The company's hubris after a decade of success led it to ignore smaller competitors, whose cheaper products eventually captured most of its market.

humdrum.text: After years of daring fieldwork abroad, the anthropologist found her humdrum office routine of meetings and paperwork almost unbearable.
The critics agreed that the first act was humdrum, with little happening beyond polite small talk, though the second act finally sparked to life.
Rather than a humdrum lecture recited from notes, the professor's talk was full of surprising demonstrations that kept students riveted.

iconoclast.text: An iconoclast by temperament, the philosopher delighted in attacking the most revered doctrines of her discipline, including those her own teachers had championed.
The architect was hailed as an iconoclast for rejecting the ornate traditions that the city's elite considered sacred, building stark concrete towers instead.
Though he began his career as a reverent student of the national epic, the critic became an iconoclast, arguing that its heroes were petty tyrants unworthy of veneration.

iconoclastic.text: The composer's iconoclastic symphony abandoned melody altogether, an affront to audiences who expected the lush romantic style of his predecessors.
Far from conventional, the chef's iconoclastic menu paired ice cream with anchovies and served the courses in reverse order.
The magazine built its reputation on iconoclastic essays that mocked cherished national myths rather than repeating them.

idiosyncrasy.text: One idiosyncrasy of the novelist was that he wrote standing at a tall lectern, a habit that none of his contemporaries shared.
Good biographers resist the temptation to catalog every idiosyncrasy of their subjects, such as a fondness for green ink, unless those quirks illuminate character.
The new manager learned to accommodate each employee's idiosyncrasies: one needed total silence, another worked only after midnight, and a third refused to use email.

ignoble.text: Although the general was celebrated as a hero, historians later uncovered the ignoble truth that he had abandoned his wounded soldiers to save himself.
The board rejected the proposal to profit from the disaster, calling it an ignoble scheme unworthy of an organization founded to help victims.
Rather than conceding defeat gracefully, the chess champion accused his opponent of cheating without any evidence, an ignoble end to a distinguished career.

ignominious.text: After promising voters a sweeping victory, the party suffered an ignominious defeat, losing even the districts it had held for generations.
The once admired financier met an ignominious end: convicted of fraud, he was stripped of his honors and shunned by his former friends.
The expedition's ignominious retreat, with soldiers abandoning their supplies and fleeing in panic, became a lasting source of national embarrassment.

illicit.text: Customs officers uncovered an illicit trade in rare orchids, smuggled across the border without the permits required by law.
Although the tavern appeared to sell only coffee, it housed an illicit gambling operation in its cellar, well hidden from the authorities.
The ban did not end consumption of the drug; it merely drove it into illicit markets where quality was uncontrolled and sellers ignored the law.

illustrious.text: The conservatory boasts an illustrious roster of alumni, including celebrated conductors, soloists and composers whose names are familiar worldwide.
Although she came from an illustrious family of statesmen, the young lawyer preferred to earn her own reputation rather than trade on her ancestors' renown.
The scientist's illustrious career, crowned by numerous prizes and honorary degrees, began modestly in a cramped basement laboratory.

imbibe.text: Children imbibe the prejudices of their surroundings long before they can articulate them, absorbing attitudes from overheard conversations and casual remarks.
Travelers crossing the desert were warned to imbibe water regularly, even when they did not feel thirsty, since dehydration can set in without warning.
The plant's roots imbibe moisture from the soil so efficiently that it can survive for months without rain.

imbroglio.text: What began as a minor dispute over a parking space escalated into a neighborhood imbroglio, involving lawyers, the city council and an embarrassing story in the local paper.
The ambassador spent weeks trying to extricate his government from the diplomatic imbroglio caused by a misdirected letter that insulted an allied leader.
The museum's board found itself in an awkward imbroglio when it emerged that a donated painting had been stolen and that two trustees had known of its origin.

immaterial.text: Whether the painting was completed on a Tuesday or a Wednesday is immaterial; what matters is that the artist was in Rome when she painted it.
The candidate's height is immaterial to the job, since the position involves analyzing data rather than performing any physical task.
Although the lawyer raised the defendant's past hobbies, the judge ruled the information immaterial, bearing no relation to the fraud at issue.

immure.text: In the gothic novel, a jealous baron immures his wife in a tower, sealing the only door with stone so that she can never leave.
Preferring solitude, the scholar immured herself in the library for months, emerging only for meals and rarely speaking to anyone.
Some medieval hermits chose to be immured in small cells built against the church wall, receiving food through a narrow window for the rest of their lives.

immutable.text: Early chemists believed that the elements were immutable, so the discovery that one element could transform into another overturned a basic assumption of their science.
Although the club's founders treated the bylaws as immutable, later members amended nearly every rule within a decade.
For the ancient philosophers, the heavens represented an immutable order, in contrast to the constant decay and change they observed on Earth.

impartial.text: Because both teams distrusted the local referees, the league appointed an impartial official from another country to oversee the final match.
A good judge must remain impartial, setting aside personal sympathies so that each side receives an equal hearing.
The researchers hired an outside firm to analyze the data, hoping that an impartial review would dispel suspicions that the drug's makers had skewed the results.

impeccable.text: The pianist's technique was impeccable, yet some critics found her playing emotionally cold, as if she cared more about hitting every note than about the music's meaning.
With his impeccable record of honesty over three decades in office, the treasurer was the last person anyone suspected of embezzlement.
Her manners were impeccable: she remembered every guest's name, wrote thank-you notes promptly and never once interrupted anyone.

impecunious.text: The impecunious graduate student lived on rice and borrowed textbooks, unable to afford even the modest fee to attend the conference.
Although he died impecunious, leaving his widow nothing but debts, the painter's canvases now sell for fortunes at auction.
Many of the city's greatest benefactors had once been impecunious immigrants who arrived with empty pockets and worked their way to wealth.

impede.text: Dense undergrowth impeded the explorers' progress, forcing them to hack a path through the jungle a few meters at a time.
Critics warned that excessive regulation might impede innovation, discouraging small firms with limited legal budgets from developing new products.
Scar tissue can impede the flow of blood, which is why surgeons try to minimize damage to the surrounding vessels.

impending.text: Aware of the impending storm, the fishermen hauled their boats onto the beach and secured their nets before the first winds arrived.
Anxious about her impending retirement, the professor began donating her books and wondering how she would fill her days.
Economists warned of an impending recession, pointing to falling orders and rising unemployment as signs that a downturn was near.

imperious.text: The imperious director demanded that the entire cast wait in silence until she arrived, and she never once thanked anyone for their work.
With an imperious wave of his hand, the landlord dismissed the tenants' complaints as unworthy of his attention and ordered them out of his office.
Although the professor was brilliant, his imperious manner toward students, whom he treated as servants summoned to hear his pronouncements, alienated many of them.

impermeable.text: Because clay is nearly impermeable, rainwater pools on its surface rather than soaking into the ground below.
The explorers wrapped their maps in an impermeable oilcloth that kept them dry even as the canoe was swamped.
Engineers lined the landfill with an impermeable membrane so that contaminated liquids could not seep into the groundwater.

impertinent.text: The intern's impertinent remark about the director's outdated methods, delivered during her first week, stunned the senior staff into silence.
Victorian children were expected to be seen and not heard, so a child who questioned an adult's authority was scolded for being impertinent.
The reporter's impertinent questions about the host's income and marriage, asked loudly in front of his guests, embarrassed everyone at the gala.

impervious.text: The new coating renders the fabric impervious to water, so that rain beads on its surface and rolls away without soaking through.
The senator seemed impervious to criticism; no matter how fiercely editorials condemned him, he never altered a single position.
Because the clay layer is impervious, groundwater collects above it rather than seeping down into the deeper rock.

impetuous.text: The impetuous investor sold all her shares the moment the market dipped, without consulting her advisers or waiting to learn the cause of the decline.
Unlike his impetuous younger brother, who proposed marriage after a week, Daniel deliberated for years before making any important decision.
The general's impetuous charge, launched before scouts had returned with information about the terrain, led his cavalry straight into a marsh.

implacable.text: Despite repeated apologies and offers of compensation, the offended landowner remained implacable, vowing to pursue the lawsuit to the highest court.
The two clans were implacable enemies whose hatred no treaty, gift, or marriage between their families could ever soften.
Negotiators hoped that generous concessions would soothe the union, but its leaders proved implacable, rejecting every offer as an insult.

implausible.text: The defendant's alibi, that he had been sleepwalking across town at the time of the robbery, struck the jury as wholly implausible.
While the novel's premise is implausible, the author renders her characters so vividly that readers willingly suspend their disbelief.
Physicists dismissed the inventor's claim of a perpetual motion machine as implausible, since such a device would violate the basic laws of thermodynamics.

implicate-v1.text: The pattern of the ruins implicates a gradual abandonment rather than a sudden catastrophe, since the inhabitants appear to have removed their valuables before leaving.
Although the report never states it outright, its careful wording implicates that the delays were foreseeable, a conclusion few readers could miss.
The recurring image of locked doors implicates a theme of isolation that runs through the entire novel, even though the narrator never names it.

implicate-v2.text: The accountant's testimony implicated the firm's director in the fraud, revealing that he had personally approved the falsified statements.
Although the burglar confessed, he refused to implicate his accomplices, insisting that he had acted entirely alone.
Forensic evidence found at the scene implicated the gardener, whose fingerprints appeared on the forced window latch.

imponderable.text: The planners could estimate construction costs, but the long-term effects of the new highway on the region's culture remained imponderable.
Philosophers have long wrestled with imponderable questions, such as why anything exists at all, that seem to resist any definitive answer.
Because the success of a debut novel depends on imponderable factors like timing and public mood, publishers cannot reliably predict which books will sell.

importuned.text: The street vendors importuned every tourist who passed, following them for blocks and pleading with them to buy just one more trinket.
For months the charity importuned the foundation for a grant, submitting letter after letter until the directors finally agreed to meet.
Tired of being importuned by relatives seeking loans, the lottery winner changed her phone number and moved to another city.

impregnable.text: Built on a sheer rock outcrop and ringed by triple walls, the fortress was considered impregnable, and no army ever managed to breach it.
