The company's encryption was once thought impregnable, but a team of researchers eventually found a flaw that allowed them to break in.
Her reputation seemed impregnable; decades of scrupulous scholarship had made it proof against the attacks of even her fiercest rivals.

improvident.text: The improvident decision to build the stadium on a floodplain, made without any environmental study, cost the city millions when the river rose.
Economists blamed the crisis on improvident lending, as banks had extended credit to borrowers without examining whether they could ever repay.
Having spent his entire inheritance in a single year, the improvident heir had nothing left when the harvest failed and his creditors called in their debts.

imprudent.text: It would be imprudent to invest one's entire savings in a single untested company, however persuasive its founders may seem.
The mountaineers made the imprudent decision to continue toward the summit despite the gathering storm, and they barely made it back to camp alive.
Critics called the city's decision to build on the floodplain imprudent, noting that the area had flooded repeatedly within living memory.

impudent.text: The impudent apprentice corrected the master carpenter in front of a client, a breach of workshop etiquette that nearly cost him his position.
When the teacher asked the class to be quiet, one impudent student replied that he would talk whenever he pleased.
Far from being grateful for the scholarship, the young man made the impudent demand that the committee also pay for his travel and lodging.

impugn.text: The defense attorney tried to impugn the witness's credibility by pointing out inconsistencies between her testimony and her earlier statements to police.
Critics impugned the study's conclusions, arguing that its small sample and flawed controls made its findings unreliable.
Rather than engaging with her argument, her opponents chose to impugn her motives, claiming she was secretly funded by the industry she criticized.

impute.text: The inquiry imputed the collapse to faulty welding rather than to the design itself, clearing the architects of blame.
It is unfair to impute malice to a colleague whose mistake was plainly the result of inexperience rather than ill will.
Historians once imputed the empire's fall entirely to moral decay, but newer research emphasizes drought, disease and economic strain.

inadvertent.text: The spill was inadvertent, caused by a worker who misread a gauge, but it still contaminated miles of the river.
The novelist's inadvertent revelation of the ending during an interview dismayed her publisher, who had carefully kept it secret.
Rather than a calculated snub, his omission of her name from the acknowledgments was inadvertent, the result of a hasty final edit.

inanity.text: The talk show's inanity was relentless: for an hour, the hosts traded empty chatter about nothing in particular while serious news went unmentioned.
After reading dozens of applications filled with vague slogans, the committee was relieved to find one essay that rose above the inanity with a genuine argument.
The satirist mocked the inanity of corporate jargon, quoting memos so full of meaningless buzzwords that they conveyed no information whatsoever.

inarticulate.text: Overcome with grief at the funeral, the normally eloquent senator was inarticulate, able only to nod at mourners who offered condolences.
The toddler's inarticulate cries grew louder as she pointed at the shelf, since she lacked the words to say which toy she wanted.
Although his paintings convey profound emotion, the artist was nearly inarticulate in interviews, groping for words and falling silent in the middle of sentences.

incense.text: The proposal to demolish the historic library incensed residents, who packed the council meeting and shouted down the mayor.
The reviewer's dismissive remarks about her life's work so incensed the elderly composer that she wrote a furious rebuttal to the newspaper.
Workers were incensed to learn that executives had awarded themselves bonuses while freezing everyone else's wages.

incessant.text: The incessant hammering from the construction site next door, which continued from dawn until dusk every day, made it impossible for the writer to concentrate.
Villagers grew weary of the incessant rain, which had fallen without a break for three weeks and turned every road to mud.
Her incessant chatter, which did not pause once during the entire three-hour journey, left her fellow passengers longing for silence.

inchoate.text: The student's thesis was still inchoate; she had a promising intuition but had not yet shaped it into a coherent argument.
The protest movement remained inchoate for months, a loose collection of grievances without leaders, demands or a clear strategy.
In the composer's sketchbooks one can see the symphony's inchoate themes, rough fragments that would later be developed into its soaring melodies.

incisive.text: The critic's incisive review distinguished between the novel's genuine innovations and its merely fashionable gimmicks, a distinction other reviewers had missed.
Although the debate was long and muddled, the moderator's incisive questions cut straight to the key differences between the two proposals.
Her incisive analysis of the survey data revealed that what appeared to be a single trend was actually two separate patterns affecting different age groups.

inclement-adj1.text: Inclement weather forced the organizers to move the outdoor concert into the gymnasium, as heavy rain and gusting winds battered the park.
Sailors in the region learned to watch the sky for signs of inclement conditions, since sudden squalls could capsize small boats.
Because of the inclement winter, with blizzards arriving week after week, construction of the bridge fell months behind schedule.

inclement-adj2.text: Debtors who came before the inclement magistrate knew that pleading poverty was useless, since he sentenced even those who owed trifling sums to long terms in prison.
Unlike his forgiving father, the young king proved inclement toward rebels, refusing every plea for pardon and punishing entire villages for the acts of a few.
Students dreaded the inclement headmaster, who punished the slightest infraction severely and never once granted a reprieve.

incongruous.text: The modern glass tower looks incongruous among the medieval churches of the old town, clashing with their weathered stone facades.
It seemed incongruous that a festival celebrating local farmers would be sponsored by a corporation that had bought up most of their land.
The comedian relies on incongruous pairings, such as a solemn funeral march played on a kazoo, to provoke laughter from his audience.

incontrovertible.text: The DNA results provided incontrovertible proof that the man had been wrongly convicted, and he was released within the week.
Although some still dispute the details, the core finding is incontrovertible: every independent laboratory that repeated the experiment obtained the same result.
The auditor presented incontrovertible evidence of the fraud, including signed invoices and bank records that no explanation could reconcile with the company's claims.

incorrigible.text: Despite detentions, suspensions, and countless meetings with his parents, the boy remained incorrigible, returning to his pranks the moment each punishment ended.
An incorrigible gambler, the count lost the family estate even after his creditors had twice seized his property and barred him from the casino.
Prison reformers argued that few offenders are truly incorrigible; given education rather than ever harsher penalties, most could be rehabilitated.

incumbent.text: Because Dr. Reyes was the senior physician on duty, it was incumbent on her to inform the family of the diagnosis, however painful the conversation.
Scholars who publish controversial claims should recognize that it is incumbent upon them to share their data, so that others can verify the results.
Once the city accepted the grant, it became incumbent on officials to report precisely how every dollar had been spent, a duty they could not ignore.

indecorous.text: At the solemn memorial service, the guest's loud laughter and ringing phone struck the mourners as deeply indecorous.
Under the rigid court etiquette of the era, it was considered indecorous for a courtier to turn his back on the king, however briefly.
The senator apologized for his indecorous remarks, conceding that insulting a colleague's family on the chamber floor violated the norms of legislative debate.

indict.text: After a lengthy investigation, the grand jury indicted the former treasurer on charges of embezzlement and filing false reports.
Prosecutors lacked sufficient evidence to indict the executive, so although suspicion lingered, he was never formally charged.
Because the statute of limitations had expired, the state could no longer indict the retired official, even though fresh evidence of his bribery had surfaced.

indifference.text: The scientist was dismayed by the public's indifference to her findings; despite the alarming data, few people bothered even to read the report.
Although the novel's hero professes indifference to wealth, he spends most of the story scheming to marry an heiress.
Teachers often find apathy harder to address than hostility, since a student's indifference offers no strong feeling that might be redirected toward learning.

indigenous.text: The botanist catalogued plants indigenous to the valley, distinguishing them from species introduced by settlers in later centuries.
Rather than importing foreign stone, the architect built the museum from indigenous materials, using timber and slate quarried within a few miles.
Many indigenous languages of the region, spoken there long before colonization, now survive only among a few elderly speakers.

indigent-adj.text: The clinic provides free care to indigent patients, many of whom cannot afford even the bus fare to reach a hospital.
Born to indigent parents who often lacked money for food, the novelist later wrote vividly about childhood hunger.
The law guarantees that indigent defendants, who cannot pay for their own lawyers, will be represented by counsel at public expense.

indigent-n.text: The charity's founders devoted their fortune to feeding indigents, opening soup kitchens in every district where poverty was most severe.
Under the old poor laws, an indigent could be sent to the workhouse, where food and shelter were provided in exchange for grueling labor.
The hospital's charter required it to treat any indigent who arrived at its doors, regardless of whether the patient could pay.

indignant.text: The scientist was indignant when a rival claimed credit for her discovery, and she promptly published her dated notebooks to prove her priority.
Customers grew indignant after learning that the airline had overbooked the flight and bumped them without compensation.
Far from accepting the unfair penalty quietly, the indignant player protested to the referee that he had never touched his opponent.

industrious.text: The industrious apprentice rose before dawn each day, finishing her chores and practicing her craft long after the others had gone to bed.
Unlike her easygoing brother, Anna was industrious, turning the neglected family farm into a thriving business through years of relentless work.
Historians credit the town's prosperity to its industrious artisans, who labored tirelessly to produce textiles admired across the region.

ineffable.text: Mystics across many traditions describe an ineffable experience of union with the divine, and their writings are full of apologies for the inadequacy of the words they must use.
The mountaineer tried to convey the view from the summit, but finally admitted that its beauty was ineffable and that photographs did it no justice.
Some names were considered too holy to speak aloud, so worshippers substituted a title for the ineffable word whenever they prayed.

ineluctable.text: The tragedy's power lies in its sense of ineluctable fate: from the first scene, the audience knows the hero cannot escape his doom.
Many economists regard some degree of automation as ineluctable, arguing that no policy can halt it and that societies should plan for its consequences.
Though the climbers tried every route, the storm made retreat ineluctable, and they descended without reaching the summit.

inequity.text: The report documented a glaring inequity in school funding: districts in wealthy suburbs spent twice as much per student as those in poorer towns.
Workers protested the inequity of a pay system in which newcomers doing identical jobs earned far less than their longer-serving colleagues.
Reformers argued that the tax code's many loopholes created inequities, allowing some to pay almost nothing while others with similar incomes paid in full.

inexorable.text: The glacier's inexorable advance, though only a few centimeters a day, eventually buried the entire village despite every effort to divert it.
Many historians reject the idea that the empire's decline was inexorable, arguing that wiser leaders could have averted collapse.
Like the tide, the aging process is inexorable; cosmetics and surgery may disguise its effects, but nothing can halt it.

infelicitous.text: The speaker's infelicitous choice of a joke about illness at a hospital fundraiser drew uncomfortable silence rather than laughter.
The translation is accurate but often infelicitous, rendering the poet's graceful lines in awkward phrasing that jars the ear.
'Exciting opportunity' was an infelicitous way to describe the layoffs, and the chief executive later apologized for the insensitivity of the phrase.

inflammable.text: The editor refused to print the letter, judging its inflammable accusations likely to provoke riots in an already tense city.
Moderators quickly removed the inflammable post, whose insults toward a minority group had already sparked furious arguments in the forum.
Diplomats avoided the inflammable subject of the disputed border, fearing that even mentioning it might derail the fragile negotiations.

ingenuity.text: With no spare parts available, the stranded crew relied on sheer ingenuity, fashioning a working filter from socks, charcoal and a plastic bottle.
The museum celebrates the ingenuity of medieval engineers, whose inventive use of pulleys and counterweights allowed them to raise enormous stones.
Faced with a tiny budget, the set designer displayed remarkable ingenuity, transforming cardboard and old curtains into a convincing palace.

ingenuous.text: The ingenuous young clerk believed every promise the salesman made, never suspecting that the bargain was a trap.
Critics found the film's heroine too ingenuous to be credible: after years in the political capital, she still trusts every smiling official she meets.
His ingenuous question about why the adults were whispering revealed that the child had no idea his parents were separating.

ingratiate.text: Hoping to ingratiate himself with the new director, the junior curator praised her every decision and volunteered for the tasks nobody else wanted.
The ambassador ingratiated herself with the local elite by learning their dialect and hosting lavish dinners in their honor.
Candidates who try too obviously to ingratiate themselves with voters, praising every town they visit as the finest in the nation, often provoke suspicion rather than affection.

inimical.text: The high salinity of the lake is inimical to most fish, so only a few hardy species of brine shrimp survive in its waters.
Economists warned that sudden, unpredictable changes in tax policy are inimical to long-term investment, because firms cannot plan under such uncertainty.
The open-plan office, with its constant chatter and interruptions, proved inimical to the deep concentration that the programmers' work required.

inimitable.text: No other cook could reproduce the grandmother's inimitable stew, though many relatives tried to copy it from her handwritten recipe.
The comedian's inimitable timing, a split-second pause before each punchline, has baffled generations of performers who have attempted to reproduce it.
Critics agree that the novelist's style is inimitable; the many writers who have tried to copy her sentences produce only pale parodies.

inkling.text: Until the letter arrived, Maria had no inkling that her grandfather had once been a celebrated violinist; he had never mentioned it.
The early experiments gave the researchers only an inkling of the compound's potential, a faint suggestion that would take years to confirm.
Although the plot twist seems obvious in hindsight, most readers have barely an inkling of the truth until the final chapter.

innocuous.text: What seemed an innocuous question about the budget provoked a furious reaction from the minister, who evidently had something to hide.
Although the mushroom closely resembles a deadly species, it is entirely innocuous and can be eaten safely by anyone who identifies it correctly.
Most of the bacteria living on human skin are innocuous; only a small fraction ever cause infection, and many actually help to protect their host.

inscrutable.text: The poker champion's inscrutable expression gave her opponents no hint as to whether she held a winning hand or nothing at all.
To modern readers the medieval manuscript remains inscrutable, written in a cipher that no scholar has yet managed to decode.
The villain's motives are deliberately inscrutable; the author never explains why he betrays his closest friend, and critics still argue about it.

insidious.text: High blood pressure is especially insidious because it produces few symptoms while steadily damaging the heart and kidneys over many years.
The propaganda was insidious rather than blatant, slipping small distortions into otherwise accurate reports until readers' views had quietly shifted.
Rot is an insidious threat to wooden buildings: it spreads unseen behind walls for years before a floor suddenly gives way.

insipid.text: The critic found the film's dialogue insipid, a string of bland platitudes that failed to reveal anything about the characters.
The developer's insipid design, a beige box indistinguishable from a thousand others, drew yawns rather than objections from the planning board.
Although the band's early albums were daring and inventive, its later work struck reviewers as insipid, polished but utterly lacking in character.

insolent.text: When the customs officer asked for his papers, the smuggler responded with an insolent sneer and tossed them onto the ground at the man's feet.
The household dismissed the insolent servant, who had openly mocked his master's guests and then refused to apologize.
Though merely a junior partner, he adopted an insolent tone with the firm's founders, openly calling their strategy foolish and their experience irrelevant.

insolvent.text: Although the startup's product won several design awards, years of reckless borrowing left the company insolvent, and its creditors seized the warehouse to recover what they could.
Economists warned that if the city kept funding pensions through short-term loans, it would soon be insolvent, and its employees might one day find their paychecks bouncing.
In the novel, the once-wealthy merchant hides from his creditors, too proud to admit that he has become insolvent and can no longer settle even his tailor's bill.

insouciance.text: The pianist approached the fiendishly difficult concerto with remarkable insouciance, chatting with the conductor minutes before walking onstage as if nothing were at stake.
Investors were alarmed by the chief executive's insouciance about mounting debts, since he seemed not the least bit worried about the looming payments.
Far from displaying the anxiety one might expect, the defendant sat through the trial with insouciance, idly sketching in a notebook while witnesses testified.

insufferable.text: The critic's insufferable arrogance, evident in his habit of correcting everyone's pronunciation at dinner, eventually cost him most of his friends.
The heat in the unventilated factory became insufferable by midafternoon, and several workers fainted before management opened the doors.
Though his early novels were charming, his later narrators became insufferable, lecturing readers for pages on subjects no one had raised.

intermittent.text: The rover's signal was intermittent, arriving in brief bursts separated by long, unpredictable silences that left the engineers anxious for hours at a time.
Because the drug's side effects were intermittent rather than constant, patients often failed to mention them to their doctors during routine appointments.
The composer punctuates the otherwise continuous string melody with intermittent brass chords, so that the listener never quite knows when the next interruption will come.

internecine.text: The party spent the campaign in internecine squabbling, as rival wings attacked one another instead of addressing the voters.
The empire's collapse owed less to foreign invaders than to internecine struggles among the emperor's sons, each of whom sought the throne for himself.
Internecine feuds within the research institute, in which departments sabotaged one another's grant applications, left it unable to compete with outside laboratories.

intimate.text: Without saying so directly, the editor intimated that the manuscript would need substantial revisions before it could be accepted.
Choosing her words carefully, the diplomat intimated that her government might soon change its position, though she never stated any such intention outright.
The board's statement seemed to intimate that the chief executive would soon step down, although no one would confirm it openly.

intimation.text: The first intimation that the company was in trouble came when the executives quietly canceled the annual holiday party.
Rather than state her objections outright, the editor offered only an intimation of her displeasure, a raised eyebrow and a pointed question about the deadline.
The late poems contain faint intimations of the poet's illness, hints that most readers noticed only after her death.

intransigent.text: Because both sides remained intransigent, refusing to budge on a single demand, the negotiations collapsed after only two days.
The committee chair was intransigent about the deadline, rejecting every request for an extension no matter how compelling the reason.
Although she welcomed criticism in most matters, the author was intransigent when editors tried to alter her novel's bleak ending.

intrepid.text: The intrepid reporter ventured into the war zone without an escort, determined to document conditions that other journalists were too frightened to approach.
Early polar explorers had to be intrepid, since they faced months of darkness, bitter cold, and the constant risk of death.
Though timid in social settings, the botanist became intrepid in the field, scaling cliffs and wading through rivers to collect rare specimens.

inundate.text: After the museum announced free admission for a single weekend, it was inundated with visitors, and the guards struggled to manage lines that wrapped around the block.
Rather than being ignored as she had feared, the young scholar found herself inundated with requests for interviews once her dissertation on urban migration was published.
When the levee failed, rising water inundated the low-lying farmland, submerging fields that had produced corn for generations.

inure.text: Years of working in the emergency ward had inured the nurse to scenes that would have unsettled most visitors, and she remained calm amid the chaos.
Residents of the flood-prone delta have become inured to hardship, rebuilding their homes after each storm without complaint.
The acoustician warned that constant exposure to background noise would inure listeners to it, so that they would no longer notice or object to the din.

invective.text: The debate degenerated into invective, with each candidate hurling insults at the other rather than discussing policy.
Although the critic was known for scathing reviews, his invective against the new museum, which he called a monument to vulgarity, shocked even his admirers.
The pamphlet abandoned reasoned argument for pure invective, denouncing its opponents as traitors, liars and fools.

inveterate.text: An inveterate traveler, the historian spent nearly every summer of her adult life exploring remote archives in a different country.
The senator was an inveterate interrupter: for thirty years, in committee and on the floor, he had never let a colleague finish a sentence, and no rebuke could break the habit.
His inveterate habit of arriving late, formed in childhood and never broken, eventually cost him his position at the firm.

invidious.text: The manager avoided invidious comparisons between team members, knowing that praising one employee at another's expense would breed resentment.
Awarding the corner offices only to senior partners' relatives proved invidious, and junior staff grumbled about favoritism for months.
Scholarship committees must make invidious choices among equally deserving applicants, inevitably disappointing and embittering those who are passed over.

inviolable.text: For the monks, the vow of silence was inviolable; not even a fire in the kitchen could persuade them to speak.
The constitution treats freedom of conscience as an inviolable right, one that no legislature may abridge under any circumstances.
Among the old merchants, a handshake agreement was inviolable, and breaking one meant permanent exclusion from the guild.

inviolate.text: Although the invading army looted the city, the ancient shrine remained inviolate, as even the conquerors feared to desecrate it.
The founder insisted that the trust's central principle remain inviolate: the land was never to be sold or developed, no matter the offer.
Throughout decades of upheaval, the family kept its grandmother's letters inviolate, sealed in a chest that no one was permitted to open.

involved.text: The plot of the opera is so involved, with its disguised twins, secret marriages, and mistaken identities, that most audiences rely on the program notes to follow it.
Applying for the grant proved an involved process, requiring dozens of forms, three separate budgets, and letters of support from several institutions.
Rather than giving a simple explanation, the lawyer offered an involved argument whose many clauses and exceptions left the jury more confused than before.

irascible.text: The irascible conductor was notorious for hurling his baton at musicians over the slightest missed entrance, so new members of the orchestra approached rehearsals with dread.
Although his letters reveal a tender side, the philosopher was irascible in public, prone to sudden outbursts whenever a student questioned one of his premises.
Chronic pain had made the old sailor irascible; the most innocent question about the weather could provoke a torrent of angry complaint.

irk.text: What irked the reviewers most was not the novel's length but its author's habit of repeating the same point in nearly identical words every few chapters.
The constant interruptions during the budget meeting irked the director, who finally snapped that she would take no further questions until she had finished.
Although the delay was minor, it irks passengers to be told nothing about its cause, and many complained more about the silence than about the wait itself.

irrefutable.text: The fingerprints on the vault provided irrefutable evidence that the guard had been involved, and he confessed shortly afterward.
Her logic was irrefutable; although her opponents searched for a flaw in the proof, none could find a step that failed.
Satellite images offered irrefutable confirmation that the forest was shrinking, silencing officials who had long denied any deforestation.

irresolute.text: The committee remained irresolute for months, unable to decide whether to renovate the aging library or demolish it, and meanwhile the roof continued to leak.
Unlike her decisive predecessor, the new manager was irresolute, reversing her instructions so often that employees began waiting a day before acting on any of them.
Faced with two equally attractive job offers, Daniel grew irresolute, writing and then deleting acceptance emails to each company throughout the night.

irrevocable.text: Once the treaty was ratified, its provisions were irrevocable, so the delegates debated each clause with great care beforehand.
The decision to demolish the historic theater was irrevocable; once the wrecking crews finished, no amount of regret could restore it.
Some philosophers argue that promises are not irrevocable, since circumstances may change so drastically that keeping one would cause great harm.

itinerant.text: In the nineteenth century, itinerant preachers rode from settlement to settlement, holding services wherever a crowd would gather.
Unlike the settled farmers of the valley, the itinerant shearers moved with the seasons, finding work wherever flocks needed tending.
Because her work as an itinerant consultant took her to a different city every week, she kept only a small apartment that she rarely saw.

jargon.text: The consultant's report was so thick with financial jargon that the town council, composed mostly of teachers and shopkeepers, could make little sense of its recommendations.
Good science writers translate the jargon of specialists into plain English, so that readers without a laboratory background can follow the argument.
Within weeks of joining the software team, Priya had absorbed its jargon, casually tossing around acronyms and shorthand that had baffled her on her first day.

jaundice.text: After years of broken campaign promises, voters regarded every new pledge with a jaundiced eye, assuming it would be abandoned after the election.
The critic's jaundiced view of the young novelist, whose success he openly resented, colored every review he wrote of her work.
Having been passed over for promotion, Martin grew jaundiced toward his rival, dismissing even her genuine achievements as luck or flattery.

jejune-adj1.text: Students struggle to stay awake through a single chapter of the textbook, whose jejune prose reduces even the most dramatic events of the century to a list of dates.
Diners expecting the bold spices promised on the menu were disappointed by the jejune curry, which tasted of little more than boiled vegetables.
Compared with the vivid, witty letters of her youth, the aging writer's final essays seem jejune, as though the years had drained all the flavor from her prose.

jejune-adj2.text: The senior diplomats dismissed the intern's proposal as jejune, the kind of naive scheme that ignores every practical obstacle an experienced negotiator would foresee.
Although the poet later disowned her jejune early verses, with their adolescent posturing and borrowed melodrama, they reveal the roots of her mature style.
The professor found the debate club's arguments jejune, relying on schoolyard taunts and simplistic slogans rather than the reasoning expected of adults.

jingoism.text: Wartime newspapers were filled with jingoism, portraying the enemy as subhuman and urging readers to accept any sacrifice for the nation's glory.
The historian warned that jingoism can masquerade as ordinary patriotism, though it differs in its eagerness for war and its contempt for other nations.
Critics accused the film of jingoism, noting that it celebrated every battlefield victory while ignoring the suffering of civilians on both sides.

jingoist.text: The jingoist newspaper editor called for an immediate invasion after the border incident, mocking anyone who urged diplomacy as a coward.
Historians have noted how quickly moderate voices were drowned out by jingoists eager for battle once the naval dispute became public.
Though he had once been a jingoist, demanding war with every neighboring state, the veteran returned from the front a committed advocate for peace.

jocular.text: Despite the gravity of the negotiations, the ambassador maintained a jocular manner, teasing his counterparts and telling anecdotes that eased the tension in the room.
The eulogy was surprisingly jocular, yet the mourners who laughed through it agreed that nothing could have captured the deceased's irreverent spirit more faithfully.
Readers who know the poet only through his somber elegies may be surprised by his jocular letters, which brim with puns and playful teasing of his friends.

jovial.text: The jovial innkeeper greeted every guest with a hearty laugh and a joke, and his cheerful mood soon spread through the dining room.
Although the meeting began tensely, the atmosphere became jovial once the unexpected profits were announced and the directors began trading toasts.
Known for his jovial manner, the professor opened each lecture with a humorous anecdote that set his nervous students at ease.

jubilant.text: The jubilant fans poured onto the field after their team's unlikely championship victory, hugging strangers and singing late into the night.
The scientists were jubilant when the probe finally transmitted its first images, the triumphant culmination of two decades of work.
Though exhausted after the long campaign, the volunteers were jubilant when the final count confirmed that the referendum had passed.

juggernaut.text: The upstart retailer grew into a juggernaut, crushing small competitors and expanding into every market it entered despite regulators' efforts to slow it.
The campaign seemed an unstoppable juggernaut until a single scandal, revealed days before the vote, finally halted its momentum.
Once the reform movement gained broad public support, it became a juggernaut that no coalition of entrenched interests could resist.

junta.text: After the army overthrew the elected government, a junta of three generals ruled by decree, suspending the constitution and closing the independent newspapers.
The novel depicts a small island nation where a military junta, having seized power in a single night, struggles to convince the population that its rule is only temporary.
Diplomats hoped that sanctions would pressure the junta to restore civilian rule, but the colonels who had taken over showed no sign of relinquishing control.

juxtapose.text: The exhibition juxtaposes ancient masks with contemporary portraits, inviting viewers to compare how different eras represented the human face.
By juxtaposing the lavish banquet with the starving crowds outside the palace gates, the director makes the film's critique of inequality unmistakable.
The poet likes to juxtapose images of industrial decay and natural beauty, setting a rusted factory beside a field of wildflowers in the same stanza.

kowtow.text: Rather than kowtow to the wealthy donor's demands, the museum director refused to alter the exhibition and risked losing the gift.
Courtiers kowtowed to the emperor, bowing low and agreeing with every pronouncement, however absurd.
The editorial accused the regulators of kowtowing to the industry they were supposed to police, approving every request without objection.

laborious.text: Before the invention of the printing press, copying a manuscript was a laborious process, requiring months of painstaking work by a single scribe.
Restoring the fresco proved far more laborious than the conservators expected: each square inch had to be cleaned by hand with tiny swabs over many exhausting months.
Although the new harvesting machine is expensive, farmers welcome it, since it replaces the laborious task of cutting and bundling the stalks by hand under the summer sun.

lacerate.text: The review lacerated the young playwright, who had poured years into the script and was devastated to see it described as worthless.
Her sister's cruel remarks at the wedding lacerated Julia's feelings, and the two did not speak for nearly a year.
Though intended as constructive, the supervisor's criticism lacerated the sensitive intern, who left the meeting in tears.

lachrymose.text: The lachrymose widower wept openly throughout the memorial service, unable to finish the eulogy he had prepared.
Critics complained that the film was lachrymose to excess, with nearly every scene engineered to make the audience cry.
Although the children's author usually wrote cheerful adventures, her final book was lachrymose, dwelling on loss and ending with a tearful farewell.

laconic.text: Asked to explain his victory, the laconic champion replied only, 'I trained,' and then left the press conference.
Whereas her predecessor gave lengthy speeches, the new chair was laconic, often ending meetings after a few terse sentences.
The general's laconic dispatches, rarely more than a line or two, frustrated officials in the capital who wanted detailed accounts of the campaign.

lambast.text: Critics who had praised the director's early work lambasted his latest film, calling its plot incoherent and its dialogue embarrassingly clumsy.
The auditor's report lambasts the agency for wasting millions on consultants, describing its oversight as negligent in the extreme.
Although the coach privately praised the players, in public she chose to lambast their lazy defense, hoping the harsh words would spur improvement.

lampoon.text: The satirical magazine lampooned the city's pompous officials, depicting them as bumbling peacocks strutting about the town hall.
The playwright lampoons the pretensions of the art world, portraying collectors who pay fortunes for blank canvases they cannot tell apart.
Rather than argue earnestly against the bureaucracy, the columnist chose to lampoon it, inventing absurd regulations so plausible that readers mistook them for real ones.

languid.text: The novel captures the languid pace of summer in a southern town, where residents spend long afternoons dozing on shaded porches.
After the frenetic first movement, the symphony shifts to a languid adagio, its phrases drifting unhurriedly as if the orchestra itself had grown drowsy in the afternoon heat.
The cat stretched in a languid way, clearly in no hurry to abandon its sunny spot on the windowsill.

languish.text: Deprived of sunlight in the dim apartment, the potted ferns languished, their fronds yellowing and drooping week by week.
Without regular visits from family, the elderly patient began to languish, eating little and growing weaker each day.
The once thriving port languished after the railway bypassed it, its warehouses emptying and its population steadily declining.

largess.text: The university's new library was made possible by the largess of an anonymous donor, who gave far more than the fundraisers had dared to request.
The king's largess toward his courtiers, showering them with estates and titles, eventually emptied the royal treasury.
Although the company advertised its charitable largess, critics noted that its donations amounted to a tiny fraction of its annual profits.

lascivious.text: The censor objected to the novel's lascivious passages, which dwelt so openly on lust that he feared they would corrupt young readers.
In the morality play, the lascivious courtier, forever leering at the ladies of the household, serves as a warning against unchecked desire.
The curator defended the painting against charges that it was lascivious, arguing that its nude figures were depicted with classical restraint rather than lecherous intent.

laudable.text: The charity's goal of providing clean water to every village is laudable, though critics question whether its methods are effective.
Her laudable decision to return the reward money to the family she had helped earned her admiration throughout the city.
While the committee found the student's ambition laudable, it worried that the proposed project was far too large to complete in a single year.

leery.text: Having been misled by glowing projections before, the investors were leery of the founder's promises and insisted on examining the company's books themselves.
Villagers who had watched earlier development schemes fail were understandably leery of the outsiders, answering their questions politely but revealing little.
Although the new treatment showed promise in early trials, many physicians remained leery of prescribing it until independent studies confirmed its safety.

lethargic.text: The heat wave left the entire office lethargic; even the most diligent employees spent the afternoon staring at their screens, too drained to begin new tasks.
Although the zoo's lions appear lethargic during the day, dozing for hours in the shade, they become far more active after sunset.
Economists described the recovery as lethargic: growth was sluggish, hiring was slow, and consumers seemed to lack the energy to spend.

limpid.text: Her limpid explanation of quantum mechanics, free of jargon and needless complication, allowed even novices to follow the argument.
The philosopher's early essays are dense and tangled, but his later prose became limpid, each sentence as transparent as a pane of glass.
Students prize the textbook for its limpid style: even the most difficult proofs are laid out so clearly that the logic seems obvious.

lionize.text: After his first novel became a surprise success, the young writer was lionized by the city's literary society, which invited him to every salon and gala.
Popular culture tends to lionize the few daring entrepreneurs who struck it rich, celebrating them in magazines and films while ignoring the many whose ventures failed.
Although she was lionized in her lifetime as the greatest actress of her generation, she is now largely forgotten.

litany.text: The customer recited a litany of complaints, from the late delivery to the scratched table to the rude driver, that lasted nearly half an hour.
The report is less an analysis than a litany of failures, listing one missed deadline after another without explaining why any occurred.
Voters, weary of the candidate's litany of grievances against his opponents, began to wonder whether he had any proposals of his own.

loath.text: The committee was loath to abandon a tradition that had lasted a century, even though few members could remember why it had begun.
Scientists are often loath to speculate in public, preferring to wait until the data are conclusive before making any claims.
Though she needed the money, Elena was loath to borrow from friends, since she had always prided herself on paying her own way.

lucid.text: Although the subject is notoriously difficult, the textbook's lucid explanations allow first-year students to grasp statistical inference without confusion.
The lawyer's closing argument was admirably lucid, reducing a tangle of conflicting testimony to three simple points that every juror could follow.
Her early essays are dense and obscure, but her later work is lucid, as though she had finally learned to trust plain words to carry her meaning.

lugubrious.text: The actor's lugubrious expression, with drooping eyes and a mournful sigh, made even his comic lines sound like announcements of a death.
The chair delivered the minor budget news in such a lugubrious tone that several members assumed the organization was about to close.
Visitors found the memorial garden's music lugubrious, a slow, funereal dirge played on repeat that seemed designed to deepen rather than console their grief.

macabre.text: The exhibit on Victorian mourning customs held a macabre fascination for visitors, displaying jewelry woven from the hair of the dead alongside elaborate coffin fittings.
The painter's later canvases turned macabre, filled with grinning skulls, rotting fruit, and figures that seemed to be decaying before the viewer's eyes.
Although the story begins as a light comedy of manners, it takes a macabre turn when the guests discover a coffin hidden beneath the dining room floor.

machinate.text: While publicly pledging loyalty to the king, the ambitious duke machinated with foreign envoys to seize the throne.
The board members who had machinated to oust the founder met secretly for months, drafting their plan before a single employee suspected it.
The novel's villain spends every chapter machinating against the heroine, forging letters and bribing servants to ruin her reputation.

magisterial.text: The new supervisor's magisterial manner, issuing decrees without consultation and brooking no dissent, quickly alienated a staff accustomed to collaboration.
In a magisterial tone that invited no disagreement, the senior partner informed the associates that his interpretation of the contract was final.
Readers bristled at the critic's magisterial pronouncements, which dismissed entire genres as unworthy without offering any reasons.

magnanimous.text: In victory the general was magnanimous, allowing the defeated soldiers to return home with their weapons and their dignity intact.
Rather than gloating over the bankruptcy of the rival firm that had tried to ruin her, the magnanimous chief executive offered jobs to its laid-off employees.
The former champion's magnanimous tribute to the young challenger who had just dethroned him surprised fans who had expected bitterness.

maintain.text: Despite mounting evidence against him, the defendant maintained throughout the trial that he had never met the victim and had been abroad that week.
Some linguists maintain that all human languages share a common underlying grammar, though others dismiss the claim as untestable.
The architect maintains that ornament is not a luxury but a necessity, arguing that bare facades alienate the people who must live beside them.

maladroit.text: The maladroit waiter managed to spill soup on two guests and drop a tray of glasses within the first hour of the banquet.
Although she was maladroit on the dance floor, stumbling over every step, the young diplomat moved with great grace through tense negotiations.
His maladroit handling of the chisel left the sculpture scarred with gouges, and the master quietly reassigned him to sweeping the studio.

malady.text: Physicians of the era had no name for the malady that swept through the port each summer, though they noticed it struck hardest near stagnant water.
The essayist argues that loneliness is not merely a mood but a genuine malady, one that can undermine the body's health as surely as any infection.
Although the patient's symptoms suggested a rare tropical malady, tests eventually revealed a common infection that responded quickly to antibiotics.

malapropism.text: Students laughed at the malapropism when their classmate announced that the explorer had died of 'ammonia' rather than pneumonia.
The sitcom's landlord speaks almost entirely in malapropisms, confidently assuring tenants that the lease is 'legally biting' and that he will never 'take them for granite.'
The best man's toast is remembered chiefly for one malapropism: he wished the newlyweds a lifetime of 'marital blitz,' and the guests laughed so hard that he never finished his speech.

malevolent.text: In the folktale, the kindly old woman turns out to be a malevolent witch who lures travelers into her cottage in order to do them harm.
The biographer rejects the view that the minister was malevolent; his disastrous policies, she argues, arose from incompetence rather than any desire to hurt his rivals.
Far from being a mere prank, the computer virus was malevolent by design, engineered to destroy hospital records and cause as much suffering as possible.

malfeasance.text: The auditors uncovered evidence of malfeasance in the treasurer's office, where public funds had been diverted to accounts controlled by the treasurer's relatives.
Although the commissioner insisted that his errors were honest mistakes, investigators concluded that his conduct amounted to deliberate malfeasance in office.
Voters who had tolerated the council's inefficiency lost patience once they learned of outright malfeasance, including bribes accepted in exchange for zoning approvals.

malingerer.text: The foreman suspected that the worker was a malingerer, since his mysterious back pain always seemed to flare up on the days heavy crates arrived.
Army doctors were trained to distinguish genuinely wounded soldiers from the occasional malingerer who feigned illness to avoid returning to the front.
Far from being a malingerer, as her skeptical manager had assumed, the employee turned out to have a serious illness that she had tried to work through.

malleable-adj1.text: Gold is so malleable that a single small nugget can be hammered into a sheet thin enough to let light pass through it without tearing.
Heated in the forge until it glowed, the iron became malleable enough for the blacksmith to bend it into an elaborate scroll for the garden gate.
Engineers chose aluminum for the panels because it is malleable, allowing the sheets to be pressed into curved shapes without cracking.

malleable-adj2.text: Advertisers target young children because their preferences are malleable, readily swayed by a catchy jingle or a cartoon mascot.
The dictator preferred malleable advisers who would echo his opinions, and he quietly dismissed anyone who dared to contradict him.
Research suggests that eyewitness recollections are surprisingly malleable: a single leading question from an investigator can alter what a witness believes she saw.

malodorous.text: The tannery was moved to the edge of town because its vats were so malodorous that residents complained of the stench from half a mile away.
Although the durian is prized for its creamy flesh, the fruit is so malodorous that some hotels forbid guests from bringing it inside.
When the sewage plant malfunctioned, a malodorous haze settled over the neighborhood, forcing residents to keep their windows shut despite the heat.

martial.text: The parade's martial music, with its pounding drums and brassy fanfares, seemed out of place at what was supposed to be a celebration of peace.
The new principal ran the school with an almost martial discipline, insisting that students march in straight lines and stand at attention when a teacher entered.
Although the statue commemorates a general, the sculptor avoided any martial imagery, depicting him without sword or uniform as a weary old man reading a letter.

martinet.text: The conductor was a notorious martinet, dismissing musicians for arriving a minute late and demanding that every note be played exactly as marked.
Cadets who expected a lenient commander were dismayed to find that the new colonel was a martinet who inspected their boots and beds every morning.
Although her students called her a martinet for her rigid rules about deadlines and formatting, many later credited her discipline with their success.

maudlin.text: By the end of the reunion, the guests had grown maudlin, tearfully toasting departed friends and lamenting lost youth in speeches that went on far too long.
The screenplay avoids the maudlin sentimentality typical of the genre; even the grandmother's death is handled with restraint rather than swelling violins and weeping relatives.
Critics found the singer's ballad maudlin, its syrupy lyrics about lost love wallowing in self-pity rather than expressing genuine grief.

maunder-v1.text: With no destination in mind, the retired professor would maunder through the old quarter each afternoon, drifting from bookshop to bookshop without any plan.
The stray cattle maundered across the open range, ambling wherever the grass looked greenest rather than following any path.
Lacking a map, the tourists maundered along the riverbank for hours, idly turning down one lane and then another until the sun had set.

maunder-v2.text: The guest speaker maundered on about his vacation photographs for forty minutes, never reaching the topic the audience had come to hear.
Rather than answer the question directly, the witness maundered about the weather, his neighbors and his health until the judge interrupted him.
Her uncle would maunder endlessly over dinner about trivial grievances, chattering so incessantly that no one else could get a word in.

maverick.text: A maverick among economists, she ignored the prevailing models and built her own, which turned out to predict the crisis far better.
The legislator earned a reputation as a maverick by voting against his own party whenever he disagreed with its position.
Unlike the studio directors who followed established formulas, the maverick filmmaker financed his own projects and shot them without scripts.

mawkish.text: The film's ending, with its swelling violins, tearful reunions, and orphaned puppy, struck critics as mawkish rather than moving.
Though the eulogy began with genuine feeling, it soon became mawkish, dwelling so heavily on sentimental commonplaces that several mourners winced.
The editor urged the poet to cut the mawkish final stanza, arguing that its gushing tributes to childhood innocence would make readers cringe.

maxim.text: The old investor lived by a simple maxim, 'never buy what you do not understand,' and he refused to touch any company whose business he could not explain.
Proverbs often contradict one another; for every maxim urging caution, such as 'look before you leap,' there is another that praises boldness.
The essay opens with a confident maxim about ambition and then spends twenty pages qualifying it until almost nothing of the original claim remains.

meander.text: With no particular destination in mind, the tourists meandered through the old quarter, pausing wherever a courtyard or bookshop caught their eye.
The lecture meandered from Greek architecture to medieval farming to modern traffic laws, and by the end the students had no idea what its main point had been.
Rather than walking directly to the station, Ana meandered along the riverbank, content to let the afternoon drift by without any plan.

melancholy.text: A deep melancholy settled over the composer after his wife's death, and for years he wrote only slow, mournful pieces in minor keys.
Although the novel's characters laugh often, an undercurrent of melancholy runs through every chapter, as each of them mourns a life that might have been.
Travelers often describe a strange melancholy that overtakes them in abandoned towns, a lingering sorrow that persists long after they have left.

melee.text: When the referee's disputed call ended the match, fans poured onto the field and a chaotic melee broke out, with dozens of people shoving and swinging at one another.
The painting depicts the battle not as an orderly clash of ranks but as a confused melee, in which soldiers can barely distinguish friend from foe.
What began as a polite argument over a parking space escalated into a melee involving half the street, and the police needed an hour to sort out who had struck whom.

mellifluous.text: Listeners who found the audiobook's chapters dull kept listening anyway, because the narrator's voice was so mellifluous that even lists of dates sounded pleasant.
Unlike the harsh, clattering consonants of the northern dialect, the southern accent sounded mellifluous to visitors, its vowels flowing gently together.
The violinist's tone was praised as mellifluous, though some critics felt that such unfailing sweetness suited Mozart better than the jagged modern works on her program.

mendacity.text: The minister's mendacity became so well known that journalists routinely checked even his most trivial statements against independent sources.
Critics of the advertising industry decry its mendacity, arguing that many campaigns rely on claims the companies know to be false.
Although the memoirist presents herself as scrupulously honest, readers soon discover her mendacity, as one invented anecdote follows another.

mendicant.text: Having given away his possessions, the friar lived as a mendicant, relying on the charity of villagers for every meal he ate.
Pilgrims approaching the medieval shrine passed long lines of mendicants holding out bowls and pleading for coins.
The novel's hero falls from wealthy merchant to mendicant, and in the final chapter he stands with an outstretched hand outside the very warehouses he once owned.

mercurial.text: Martha Argerich's mercurial nature is perfectly matched with playing Chopin: she'll toss off, with aplomb, effervescent passages, before moments later plumbing the depths of her soul to give voice to bars of music steeped in the utmost melancholy.
The orchestra struggled to work with its mercurial conductor, who might praise the musicians warmly one moment and storm out of rehearsal the next.
Biographers attribute the poet's uneven output to his mercurial temperament, which swung without warning from euphoria to despair.
Investors grew wary of the founder's mercurial leadership, since her sudden changes of mood often produced abrupt reversals in strategy.

mesmerize.text: The pianist's performance mesmerized the audience; for nearly an hour no one coughed, whispered, or even shifted in their seats.
Children at the aquarium stood mesmerized by the jellyfish, watching the glowing creatures pulse through the dark water as if in a trance.
Some critics complain that the documentary's gorgeous aerial footage is meant to mesmerize viewers so thoroughly that they stop questioning its dubious claims.

meteoric.text: The startup's meteoric rise, from a garage workshop to a billion-dollar valuation in three years, astonished even its founders.
Her fame was meteoric in every sense: dazzling for a single season, it faded almost as abruptly as it had appeared.
Few scientists enjoy so meteoric a career; within five years of his doctorate, he directed an institute and had won nearly every major award.

meticulous.text: The restorer was meticulous, spending weeks cleaning a single square inch of the fresco with tiny brushes to avoid damaging the original pigment.
Because the experiment depended on precise measurements, the lab kept meticulous records, logging every temperature reading to a hundredth of a degree.
Although his early drafts were careless, the novelist became meticulous in revision, checking every date and name against his sources.

mettlesome.text: The mettlesome reporter continued to investigate the cartel despite repeated threats, refusing to abandon the story.
Though hers was the smallest boat in the regatta, it had a mettlesome crew that sailed straight into the storm while larger vessels turned back.
The seventeen-year-old proved a mettlesome advocate for her village, confronting the mining company's executives at a public hearing where adults had stayed silent.

misanthrope.text: The novel's hero is a bitter misanthrope who retreats to a mountain cabin, convinced that every human being is fundamentally selfish and cruel.
Although the philosopher was often called a misanthrope, his letters reveal a man who despised not humanity itself but the vanity of the society around him.
After decades of watching colleagues betray one another for promotions, the retired diplomat had become a misanthrope, avoiding company and expecting the worst of everyone he met.

misattribute.text: Quotations are frequently misattributed to famous figures, since a clever line gains authority when it seems to come from a celebrated author.
The museum had long misattributed the portrait to the master himself, until an analysis of the brushwork revealed that one of his apprentices had painted it.
Historians warn against misattributing the anonymous pamphlet to the revolutionary leader simply because its style resembles his; several contemporaries wrote in the same manner.

misconstrue.text: The ambassador's cautious silence was misconstrued as approval, and the neighboring government proceeded with plans he actually opposed.
Students often misconstrue the principle of natural selection, wrongly believing that organisms change deliberately to suit their environments.
Fearing that readers might misconstrue her satire as a sincere endorsement, the author added a preface explaining her ironic intent.

miscreant.text: The mayor promised to install more streetlights so that the miscreants who had been vandalizing the park at night would have nowhere to hide.
In the colonial settlement, any miscreant caught stealing from the common storehouse was sentenced to months of hard labor on the fortifications.
The detective suspected that the burglaries were the work of a single miscreant, since each break-in followed exactly the same method.

miser.text: Although he owned three factories, the old miser heated only one room of his house and wore the same threadbare coat for decades, unwilling to part with a single coin.
The play satirizes a miser who hoards gold in a locked chest while his servants go hungry and his daughter is denied a dowry.
Neighbors assumed the reclusive widow was a miser, but after her death they learned she had quietly given a fortune to the local hospital.

misogynist.text: The critic argues that the poet was a misogynist, pointing to the contempt with which nearly every female character in his work is portrayed.
The club's rule barring women was defended as tradition, but many saw it as the legacy of a misogynist founder whose diaries ridicule women as unfit for serious conversation.
Although the philosopher was long dismissed as a misogynist, recent scholars note that he championed women's education at a time when few others did.

mitigate-v1.text: Planting trees along city streets can mitigate the effects of summer heat, lowering surface temperatures by providing shade.
The company introduced flexible schedules to mitigate the stress of the long commute, although many employees still arrived exhausted.
Although nothing could undo the damage of the flood, the relief fund mitigated the hardship of families who had lost their homes.

mitigate-v2.text: The judge accepted that the defendant's youth and genuine remorse mitigated his crime, and she imposed a far lighter sentence than the prosecution had sought.
His lawyer argued that the extreme provocation he had endured mitigated the assault, though it could not excuse it entirely.
The review board condemned the officer's misconduct but agreed that his lack of training did mitigate his culpability, so it recommended retraining rather than dismissal.

modicum.text: The reforms granted the colonies only a modicum of self-government; the governor still appointed every official and could veto any law.
Although the documentary is mostly bleak, it offers a modicum of hope in its final scenes, showing a few families returning to rebuild.
The negotiators agreed that at least a modicum of trust, however slight, would be necessary before any larger agreement could be reached.

mollify.text: To mollify the furious customers whose flights had been canceled, the airline offered free hotel rooms and vouchers for future travel.
The mayor's apology did little to mollify residents who were outraged by the sudden rise in water rates.
Hoping to mollify his irate editor, the reporter promised to deliver the overdue article before the morning deadline.

moment.text: Although the treaty was signed with little fanfare, it proved to be of great moment, reshaping trade in the region for the next century.
The committee spent hours on matters of little moment, such as the color of the letterhead, while the urgent question of the budget went undiscussed.
Few at the time recognized the discovery as an event of real moment; only decades later did historians see that it had transformed the practice of medicine.

moot.text: Whether the bridge should be painted blue or green became a moot question once engineers declared the structure unsafe and scheduled it for demolition.
Since the company had already gone bankrupt, the lawsuit over its advertising practices was moot, and the judge dismissed it without hearing arguments.
Whether the portrait is the artist's own work remains a moot point among scholars, who have argued over the brushwork for decades without reaching agreement.

mordant.text: The columnist's mordant wit spared no one; her caustic remarks about the city council were quoted, and resented, for weeks.
Though his novels deal with grim subjects, they are leavened by a mordant humor that skewers the pretensions of his characters.
Rather than offering gentle suggestions, the editor scrawled mordant comments in the margins, mocking clumsy sentences with biting sarcasm.

moribund.text: The once bustling mill town is now moribund, its factories shuttered and its young people departing for cities elsewhere.
Critics declared the epic poem a moribund form, but a few contemporary writers have revived it with surprising vigor.
The physician recognized that the patient was moribund and gently advised the family to gather at her bedside while there was still time.

morose.text: After losing the election, the candidate grew morose, retreating to his study and answering his aides' questions with sullen grunts.
Although she had been lively at dinner, Marta became morose on the drive home, staring out the window and ignoring every attempt at conversation.
The novel's narrator is a morose clerk whose sullen silences contrast sharply with the cheerful chatter of his coworkers.

morph.text: Over several decades, the small neighborhood bakery morphed into a regional chain, its transformation so gradual that longtime customers hardly noticed.
In the animated film, the villain's face slowly morphs into that of a wolf, each feature shifting so smoothly that viewers cannot pinpoint when the change occurred.
The protest began as a campaign against a single tax but gradually morphed into a broad challenge to the government's legitimacy, without any single moment marking the shift.

mulct.text: The fraudulent contractor mulcted elderly homeowners of their savings, charging for roof repairs that were never performed.
Investigators found that the fund's managers had mulcted investors by inflating fees and concealing losses for nearly a decade.
Posing as a tax official, the con artist mulcted dozens of shopkeepers, collecting fictitious penalties that went straight into his own pocket.

mundane-adj1.text: Although the job came with a glamorous title, most of her days were consumed by mundane tasks such as filing reports and answering routine email.
The novelist's precise and lyrical prose makes even mundane chores like washing dishes and sorting mail seem fascinating, a feat few writers achieve.
Astronauts report that, contrary to popular belief, much of life in orbit is mundane: repeated maintenance checks and exercise routines fill most of each day.

mundane-adj2.text: The monks were expected to renounce mundane concerns such as property and politics in order to devote themselves wholly to prayer.
Medieval painters often placed saints in mundane settings, such as a merchant's kitchen or a busy marketplace, linking the sacred with the everyday world.
The anthropologist cared less about the tribe's sacred rituals than about its mundane life: how people farmed, traded, and raised their children.

munificent.text: Thanks to a munificent bequest from a former student, the college was able to offer full scholarships to every admitted applicant.
The patron was munificent toward young composers, funding their studies, commissioning their works, and even paying their rent.
Though notoriously stingy with his own family, the industrialist was munificent in public, endowing museums and hospitals across the city.

muted.text: Unlike the garish murals downtown, the interior of the chapel was painted in muted grays and soft blues that invited quiet reflection.
The critics' response to the novel was muted: reviewers praised a few passages but showed none of the enthusiasm that had greeted the author's debut.
Through the thick walls of the recording studio, the traffic outside was reduced to a muted hum that the microphones barely picked up.

myopic.text: Cutting the research budget to boost this quarter's profits was a myopic decision that left the company without new products a few years later.
Critics called the zoning plan myopic, arguing that it ignored the population growth the region would certainly experience over the next two decades.
Far from being myopic, the city's founders laid out avenues wide enough to accommodate a population ten times larger than the one they governed.

myriad.text: The rainforest canopy is home to a myriad of insect species, many of which scientists have not yet even named.
A newcomer to the city faces a myriad of decisions, from choosing a neighborhood to navigating an unfamiliar transit system.
Myriads of stars, too faint to be seen individually, combine to produce the pale glow of the galaxy's band across the night sky.

nadir.text: Mike had walked in cold to the new GRE and was not surprised afterwards that he'd hit a standardized test nadir.
The team reached its nadir in the final month of the season, losing ten straight games and finishing in last place.
Historians regard the famine years as the nadir of the kingdom's fortunes, after which a slow recovery began.
At the nadir of his career, with no publisher willing to read his manuscripts, the novelist took a job washing dishes to pay the rent.

negligible.text: The new filter's effect on water quality was negligible; tests showed virtually no difference in contaminant levels before and after installation.
Although the tax increase was negligible for wealthy households, it imposed a real burden on families with lower incomes.
The engineers dismissed the risk as negligible, since the probability of both backup systems failing at once was less than one in a billion.

nettlesome.text: The software's nettlesome habit of freezing whenever a file was saved drove the office staff to distraction.
Negotiators set aside the most nettlesome issue, the division of water rights, to avoid derailing agreement on the rest of the treaty.
The constant hum of the neighbor's generator was more nettlesome than genuinely harmful, but it frayed everyone's nerves by the end of the week.

noisome.text: The noisome odor of rotting fish drifted from the abandoned cannery, forcing pedestrians to cover their noses as they passed.
Before the sewer system was built, the city's canals were noisome channels whose stench sickened residents every summer.
The chemist opened the flask and immediately regretted it, as noisome fumes reminiscent of rotten eggs filled the entire laboratory.

nonchalant.text: Despite having just won the championship, the player gave a nonchalant shrug when reporters asked how she felt, as though the victory meant little to her.
The pilot's nonchalant announcement that one engine had failed, delivered in the tone of a weather update, somehow reassured the anxious passengers.
Though his hands trembled beneath the table, the candidate tried to appear nonchalant during the interview, leaning back and answering questions with studied indifference.

nonplussed.text: The seasoned lecturer was nonplussed by the student's question, which exposed a flaw he had never considered, and he stood silent for a long moment.
Nonplussed by the conflicting instructions from her two supervisors, the new employee simply did not know which task to begin first.
Visitors are often nonplussed by the old city's nameless streets, unsure which way to turn at each intersection and unable to find their hotels.

nuance.text: The translator struggled to capture every nuance of the poem, since a single word in the original could carry shades of both irony and tenderness.
Although the two philosophers' positions look identical at first, careful readers notice a nuance: one treats duty as absolute, while the other allows exceptions.
The actor's performance was praised for its nuances, conveying the character's grief through slight changes in posture and tone rather than dramatic outbursts.

obdurate.text: Despite months of petitions and protests, the landlord remained obdurate, refusing even to discuss repairs to the crumbling building.
The general's obdurate insistence on a frontal assault, even after his officers presented evidence of its folly, cost the army dearly.
Diplomats hoped that economic pressure would soften the regime's position, but it proved obdurate, rejecting every compromise put forward.

objurgate.text: Rather than offering the gentle correction the young clerk expected, the magistrate chose to objurgate him before the entire courtroom, denouncing his carelessness in the harshest terms.
Critics who had once praised the architect's daring now objurgated her latest tower, condemning its blank facade as an insult to the historic square it overshadowed.
Although the committee chair was known for her mild manners, she objurgated the auditors sharply for concealing the deficit, making clear that such conduct would not be tolerated.

obliging.text: The hotel's obliging concierge not only recommended a restaurant but also called ahead to reserve a table and arranged a taxi for us.
Though I had expected the archivist to resent my endless requests, she was remarkably obliging, retrieving dozens of dusty boxes without a word of complaint.
Neighbors described the old man as obliging, and during any vacation on the street it was usually he who watered the plants, collected the mail, and fed the cats.

oblique.text: Instead of stating her objection outright, the diplomat made only an oblique reference to 'certain unresolved concerns,' leaving her counterparts to guess what she actually opposed.
The novel's criticism of the regime is oblique rather than explicit: the author never names the dictator, conveying her judgment through allegory and carefully chosen silences.
Because direct questions about his finances made the tycoon defensive, the biographer took an oblique approach, asking about his childhood and letting the subject of money arise on its own.

obscure-adj.text: The scholar built her career on obscure poets of the eighteenth century, figures whose names appear in few anthologies and on fewer syllabi.
Although the composer was obscure during his lifetime, performing only for small provincial audiences, his symphonies are now staples of the concert repertoire.
The foundation often gives its prize to obscure researchers rather than celebrated ones, hoping to draw attention to work that has been overlooked.

obscure-v.text: The report's dense technical jargon tends to obscure its central finding, so many readers never realize that the study contradicts earlier research.
The translator's heavy footnotes obscured rather than clarified the poem's meaning, burying each simple image beneath paragraphs of commentary.
Critics accused the company of using convoluted accounting to obscure its mounting losses, leaving investors unable to judge its true condition.

obsequious.text: The obsequious courtier praised every decree the king issued, however foolish, hoping to secure a lucrative appointment.
Diners complained that the obsequious staff hovered over them, refilling glasses after every sip and bowing whenever the owner's wealthy friends arrived.
Although he was obsequious toward the board members who controlled his salary, the manager treated his own subordinates with open contempt.

obstinate.text: The farmer coaxed, pulled and bribed with apples, but the obstinate mule refused to take a single step across the shallow stream.
Although the evidence against his theory had become overwhelming, the professor remained obstinate, clinging to his original conclusions and dismissing every critic.
Teachers found the boy obstinate rather than slow: he understood the lessons perfectly well but refused to complete any assignment he considered pointless.

obstreperous.text: The seminar ran smoothly until an obstreperous attendee began shouting objections over every speaker and refused to yield the microphone even when the moderator pleaded with him.
Far from the docile animals described in the brochure, the goats proved obstreperous, bleating loudly, butting the gate, and resisting every attempt to lead them into the pen.
The conductor could manage temperamental soloists, but the obstreperous brass section, which played loudly out of turn and ignored his cues, finally exhausted his patience.

obtain.text: Customs that obtain in a small village, where everyone knows everyone else, often fail to hold in a large city, where anonymity changes how people behave.
The economist cautioned that the link between interest rates and inflation, though reliable in the past, may no longer obtain under the new global conditions.
Newton's laws obtain for everyday objects such as falling apples and rolling carts; at the scale of atoms, however, they cease to apply and quantum mechanics must take over.

obtuse.text: The clues in the detective story were so heavy-handed that only the most obtuse reader could fail to identify the murderer by the second chapter.
Though brilliant with numbers, the analyst was strangely obtuse about people, never noticing that his colleagues' polite smiles concealed growing irritation.
The editor's letter was gently worded, but the author was so obtuse that he mistook her rejection for a request to submit more chapters.

officious.text: The officious hall monitor insisted on inspecting every visitor's bag and lecturing each one on the building's history, though no one had asked for either service.
Maria appreciated help with the move, but her officious neighbor rearranged the kitchen cabinets without asking and then criticized where she had placed the dishes.
Tourists found the museum guard officious: he hovered beside each group, correcting their pronunciation of artists' names and telling them how long to look at each painting.

opaque.text: The contract's language was so opaque that even the company's own lawyers disagreed about what obligations it imposed.
Critics complain that the agency's decision-making process remains opaque, since it never publishes the criteria it uses to award grants.
Although the philosopher's early essays are lucid, his later work is opaque, full of invented terminology that few readers can decipher.

opulence.text: Visitors to the palace are struck by its opulence: gilded ceilings, marble staircases, and chandeliers of hand-cut crystal fill every room.
The novel contrasts the opulence of the banker's mansion with the squalid tenements where the workers in his factories live.
During the port city's commercial boom, merchant families displayed their opulence through lavish balls, imported silks, and private art collections.

ornate.text: The architect rejected the ornate style of the previous century, stripping away carved garlands and gilded moldings in favor of clean, unadorned surfaces.
Readers accustomed to plain modern prose often find the novelist's ornate sentences exhausting, weighed down as they are with elaborate metaphors and nested clauses.
The ceremonial sword was far too ornate for battle; its hilt was encrusted with jewels and engraved with intricate hunting scenes.

ossify.text: Once a lively forum for dissent, the academy gradually ossified, its members repeating the same doctrines year after year and rejecting any painter who departed from them.
The reformer warned that without periodic review, even well-intentioned regulations tend to ossify into rigid procedures whose original purpose no one remembers.
Linguists note that phrases once used creatively can ossify into cliches, fixed expressions that speakers repeat without any awareness of their original imagery.
