ostentatious.text: The newly rich banker built an ostentatious mansion with gold-plated faucets and a fountain in the foyer, determined that no visitor would overlook his wealth.
Although she could easily afford luxury, the heiress avoided ostentatious displays, preferring plain clothing and a modest car.
Critics found the monument ostentatious, arguing that its towering columns and gilded eagles were designed to impress rather than to honor the dead.

ostracize.text: After he reported the fraud to regulators, the accountant was ostracized by his colleagues, who stopped inviting him to meetings and refused to eat lunch with him.
In many small villages, a family that broke the community's customs risked being ostracized, cut off from trade and social life alike.
Rather than ostracize the dissenting member, the society invited her to present her objections at its annual meeting.

overweening.text: The general's overweening confidence led him to dismiss his scouts' warnings, and he marched his army straight into the ambush they had predicted.
Her colleagues admired her talent but resented her overweening manner: she routinely claimed credit for group projects and interrupted senior partners to correct them.
Critics faulted the new director's overweening ambition, noting that he had presumed to redesign the historic galleries without consulting a single curator.

palatable.text: The proposal to raise taxes was unpopular, but the mayor made it more palatable by pairing it with a promise to repair every school roof in the district.
Though the medicine was bitter, the pharmacist mixed it with honey so that it would be palatable to the children who had to take it.
Many voters found neither candidate appealing, yet the moderate's platform was at least palatable, containing nothing they considered outright objectionable.

palaver.text: While the kitchen prepared the next course, the waiters palavered by the door about the weather and their weekend plans, ignoring the diners who needed attention.
The committee members palavered for an hour about parking spaces and coffee brands, so the substantive budget question was never even raised.
Rather than get to the point, the salesman would palaver endlessly about his vacation and his nephew's soccer games until the customer finally walked out.

palimpsest.text: The old manor house is a palimpsest: Victorian wallpaper peels away to reveal Georgian paneling, and beneath the modern floor lie traces of a medieval hearth.
Scholars read the heavily amended constitution as a palimpsest, since each revision layered new principles over older clauses that were never fully erased.
The artist's canvas became a palimpsest of her changing intentions; x-rays revealed at least three earlier compositions beneath the final painted surface.

panacea.text: Enthusiasts touted the new software as a panacea for every inefficiency in the office, but staff soon found that it solved some problems while creating several others.
Economists cautioned that free trade is not a panacea; although it can raise overall wealth, it cannot by itself cure unemployment, inequality, or poor infrastructure.
Nineteenth-century peddlers hawked tonics said to cure everything from baldness to heartbreak, yet each supposed panacea usually contained little but alcohol and sugar.

panache.text: The pianist played with such panache, flourishing her hands and adding improvised ornaments, that even the plainest etude seemed dazzling.
Although the restaurant's food was ordinary, the owner ran it with panache, greeting guests in a velvet jacket and presenting each dish with theatrical flair.
The architect's designs lacked panache; they were sound and practical but so plain that they rarely attracted a second glance.

panegyric.text: The retirement dinner featured a lengthy panegyric in which the dean praised the professor's scholarship, generosity, and wit in the most elevated language.
Reviewers expected a balanced biography, yet the book reads as a panegyric, lavishing admiration on its subject while ignoring his well-documented failures.
Far from delivering the sharp critique the audience anticipated, the rival poet offered a panegyric, extolling the laureate's verse as the finest of the century.

paradoxical.text: It seems paradoxical that adding a new road can worsen traffic, yet planners have found that extra lanes often attract so many new drivers that congestion increases.
The philosopher's paradoxical claim that we are most free when we bind ourselves to rules puzzled his students until he illustrated it with the example of language.
Though it sounds paradoxical, some patients report feeling less anxious after learning a grim diagnosis, because certainty is easier to bear than doubt.

paragon-n1.text: Among the violinists of her generation, she was considered a paragon, the standard against which every young performer's technique and tone were measured.
The old textbook held up the cathedral as a paragon for students of architecture to emulate, arguing that no later building had matched its harmony of proportion.
Colleagues regarded the surgeon as a paragon without rival in the hospital; when difficult cases arrived, other doctors sought her judgment before making any decision.

paragon-n2.text: With its punctual trains, spotless stations, and clear signage, the city's transit system is often cited as a paragon of efficiency.
The novelist's heroine is a paragon of patience: through years of betrayal and hardship, she never once loses her temper or her compassion.
Though the founder was celebrated as a paragon of thrift, his private letters reveal lavish spending that contradicted the frugal image he cultivated.

pariah.text: After testifying against his former partners, the accountant became a pariah in the financial district; old friends crossed the street to avoid him.
After the novelist mocked the town's founding family in a thinly veiled satire, she became a pariah there, greeted with silence at the market and barred from the reading club she had started.
Once welcomed at every gala, the collector found himself a pariah after the forgeries were exposed, shunned by the very circles that had courted him.

parochial.text: The newspaper's parochial coverage, focused almost entirely on local gossip, left readers ignorant of events beyond the county line.
Critics accused the committee of parochial thinking, since it judged every proposal solely by its effect on a single department rather than on the university as a whole.
Traveling abroad for the first time, the student realized how parochial her views had been, shaped entirely by the small town where she had grown up.

parsimonious.text: Even with millions in his bank account, Fred was so parsimonious that he followed a diet consisting of nothing more than bread and canned soup.
The parsimonious landlord refused to repair the broken heater, insisting that tenants could simply wear more sweaters during the winter.
Although he was a millionaire, the collector was so parsimonious that he reused tea bags and walked miles to avoid paying bus fare.
The foundation's parsimonious grants, rarely enough to cover even basic expenses, disappointed researchers who had hoped for generous support.

parvenu.text: Although the parvenu had purchased the grandest house on the avenue, the old families never invited him to dinner, regarding his fortune as too recent to be respectable.
In the novel, the heroine's father is a parvenu who made millions in railways, yet his ostentatious carriages only confirm the aristocrats' view that money cannot buy breeding.
The dowager dismissed the young industrialist as a parvenu, observing that he had acquired a fortune in a single decade but none of the manners that old wealth supposedly confers.

pastoral.text: The painting offers a pastoral vision of shepherds resting beneath oak trees, a far cry from the grimy industrial cities where most of its buyers lived.
Weary of the noise of the capital, the poet retreated to a pastoral village of meadows and grazing sheep, where he wrote his most tranquil verses.
The symphony's slow movement is pastoral in mood, evoking birdsong, flowing streams and gentle green hills rather than the storms of the preceding section.

patent.text: The witness's story was a patent fabrication; she claimed to have seen the suspect clearly from a window that, as the photographs showed, faced a brick wall.
Despite the manager's efforts to appear calm, his anxiety was patent to everyone in the room: he stammered, fumbled with his notes, and kept glancing toward the door.
The flaw in the argument was so patent that even first-year students spotted it at once, which made the author's failure to address it all the more puzzling.

patronize.text: The tour guide patronized the visitors, explaining the simplest facts in a slow, exaggerated voice as though they were small children.
Although the senior partner meant to be encouraging, his habit of praising junior colleagues for 'trying so hard' made them feel patronized.
Critics accused the documentary of patronizing its rural subjects, portraying them as quaint and simple rather than as people capable of understanding their own lives.

paucity.text: The paucity of reliable records from the period means that historians must reconstruct daily life largely from a handful of letters and tax receipts.
Despite the paucity of rainfall, the desert farmers coaxed impressive harvests from the land by using ancient irrigation techniques.
Reviewers praised the film's visuals but lamented the paucity of genuine ideas in its script, which relied almost entirely on stock situations and cliches.

pecuniary.text: The volunteers insisted their motives were entirely charitable, and indeed none of them received any pecuniary reward for the hundreds of hours they contributed.
Although the scholarship carried great prestige, its pecuniary value was modest, covering little more than the cost of textbooks for a single semester.
The ethics board required each member to disclose any pecuniary interest in the project, such as stock holdings or consulting fees, before voting on it.

pedantic.text: The pedantic reviewer devoted half of his critique to the author's misuse of a semicolon, ignoring the novel's ambitious themes entirely.
Students found the lecturer pedantic, since he interrupted every discussion to correct minor points of Latin grammar.
Although the scholar's footnotes are exhaustive, they are never pedantic; each one illuminates the argument rather than merely displaying erudition.

pedestrian.text: Critics dismissed the novel as pedestrian, noting that its predictable plot and flat prose offered nothing readers had not seen many times before.
Although the architect's early sketches were daring, the final building was pedestrian: a plain box indistinguishable from the offices around it.
The menu was surprisingly pedestrian for a restaurant with such lofty ambitions, relying on familiar dishes prepared without any creative twist.

peevish.text: Deprived of his afternoon nap, the toddler grew peevish, whining at every small frustration and pushing away the toys he usually loved.
The editor's peevish marginal notes, complaining about everything from comma placement to the font, made the author dread receiving her manuscripts back.
Long delays at the airport had made the passengers peevish, and the gate agent endured a steady stream of petty complaints about trivial inconveniences.

pejorative.text: The word 'bureaucrat' has acquired such a pejorative sense that many civil servants prefer to describe themselves as public administrators.
Many art historians note that 'Gothic' began as a pejorative label, applied by critics who regarded medieval architecture as crude and barbaric.
The editor removed several pejorative terms from the article, explaining that such disparaging language undermined the author's claim to objectivity.

pellucid.text: Unlike the dense treatises of his predecessors, the philosopher's essays were pellucid, explaining even abstract questions of logic in prose that any educated reader could follow.
The instruction manual, written by engineers for engineers, was anything but pellucid; lay readers found its jargon and diagrams utterly baffling.
Her lecture on tax law was so pellucid that students who had dreaded the topic left the hall confident they understood every provision she had discussed.

penurious-adj1.text: The composer spent his final years penurious, living in a single unheated room and selling his manuscripts for whatever meager sums the local publishers would pay.
Many of the immigrant families were penurious when they arrived, possessing only the clothes they wore and a few borrowed coins.
Though the family had once owned vast estates, a series of disastrous investments left them penurious, unable even to afford the rent on a modest cottage.

penurious-adj2.text: Sarah chose to be penurious and drive a beat-up VW, though with her wealth she could have easily afforded an Italian sports car.
Despite his considerable fortune, the landlord was so penurious that he refused to repair the building's broken heating, preferring to let tenants shiver rather than spend a dime.
The wealthy patron proved surprisingly penurious; after promising to fund the entire exhibition, she haggled over the cost of every frame and label.
Although the company earned record profits, its penurious owners cut employees' holiday bonuses and rationed office supplies as though bankruptcy were imminent.

percipient.text: A percipient critic, she noticed that the novel's seemingly random chapter titles actually formed an acrostic that the author had never publicly acknowledged.
Most visitors saw only a charming village, but the percipient anthropologist recognized in its festival calendar the remnants of an ancient agricultural cycle.
The therapist was unusually percipient, detecting from a client's hesitations and slight changes in tone the anxieties he had not yet admitted even to himself.

peremptory.text: The new supervisor's peremptory manner, issuing orders without explanation and tolerating no questions, quickly alienated a staff accustomed to collaborative decisions.
Rather than politely requesting the documents, the official sent a peremptory note demanding them by noon and threatening penalties for any delay.
Guests were taken aback by the host's peremptory tone as he directed them where to sit, when to eat, and which topics they were permitted to discuss.

perennial.text: Flooding is a perennial problem in the delta; every generation builds new levees, and every generation watches the river overwhelm them.
Questions about the nature of justice are perennial, debated by ancient philosophers and modern jurists alike without ever being settled.
Although fashions in children's literature come and go, fairy tales remain perennial favorites, read aloud to children century after century.

perfidy.text: The general never forgave the perfidy of his closest adviser, who had secretly sold the army's battle plans to the enemy.
Many revenge tragedies turn on an act of perfidy, as a trusted friend or relative betrays the hero for personal gain.
When the partner who had sworn loyalty to the firm was caught leaking client files to a competitor, his colleagues were stunned by such perfidy.

perfunctory.text: The inspector gave the factory only a perfunctory glance before signing the safety certificate, missing the frayed wiring that later caused a fire.
After years of performing the same role, the actor delivered his lines in a perfunctory manner, reciting them accurately but without any trace of feeling.
His apology was perfunctory, a mumbled 'sorry' offered without eye contact, and it did little to repair the trust his careless remarks had damaged.

peripatetic.text: The medieval friars led a peripatetic existence, walking from village to village to preach and seldom sleeping under the same roof two nights in succession.
Rather than lecturing from a podium, the philosopher preferred a peripatetic style of teaching, strolling along the garden paths while his students walked beside him.
A peripatetic naturalist, she covered hundreds of miles of trail on foot each year, recording birdsong along routes that no vehicle could reach.

pernicious.text: Economists warn that inflation has a pernicious effect on savings, quietly eroding their value year after year without the owners noticing.
The pernicious rumor spread slowly through the town, and by the time the mayor learned of it, his reputation had been irreparably damaged.
Some invasive vines are pernicious because they grow unnoticed beneath the canopy, gradually strangling the trees that support them.

perpetuate.text: Critics argue that the textbook perpetuates outdated stereotypes, repeating myths about immigrant groups that historians discredited decades ago.
By rewarding only short-term profits, the bonus system perpetuated the very risk-taking that had nearly ruined the firm.
The festival was founded to perpetuate the region's folk music, ensuring that songs once passed down orally would survive for future generations.

perquisite.text: A chauffeured car was among the perquisites of the ambassador's office, along with an official residence and a generous entertainment allowance.
In feudal society, the right to hunt in the royal forests was a perquisite of the nobility; a commoner caught with a deer faced severe punishment.
When the company cut costs, executives lost many of the perquisites they had come to expect, including first-class travel and memberships at exclusive clubs.

perspicacious.text: While other investors were dazzled by the company's growth, one perspicacious analyst noticed that its revenue depended almost entirely on a single contract due to expire.
The judge was perspicacious enough to see that the two witnesses, though apparently strangers, had rehearsed their testimony together.
Historians praise the minister as perspicacious, for she foresaw the consequences of the treaty's vague borders decades before disputes over them erupted.

pertinent.text: The judge ruled that the defendant's childhood was not pertinent to the charges and ordered the lawyer to limit his questions to the night of the crime.
Before the interview, the reporter gathered every pertinent document, discarding hundreds of pages that had no bearing on the story.
The student's essay was eloquent but rarely pertinent, drifting into anecdotes that had little to do with the question she had been asked.

perturb.text: The captain's calm voice over the intercom did little to reassure the passengers, who were perturbed by the sudden drop in altitude.
Nothing seemed to perturb the veteran surgeon; even when alarms sounded in the operating room, she continued working with steady hands.
Reports of irregularities in the vaccine trial perturbed regulators, who immediately ordered an independent review of the data.

peruse.text: Before signing the lease, Hana perused every clause, underlining ambiguous phrases and noting questions to raise with the landlord.
Rather than skimming the report as his colleagues had, the auditor perused it line by line, and so he alone noticed the discrepancy in the third appendix.
Scholars who have perused the diaries closely argue that the poet's supposed breakdown was exaggerated by her early biographers.

petulant.text: When the committee rejected his proposal, the petulant professor stormed out of the meeting and refused to speak to his colleagues for a week.
The toddler grew petulant whenever his nap was delayed, whining and swatting at anyone who tried to comfort him.
Critics found the tennis star's petulant outbursts, smashing rackets and snapping at line judges over minor calls, unworthy of a champion.

phantasmagorical.text: The painter's late canvases are phantasmagorical: melting towers, floating staircases, and figures that dissolve into smoke, as though each scene came from a fevered dream.
Critics found the film's plot phantasmagorical rather than realistic, a shifting parade of illusions in which viewers could never tell what was actually happening.
Recovering from a high fever, the patient described phantasmagorical visions of dancing shadows and talking statues that he knew, in retrospect, had never existed.

philistine.text: The council's philistine decision to demolish the historic theater for a parking lot outraged residents who valued the building's ornate architecture.
He scoffed at the symphony as mere noise and called poetry a waste of paper, a philistine attitude that dismayed his literature-loving wife.
Critics accused the publisher of philistine priorities, since he refused to print any novel without a car chase and dismissed literary fiction as pretentious and unprofitable.

phlegmatic.text: Even when the stock market collapsed and colleagues panicked, the phlegmatic trader merely shrugged, sipped his coffee, and continued reviewing his spreadsheets.
The fans screamed and wept as the final goal went in, but the phlegmatic coach barely changed expression, simply noting the time on his watch.
Her phlegmatic temperament made her an ideal emergency dispatcher, since frantic callers rarely managed to disturb her steady, unemotional voice.

picayune.text: The editor's comments were so picayune, quibbling over commas and fonts, that the author wondered whether she had engaged with the manuscript's actual arguments at all.
Rather than address the substance of the proposal, the council members raised picayune objections about the color of the binder and the width of the margins.
Colleagues found him picayune, a manager who would reprimand staff for arriving two minutes late while ignoring serious problems in the department's budget.

pillory.text: The tabloids pilloried the actor after his ill-judged remarks, running mocking cartoons and headlines that held him up to nationwide ridicule.
Although her findings were later vindicated, the young scientist was pilloried at the conference, where senior researchers openly mocked her data before a laughing audience.
Satirists of the eighteenth century loved to pillory pompous aristocrats, and pamphlets mocking their vanity and hypocrisy were read aloud to jeering crowds in coffeehouses.

pine.text: Exiled to a remote island, the deposed king pined for the capital, writing letter after letter begging to be allowed to return.
Though she had longed to leave her small hometown, after a year in the crowded city Clara found herself pining for its quiet streets and familiar faces.
Months at sea, the sailors pined for fresh fruit and the company of their families, and they talked of little else during the long evenings.

pinnacle.text: Winning the national prize marked the pinnacle of her career; she never again produced work that earned such acclaim.
Many critics regard the cathedral as the pinnacle of Gothic architecture, since later builders, unable to surpass its soaring vaults, turned instead to heavier and less daring designs.
Although he had risen to the pinnacle of the legal profession, the judge often said he had been happier as a struggling young lawyer.

piquant.text: A squeeze of lime and a pinch of chili made the otherwise bland stew piquant, and the guests asked for second helpings.
The chef balances the richness of the pork with a piquant sauce of mustard, vinegar and pickled peppers that sharpens every bite.
Though some diners found the aged cheese too strong, others relished its piquant flavor, which lingered pleasantly on the tongue.

pith.text: The senator's speech rambled for an hour, but its pith could be summed up in a single sentence: the bridge would be built, and taxpayers would fund it.
Good editors cut away ornamental digressions and tangents so that the pith of an argument stands out clearly, no longer buried beneath material the reader could safely skip.
After three days of testimony, the jurors struggled to identify the pith of the case amid all the technical detail and conflicting expert opinions.

pithy.text: Rather than delivering a long speech, the departing senator offered a pithy farewell of two sentences that the audience quoted for years afterward.
The editor trimmed the rambling paragraph into a single pithy line that conveyed the argument more forcefully than the original page had.
Aphorisms endure because they are pithy: a handful of words can capture an insight that would take a philosopher chapters to explain.

pittance.text: The seamstresses worked twelve-hour days for a pittance, earning barely enough to buy bread and coal for their families.
The company offered the inventor a pittance for his patent, a sum that looked absurd once his device began earning millions.
Although the grant was a pittance compared with the budgets of large laboratories, it allowed the young researcher to buy the one instrument she needed.

placate.text: To placate the angry investors, the company promised to replace its chief executive and to publish independent audits every quarter.
The ministry placated the striking dockworkers with a modest raise and a promise of safer equipment, and the ports reopened within days.
The king hoped that lowering the grain tax would placate the rebellious provinces, but the unrest only spread.

placid.text: The placid librarian listened to the patron's furious complaint without raising her voice, then calmly explained the late-fee policy once more.
Unlike his volatile brother, Tomas was placid by nature; delays, insults and broken appliances all failed to ruffle him.
Breeders prize the horse for its placid temperament, since it remains unbothered even amid the noise and crowds of a busy city street.

platitude.text: Instead of offering concrete plans, the candidate relied on platitudes such as 'the future belongs to all of us,' which no voter could possibly dispute.
Grieving families often find a platitude like 'everything happens for a reason' more hurtful than simple silence.
The critic dismissed the novel's closing moral, that honesty is the best policy, as a platitude unworthy of such a sophisticated writer.

plodding.text: The old ox moved at a plodding pace, dragging the heavy cart up the muddy slope one slow, heavy step at a time.
Weighed down by their packs, the hikers fell into a plodding rhythm, their boots sinking deep into the snow with each weary stride.
The tortoise's plodding progress across the garden seemed hopeless, yet by evening it had reached the far wall.

ploy.text: The offer of a free trial was merely a ploy to collect customers' credit card numbers, which were then charged automatically once the month ended.
The general's retreat was a clever ploy: once the enemy pursued his troops into the narrow valley, his reserves closed in from both sides.
Some critics dismissed the author's announcement that this would be her final novel as a marketing ploy designed to boost sales.

plucky.text: Though the plucky little firm had no capital and only three employees, it challenged the industry giant in court and ultimately won.
Despite a broken wrist, the plucky climber insisted on finishing the ascent, determined not to abandon her team a few hundred meters from the summit.
Critics dismissed the underfunded expedition as doomed, yet its plucky members pressed on through blizzards and food shortages until they reached the pole.

poignant.text: The documentary's most poignant scene shows an elderly man returning to the village where he was born, only to find it submerged beneath a reservoir.
Letters from soldiers to their children are especially poignant, since many of the writers never returned home to see the families they addressed.
Though the novel is often comic, its final chapter is poignant, and many readers admit to weeping as the old friends say goodbye.

polemic.text: The pamphlet was less a balanced analysis than a polemic: its author never once acknowledged a reasonable point made by the reformers, and he questioned their motives on every page.
In a fierce polemic published in the journal, the economist denounced her rivals' models as not merely flawed but intellectually dishonest.
Although the author intended the book as a calm historical survey, reviewers read it as a polemic against the modern art establishment.

pollyannaish.text: Even as floodwaters rose around the town, the mayor issued Pollyannaish statements assuring residents that the levees would certainly hold and nothing would be damaged.
The analyst warned that the company's Pollyannaish forecasts ignored rising costs and shrinking demand, projecting growth where the evidence pointed toward decline.
Critics called the novel's ending Pollyannaish, since every character, however badly wronged, is reconciled and rewarded in a single cheerful chapter.

ponderous.text: Unlike the nimble gazelles that scattered at the first sound, the elephants made their ponderous way across the plain, each heavy step raising a cloud of dust.
Burdened with heavy armor, the knights advanced at a ponderous pace, allowing the lightly equipped archers to outmaneuver them with ease.
The freighter, loaded far beyond its usual capacity, made ponderous progress through the harbor while smaller vessels darted nimbly past it.

pontificate.text: At every family dinner, Uncle Richard would pontificate about foreign policy as though he were the only person present who had ever read a newspaper.
Instead of listening to the farmers' concerns, the consultant pontificated on the principles of agronomy, lecturing them with a certainty his limited experience hardly justified.
The critic tended to pontificate rather than argue, handing down grand pronouncements on which films were masterpieces without ever explaining his reasons.

portentous.text: The sudden silence of the birds seemed portentous to the villagers, who had learned that such stillness often preceded a violent storm.
Economists found the sharp drop in shipping orders portentous, interpreting it as an early sign of the recession that arrived six months later.
In the play, a portentous dream in which the king sees his crown crack foreshadows the rebellion that will eventually cost him his throne.

posit.text: To explain the planet's irregular orbit, astronomers posited an unseen companion body, a hypothesis that later telescopes confirmed.
Classical economic models simply posit a perfectly rational consumer without testing the premise, an assumption that behavioral researchers have repeatedly challenged.
The detective's theory rested on a single unproven premise: she posited that the victim knew his attacker, and every later inference followed from that assumption.

powwow.text: Before presenting the proposal to the board, the designers held a quick powwow in the hallway to agree on who would answer which questions.
What was scheduled as a formal negotiation turned into a relaxed powwow over coffee, with both sides sketching ideas on napkins.
Every Friday afternoon the editors gather for an unstructured powwow, trading gossip and story ideas without an agenda or minutes.

pragmatic.text: Rather than waiting for a perfect theoretical model, the engineers took a pragmatic approach, testing dozens of prototypes and keeping whatever worked.
The new mayor was pragmatic rather than ideological, adopting policies from any source if experience showed that they reduced crime.
Although her training was highly theoretical, years in rural clinics made the doctor pragmatic, trusting what she observed in patients over what textbooks predicted.

precarious.text: The climbers' camp was perched on a precarious ledge, where a single misstep or a gust of wind could send them over the edge.
With no savings and a temporary job that could vanish without notice, the family's finances were precarious, one unexpected bill away from disaster.
The coalition government was precarious from the start, depending on the support of a small party that threatened to withdraw at every disagreement.

precedent.text: The judge's ruling set a precedent that later courts cited repeatedly when deciding similar disputes over digital privacy.
Administrators refused the student's request for an extension, fearing that it would create a precedent that every other student could then invoke.
Lacking any precedent for such a case, the tribunal had to reason from general principles rather than from earlier decisions.

precipitate-adj.text: The board regretted its precipitate decision to close the factory, made in a single afternoon without consulting engineers who could have fixed the problem cheaply.
Cautious by temperament, the scientist warned against precipitate conclusions drawn from a single experiment, insisting that the results be replicated first.
The general's precipitate retreat, ordered before scouts had even confirmed the enemy's strength, abandoned a position that could easily have been held.

precipitate-v.text: The minister's careless remark precipitated a diplomatic crisis, prompting both countries to recall their ambassadors within days.
A single failed harvest can precipitate famine in regions where grain reserves are already dangerously low.
Historians debate whether the assassination actually precipitated the war or merely provided a pretext for a conflict that existing tensions had made inevitable.

precipitous.text: The board's precipitous decision to fire the director, made within hours of a single critical article, was soon regretted when the accusations proved false.
Historians argue that the precipitous withdrawal of troops, ordered without any plan for transferring security, left the region vulnerable to chaos.
Rather than making a precipitous commitment to the merger, the cautious chairwoman insisted on months of study and independent review.

preclude.text: The contract's exclusivity clause precludes the author from publishing with any other house for five years, so her next two novels must go to the same firm.
A single contaminated sample may not preclude the study's publication, but it does require the researchers to repeat several experiments.
The knee injury precluded any chance of her competing in the final, so she watched from the stands as her rival won the title.

precocious.text: A precocious reader, the girl was working her way through her parents' collection of Victorian novels by the age of six.
The composer's precocious talent astonished his teachers, who found that by the age of eight he could write fugues more polished than their own.
Although precocious children often attract admiring attention, early brilliance does not necessarily predict great achievement in adulthood, and many prodigies settle into ordinary careers.

predilection.text: The critic's predilection for experimental fiction led him to champion little-known writers while ignoring more conventional bestsellers.
Despite her own predilection for fiery food, the chef designed a mild menu to suit the tastes of the conference guests.
The collector's predilection for maritime paintings was obvious to every visitor: seascapes lined each hallway, and model ships crowded the shelves.

preempt.text: Under the new treaty, national law preempts any conflicting provincial regulation, so local rules on pesticide use no longer apply.
The chief executive's surprise announcement preempted the rest of the agenda; the board set aside its planned discussion and spent the afternoon on the merger.
Urgent repairs to the roof preempted the museum's plans for a new wing, consuming the funds originally set aside for expansion.

preemptive.text: Anticipating criticism of the delay, the mayor issued a preemptive statement blaming the contractor before any reporter could raise the issue.
Suspecting that a rival firm was about to lure away her best engineer, the director made a preemptive offer of a promotion and a raise.
The chess player's preemptive advance on the queen's side prevented her opponent from launching the attack he had been preparing for several moves.

prescience.text: The economist's prescience was confirmed when the housing market collapsed exactly as she had predicted in a paper that most of her peers had ignored.
Some early science fiction writers showed remarkable prescience, describing video calls and pocket computers long before such devices existed.
Lacking any prescience about the coming drought, the farmers planted thirsty crops and lost nearly their entire harvest.

presentiment.text: Before boarding the ship, the traveler had a vague presentiment of disaster, and though he could not explain it, he canceled his passage at the last moment.
Throughout the novel, the heroine is haunted by a presentiment that her brother will not return from the war, a dread the final chapter sadly confirms.
Although the morning was bright and calm, Elena woke with a presentiment of misfortune that she could not shake as she prepared for the interview.

presumption-n1.text: The study challenges the presumption that older workers are less adaptable, showing that they learn new software as quickly as their younger colleagues.
The legal system operates on the presumption of innocence: a defendant need not prove anything, since the burden falls entirely on the prosecution.
Early astronomers worked under the presumption that the heavens were perfect and unchanging, so the appearance of a new star in the sky astonished them.

presumption-n2.text: The courtier's presumption in addressing the queen by her first name shocked the assembled nobles, who waited to see how she would punish his insolence.
She was astonished at his presumption: having met her only once, he had already announced their engagement to his friends.
The junior clerk had the presumption to rewrite his supervisor's report without asking, and he was promptly reprimanded for overstepping his role.

presumptuous.text: The campaign manager warned her overconfident staff that it would be presumptuous to plan a victory celebration before a single vote had been counted.
The graduate student's presumptuous critique of the eminent professor, delivered uninvited at their very first meeting, left the room in stunned silence.
Though he meant only to help, the guest struck his hosts as presumptuous when he rearranged their kitchen cabinets on his first evening in the house.

prevail-v1.text: In the years after the war, a mood of cautious optimism prevailed, and families spent freely on new homes and appliances.
The custom of arranged marriage still prevails in some rural districts, although it has largely disappeared from the cities.
The belief that illness was caused by bad air prevailed among physicians for centuries, until microscopes revealed the role of microorganisms.

prevail-v2.text: Although the underdog team was outmatched in size and experience, it prevailed in overtime, stunning the favored champions.
In the long legal battle between the inventor and the corporation, the inventor eventually prevailed, winning both the patent and substantial damages.
The debate grew heated, but in the end the cautious faction prevailed over the ambitious one, and the committee voted to postpone the expansion.

prevaricate.text: Bobby learned not to prevaricate when his teacher asked him where his homework was; by giving a straightforward answer, he would avoid invoking the teacher's wrath.
When asked directly whether he had seen the documents, the witness prevaricated, talking at length about the office layout without ever answering yes or no.
Rather than prevaricate about the budget shortfall, the new treasurer stated the figures plainly and proposed immediate cuts.
Journalists grew frustrated as the spokesperson continued to prevaricate, answering every pointed question with vague references to ongoing reviews.

primacy.text: The historian argued that the city's primacy among Mediterranean ports rested less on its geography than on the stability of its banking institutions.
Throughout his career, the philosopher insisted on the primacy of experience over theory, maintaining that no abstract system should override what observation reveals.
Once unchallenged, the company's primacy in the market began to erode as smaller rivals introduced cheaper and more innovative products.

pristine-adj1.text: The expedition found the valley pristine, and the surveyors, who had grown used to clear-cut slopes and polluted streams elsewhere, could scarcely believe no one had ever settled there.
Conservationists fought to keep the remote coral reef pristine, banning fishing boats and tourists from its most fragile sections.
Once pristine, the coastline is now lined with hotels and parking lots, and its wetlands have been drained for development.

pristine-adj2.text: Although the novel was printed a century ago, the collector's copy is pristine, its pages crisp and its binding uncracked as though no one had ever opened it.
The rental agency demanded that the apartment be returned in pristine condition, and it deducted fees for even the faintest scuff on the walls.
The chef insisted that every knife and cutting board be pristine before service began, and he sent back any utensil bearing the faintest smudge.

probity.text: The treasurer's probity was never questioned; in forty years of handling the charity's funds, not a single penny was misplaced or misused.
Voters had grown weary of scandal, so the candidate's reputation for probity, rather than any specific policy, became her greatest electoral asset.
The auditors expected to find fraud, but instead the records revealed the manager's probity: every expense was documented and every conflict of interest disclosed.

prodigal.text: The prodigal heir squandered his inheritance within five years, spending lavishly on racehorses, yachts, and parties for hundreds of guests.
Critics accused the government of prodigal spending, pointing to a new presidential palace built while hospitals lacked basic supplies.
Unlike her prodigal brother, who bought every expensive gadget that caught his eye, Maria saved nearly half of her modest salary.

prodigious.text: The young violinist's prodigious memory allowed her to perform dozens of concertos without ever consulting a score.
Building the cathedral required a prodigious effort, involving thousands of workers and more than a century of labor.
The storm dumped a prodigious amount of snow on the city, burying cars entirely and closing the roads for a week.

profligate-adj.text: The profligate administration borrowed heavily to fund lavish festivals and monuments, leaving its successors with debts they could scarcely repay.
Although he earned a modest salary, the clerk led a profligate life, spending each paycheck on fine wines and tailored suits within days of receiving it.
Economists warned that profligate use of the emergency fund, drawn down to cover routine expenses, would leave the state unprepared for a genuine crisis.
Far from being profligate, the museum's director stretched each small grant remarkably far, buying secondhand display cases and relying on volunteer carpenters.

profligate-n.text: The novel's hero is a profligate who gambles away three fortunes before finally learning the value of thrift.
Although his creditors dismissed the young count as a profligate, his lavish spending on artists eventually produced one of the finest collections in the country.
The bank refused to lend to such a notorious profligate, since he had already squandered his inheritance and defaulted on several previous loans.

profuse.text: The actor's profuse apologies for arriving late seemed excessive; he spent more time apologizing than the delay had actually cost.
After the spring rains, the blossoms on the hillsides were so profuse that the grass beneath them was barely visible from the road.
The patient's profuse sweating alarmed the nurse, who noticed that his sheets were soaked through within a few minutes.

profusion.text: The market offered a dazzling profusion of spices, from saffron and cardamom to dozens of chili varieties the visitors had never seen.
The Baroque chapel is decorated with a profusion of gilded angels, carved flowers and painted clouds, leaving hardly an inch of wall unadorned.
Rather than a scarcity of data, modern researchers face a profusion of it, and the challenge lies in separating meaningful signals from noise.

prognostication.text: The economist's prognostication of a housing collapse was ridiculed at the time, but within two years prices had fallen exactly as she had predicted.
Weather forecasting has progressed from folklore to science, yet any prognostication beyond ten days remains notoriously unreliable.
The astrologer's vague prognostication that great changes lay ahead was carefully worded so that almost any future event could be claimed as its fulfillment.

prolific.text: A prolific scholar, the historian published a new book nearly every year while also editing two journals.
Although she wrote only two novels, the author was prolific as an essayist, producing hundreds of reviews and columns over four decades.
The painter's prolific output, thousands of canvases over a long career, has made it difficult for curators to distinguish his masterpieces from his routine work.

prolixity.text: The lawyer's prolixity tested the jury's patience; a point that required a single sentence would stretch, in his telling, over twenty tedious minutes.
Editors trimmed the manuscript by half, since the author's prolixity had buried a genuinely original argument beneath pages of repetitive digression.
In contrast to the prolixity of his earlier novels, the writer's final book is spare and concise, with no chapter longer than a few pages.

promulgate.text: After months of deliberation, the council promulgated new building codes, publishing them in the official gazette so that every contractor would know the requirements.
The monarch promulgated the edict throughout the kingdom, ordering heralds to read it aloud in every town square.
Early advocates of the germ theory worked tirelessly to promulgate their findings, lecturing to physicians and publishing pamphlets to make the discovery widely known.

propitiate.text: The ancient farmers offered the first fruits of each harvest in an effort to propitiate the gods they believed controlled the rain.
Hoping to propitiate the furious client, the architect apologized for the delay and offered to redesign the lobby at no extra cost.
The new manager tried to propitiate the disgruntled employees with a round of raises, but their anger over the layoffs was not so easily soothed.

propitious.text: With interest rates low and consumer demand rising, the moment seemed propitious for launching the new product line.
The sailors waited for propitious winds before setting out, since a strong headwind could delay the crossing by weeks.
Although the early test results were propitious, the researchers cautioned that larger trials might yet reveal serious problems.

proponent.text: A leading proponent of renewable energy, the engineer spent decades urging legislators to fund wind and solar research.
Although she was once a vocal proponent of the plan, the council member turned against it after learning of its true cost.
Proponents of the four-day workweek argue that it improves productivity, while critics warn that it may strain small businesses.

prosaic.text: Visitors expecting a romantic castle were disappointed by the prosaic reality: a squat concrete building housing the regional tax office.
Though the poet's early work was bold and inventive, her later verse struck critics as prosaic, full of flat statements and predictable imagery.
The detective in the novel solves crimes not through brilliant leaps of imagination but through prosaic methods such as checking receipts and interviewing neighbors.

proscribe.text: The new regulations proscribe smoking in all public buildings, including the lobbies and stairwells where it had long been tolerated.
Many ancient legal codes proscribed marriage between close relatives, imposing severe penalties on those who violated the prohibition.
Although the club's charter did not explicitly proscribe political debate at dinner, members observed an unwritten rule against it that newcomers quickly learned.

proselytize.text: Having discovered the benefits of a plant-based diet, Tom began to proselytize at every dinner party, urging each guest to give up meat as he had.
The ruler allowed the foreign monks to practice their faith privately but forbade them to proselytize, fearing that they would win his subjects over to their religion.
Rather than proselytize for her economic theory, the professor presented it alongside its rivals and let students decide which account they found persuasive.

protean.text: A protean performer, she could play a tragic queen one night and a slapstick maid the next, fully convincing in both roles.
The virus proved protean, mutating so rapidly that each season's vaccine was nearly obsolete by the time it reached pharmacies.
The protean intellectual moved easily among the roles of novelist, diplomat, and composer, excelling in each while never settling into one.

provident.text: Provident farmers stored grain during the good years, so that when drought struck the region, their families did not go hungry.
Unlike his spendthrift brother, Marcus was provident, setting aside part of every paycheck for retirement and keeping an emergency fund for unexpected repairs.
The city's provident decision to build reservoirs decades earlier spared it the water rationing that afflicted its neighbors during the long dry spell.

provincial.text: Having never left his hometown, the young editor held provincial views that his cosmopolitan colleagues in the capital found quaint.
The designer's collection was criticized as provincial, reflecting fashions that the great cities had abandoned years earlier.
Sophisticated visitors from the capital once dismissed the town's theater as provincial, yet its daring productions soon made the capital's own stages look stale.

provisional.text: The rebels formed a provisional government to run the country until elections could be held and a permanent constitution drafted.
The committee reached a provisional agreement on the budget, but members stressed that several details remained to be negotiated.
Scientists regard every theory as provisional, subject to revision or even abandonment should new evidence contradict its predictions.

puerile.text: The debate degenerated into puerile name-calling, with the candidates mocking each other's hairstyles rather than discussing policy.
Although the comedy was marketed to adults, critics found its humor puerile, relying on jokes that would amuse only a young schoolboy.
Rather than responding maturely to criticism, the executive sulked and slammed doors, behavior his staff considered puerile in a man of fifty.

pugnacious.text: The pugnacious senator seemed to relish every confrontation, interrupting opponents and challenging them to debate at every opportunity.
Although he was mild-mannered at home, the critic was pugnacious in print, attacking rival scholars with a ferocity that shocked his readers.
The little terrier was absurdly pugnacious, snarling at dogs five times its size and lunging at anyone who approached the gate.

puissant.text: The duke was a puissant lord whose vast armies and wealth allowed him to defy even the king.
Once a puissant force in regional politics, the party had dwindled to a handful of elderly members with no real influence.
Myths describe the storm god as puissant enough to split mountains with a single thunderbolt, and even the other deities feared his wrath.

punctilious.text: The punctilious accountant checked every figure three times, refusing to sign off on the report until even a discrepancy of a few cents had been explained.
Guests at the embassy dinner were expected to observe punctilious etiquette, from the precise order of toasts to the correct form of address for each diplomat.
Although some authors found her tiresome, the editor's punctilious attention to citations meant that no error in her journal ever went uncorrected.

pundit.text: The committee invited a leading pundit on medieval law to testify, since none of its members could interpret the ancient charters themselves.
Although he held no formal degree, the self-taught astronomer was consulted as a pundit by professors who valued his decades of careful observation.
Recognized as a pundit in Sanskrit grammar, the elderly scholar was asked to settle a dispute that had divided younger linguists for years.

pyrrhic.text: The company won its lawsuit, but the victory was pyrrhic: legal fees exceeded the damages awarded, and the bad publicity drove away its biggest clients.
Although the army held the ridge, it lost so many soldiers doing so that the triumph proved pyrrhic, leaving it too weak to continue the campaign.
The strike secured the union a small raise, yet many regarded the outcome as pyrrhic, since the plant closed within a year and every worker lost a job.

quail.text: The young lawyer, confident in rehearsal, quailed when the stern judge fixed her with a withering stare.
Seasoned sailors did not quail before the approaching storm, but the passengers huddled below deck in terror.
Many people would quail at the prospect of speaking before thousands, yet the shy student delivered her commencement address without a tremor.

qualify-1.text: Because she had lived in the district for less than a year, the candidate did not qualify to run for the city council.
Applicants qualify for the grant only if their household income falls below the threshold set by the agency.
After passing the bar examination, he finally qualified to practice law in the state, ending years of work as a paralegal.

qualify-2.text: The scientist praised the study's methods but qualified her endorsement, noting that its small sample limited how broadly the results could be applied.
Asked whether the policy had succeeded, the minister qualified his answer, conceding that it had worked in cities but not in rural areas.
Careful historians qualify their generalizations about an era, acknowledging the many exceptions that a sweeping claim might conceal.

qualm.text: The accountant had no qualms about reporting her employer's fraud, even though she knew that speaking up might cost her the job.
Despite his qualms about the ethics of the experiment, the young researcher agreed to take part, silencing his conscience with the promise of a publication.
Voters who had once supported the project began to express qualms after reports suggested that its environmental impact had been underestimated.

quandary.text: The doctor faced a quandary: the only drug that might save the patient could also trigger a fatal allergic reaction.
Offered a promotion that required moving far from her aging parents, Leila found herself in a quandary, unable to accept or refuse without regret.
Rising sea levels have placed the island nation in a painful quandary, forced to choose between seawalls it cannot afford and abandoning its coastal towns.

querulous.text: The querulous passenger complained about the legroom, the temperature, the meal, and the pilot's announcements before the plane had even left the gate.
Although he had once been cheerful, long illness made the old sailor querulous, and his nurses dreaded his constant grumbling.
The letters reveal a querulous side of the poet, who filled page after page with grievances about his publishers, his neighbors, and his health.

quip.text: Asked whether he was nervous before the debate, the candidate replied with a quip about having survived far tougher audiences at family dinners, and the reporters laughed.
Her lectures were dry and technical, but an occasional quip about the absurdities of academic life kept the students awake.
The novelist was famous for his quips at dinner parties, though friends noted that many of his supposedly spontaneous witticisms had been rehearsed in advance.

quisling.text: When the occupying forces installed a puppet government, the resistance denounced its leader as a quisling who had sold out his own people.
The official was branded a quisling after it emerged that he had passed his country's secrets to the enemy in exchange for money.
Although he claimed to be protecting his fellow citizens, the mayor who collaborated with the invaders was remembered as a quisling who had betrayed his town.

quixotic.text: Her quixotic plan to end world hunger by planting a single orchard in every town ignored the practical problems of transport, funding, and climate.
Colleagues admired his idealism but considered the campaign quixotic: a lone candidate with no funds hoping to unseat an incumbent who had never lost.
Rather than pursue the quixotic dream of a perfectly just society, the pragmatic reformer focused on small, achievable improvements to local courts.

quotidian.text: The painter found beauty in quotidian scenes, such as a woman peeling potatoes or a child tying her shoes, that other artists overlooked.
Although the diary describes a momentous war, most entries record quotidian matters: the price of bread, the weather, a neighbor's cough.
Tourists marvel at the city's grand cathedrals, but the anthropologist studied its quotidian rhythms of commuting, shopping, and cooking.

raconteur.text: A gifted raconteur, the retired ambassador kept dinner guests enthralled for hours with tales of misadventures in distant capitals.
Although his lectures were dry, the professor was a superb raconteur at faculty gatherings, where his amusing anecdotes about eccentric scientists drew crowds.
The host fancied himself a raconteur, but his stories rambled without punch lines, and guests drifted away before he reached the end of each one.

raffish.text: The poet cultivated a raffish image, wearing rumpled velvet jackets, keeping disreputable company and paying his debts only when pressed.
The neighborhood had a raffish charm, with its dimly lit jazz clubs, secondhand bookshops and bohemian residents who ignored the conventions of polite society.
His conservative parents disapproved of his raffish friends, a band of gamblers and struggling actors who stayed out until dawn.

raft.text: The new administration introduced a raft of reforms, from changes in tax policy to an overhaul of the school curriculum.
The drug's approval was delayed after regulators raised a raft of concerns about side effects, dosage, and the design of the clinical trials.
A raft of recent studies has challenged the notion that bilingual children are slower to speak, finding instead that they reach milestones at the same pace.

raillery.text: Her colleagues' raillery about her fondness for bow ties was affectionate, and she laughed along with the good-natured jokes.
The friendly raillery between the two old rivals, full of gentle jibes about each other's golf swing, masked a deep mutual respect.
What began as playful raillery at the dinner table turned hurtful when her brother's teasing touched on her recent divorce.

rakish.text: With his hat tilted at a rakish angle and his reputation for gambling and dueling, the young officer was the despair of respectable mothers.
The novel's rakish hero drinks, duels, and runs up debts across Europe, yet readers cannot help being charmed by his careless wit.
Although she was raised in a strict household, Julia was drawn to rakish companions whose disregard for convention and propriety thrilled her.

rankle.text: Years after the contest, it still rankled the runner-up that the judges had awarded first prize to a close friend of the organizer.
The committee's decision to ignore her research rankled, and she spent months composing a detailed and indignant rebuttal.
Small slights, left unaddressed, can rankle for decades; the historian traces the bitter feud between the two families to a single unreturned greeting.

rapprochement.text: After decades of hostility, the two nations achieved a rapprochement, reopening embassies and signing trade agreements that would have been unthinkable a generation earlier.
The estranged brothers' rapprochement began slowly, with a few tentative letters, and culminated in a warm reunion at their mother's birthday.
Despite the mediator's efforts, no rapprochement between the feuding departments proved possible, since each blamed the other for the project's failure.

rarefied.text: Accustomed to the rarefied world of manuscript auctions and private collectors, the curator was bewildered by the noisy bargaining at the county fair's antique stalls.
The seminar's debates about medieval Latin grammar were so rarefied that even well-read visitors from other departments could not follow a single exchange.
Critics complained that the opera house, with its steep prices and strict dress code, had become a rarefied enclave for connoisseurs rather than a place where ordinary citizens might hear music.

rash.text: Investing his entire savings in a company he had read about only that morning was a rash decision, and he regretted it within the week.
The general urged patience, warning that a rash attack across the open field would expose his troops to devastating fire.
Although critics called the explorer rash for crossing the ice without a guide, she had in fact studied the route for years.

ravenous.text: After hiking for nine hours without food, the climbers were ravenous and devoured an entire pot of stew within minutes.
Bears emerge from hibernation ravenous, having eaten nothing for months, and they spend the spring foraging almost constantly.
The ravenous caterpillars stripped the orchard bare in a single week, consuming leaves far faster than the trees could replace them.

rebuke.text: The judge rebuked the prosecutor for withholding evidence, warning that any further misconduct would lead to sanctions.
Rather than praising the report, the director sharply rebuked its authors for their careless errors and unsupported conclusions.
The coach chose not to rebuke the young player in front of the team, preferring to discuss his mistakes privately after practice.

recapitulation.text: At the end of each chapter, the textbook provides a brief recapitulation of its main points, helping students review before the exam.
Rather than introduce new evidence, the prosecutor's closing statement was a recapitulation of the testimony the jury had already heard.
The chair opened the meeting with a brief recapitulation of last week's decisions, running through each in a sentence or two for members who had been absent.

reconcile.text: Physicists have long struggled to reconcile quantum mechanics with general relativity, since the two theories make incompatible predictions at extreme scales.
It is difficult to reconcile the company's pledge to cut emissions with its plan to open three new coal mines next year.
The committee worked late to reconcile the two budgets, trimming some programs and delaying others until the figures finally agreed.

recondite.text: The lecture on medieval numerology was so recondite that even the specialists in the audience struggled to follow its references.
Although the poet's allusions are recondite, drawing on forgotten myths and little-known treatises, the emotions of her verse are immediately accessible.
The editors rejected the article as too recondite for a general readership, advising the author to explain her technical terms.

recrimination.text: After the project failed, the meeting dissolved into bitter recrimination, with engineers blaming managers and managers blaming engineers in turn.
The divorce proceedings were marked by recriminations on both sides, each spouse accusing the other of having wrecked the marriage.
Rather than trade recriminations over the lost election, the party's leaders agreed to analyze what had gone wrong and plan together for the next campaign.

recrudesce.text: Doctors warned that the infection might recrudesce if the patient stopped taking the antibiotics before completing the full course.
Just when the border dispute seemed settled, old hostilities recrudesced, and skirmishes broke out once more along the contested river.
The historian notes that anti-intellectual sentiment tends to recrudesce in times of economic hardship, reappearing after long periods of dormancy.

redoubtable.text: The chess champion was a redoubtable opponent, and many challengers conceded defeat after only a few moves against her.
Protected by thick walls and a deep moat, the castle was redoubtable, and invading armies usually chose to bypass it rather than risk a siege.
Even seasoned lawyers were intimidated by the redoubtable judge, whose sharp questions and formidable memory left unprepared counsel speechless.

redress.text: The workers who had been injured by the faulty machinery sought redress in court, demanding compensation for their medical bills and lost wages.
When the airline lost her luggage, Emma spent weeks seeking redress, but the company offered only a voucher that barely covered a new toothbrush.
The commission was established to provide redress for families whose land had been seized without payment decades earlier.

refractory.text: The refractory mule refused to cross the bridge, planting its hooves no matter how the farmer coaxed or pulled.
Teachers who had tamed the rowdiest classes admitted defeat with the refractory students of the fourth period, who ignored every rule and defied every punishment.
The colonial governor found the northern provinces refractory, their leaders openly resisting his decrees and refusing to pay taxes.

refute.text: The new fossil evidence appeared to refute the long-held theory that the species had evolved only on the island.
The defense attorney refuted the witness's testimony by producing receipts proving that her client had been in another city on the night of the crime.
Although the claim was widely repeated, a careful study refuted it, showing that the supposed link between the two diseases was a statistical artifact.

relegate.text: Once the star of the rotation, the aging pitcher was relegated to the bullpen, appearing only in games whose outcome had already been decided.
Early historians relegated women's contributions to footnotes, treating them as marginal to the main story of the era.
After the new model arrived, the old computer was relegated to a corner of the storeroom, where it gathered dust.

remiss.text: The inspector was remiss in his duties, signing off on the building's wiring without ever actually examining it.
At the ceremony, the director said she would be remiss not to thank the volunteers, whose unpaid labor had made the entire festival possible.
Although the hospital's staff worked tirelessly, its administrators had been remiss, neglecting to replace outdated equipment despite repeated warnings.

remonstrate.text: The residents remonstrated with the council against the highway plan, pleading that it would split their neighborhood in two and destroy its historic park.
When the headmaster announced that the library would close, students remonstrated, begging him to reconsider and pointing out how many of them relied on it for study.
The scientist remonstrated with her funders, protesting the decision and urging them not to cancel the project when it was so close to yielding results.

renege.text: After promising to fund the new library, the council reneged, diverting the money to road repairs and leaving the architects unpaid.
Voters grew cynical when the governor reneged on his pledge not to raise taxes, introducing a new levy on fuel within six months of taking office.
Having signed the contract, the publisher could not easily renege, though executives privately regretted the enormous advance they had agreed to pay.

replete.text: The anthology is replete with forgotten masterpieces, poems that had languished unread in obscure journals for more than a century.
The ship's hold was replete with provisions for the long voyage: barrels of salted meat, casks of water, and sacks of flour stacked to the ceiling.
Far from being a dry legal document, the treaty is replete with poetic flourishes and elaborate expressions of goodwill.

reprisal.text: After the rebels ambushed a supply convoy, the occupying army launched a harsh reprisal, shelling the villages it suspected of sheltering them.
The treaty explicitly forbade reprisals against prisoners of war, so commanders could not punish captured soldiers for attacks carried out by their comrades.
Fearing reprisal from the enemy fleet, the admiral hesitated to strike its harbor, knowing that his own coastal cities lay undefended.

reproach.text: The teacher gently reproached the student for plagiarizing, reminding him that honesty mattered more than a perfect grade.
Although he had broken no law, the senator was reproached by his colleagues for accepting lavish gifts from lobbyists.
The reviewer was careful not to reproach the young author too harshly, framing his criticisms as suggestions for her next book.

reprobate.text: The town regarded the old gambler as an incorrigible reprobate, and mothers warned their sons never to visit his card games.
In the novel, the heroine's family disowns her brother as a reprobate after he squanders the inheritance and is jailed for fraud.
Although the press painted the defendant as a reprobate with no redeeming qualities, several witnesses described his generosity toward the poor.

repudiate.text: The scientist publicly repudiated the rumor that her data had been fabricated, releasing all of her original laboratory notebooks for inspection.
The company issued a statement repudiating the allegations of child labor in its factories, though independent investigators continued to demand evidence.
Later scholars repudiated the once popular theory that the ancient city had been destroyed by a flood, pointing to evidence of a prolonged drought instead.

rescind.text: After widespread protests, the university rescinded its decision to raise tuition, restoring the previous fees for the coming year.
The city council voted to rescind the ordinance banning street musicians, conceding that the law had been both unpopular and unenforceable.
The publisher threatened to rescind the author's contract if she failed to deliver the manuscript by the agreed deadline.

reservation.text: Although the committee approved the design, several members expressed reservations about its cost, and the vote was far from unanimous.
She accepted the job offer without reservation, confident that the position was exactly what she had been seeking for years.
Critics admired the film's visual ambition but had reservations about its ending, which seemed to undercut everything that came before.

resignation.text: When the doctor explained that nothing more could be done, the old farmer received the news with quiet resignation, thanking her and turning to gaze at his fields.
Rather than protesting the new rules, the employees greeted them with weary resignation, having learned long ago that complaints changed nothing.
The poems of her final years show not despair but resignation: she writes of failing eyesight and absent friends calmly, as facts to be lived with rather than fought.

resolve.text: After weeks of debate, the council resolved to postpone construction until an independent study of its environmental impact was complete.
Having nearly missed her flight twice, Nadia resolved never again to leave her packing until the last minute.
The delegates argued late into the night before they finally resolved that the organization would admit new members only by unanimous vote.

respite.text: The brief cease-fire gave the exhausted villagers a respite from the shelling, allowing them to repair their roofs and gather supplies.
For the overworked nurses, the quiet hour before dawn offered a welcome respite, a chance to sit down with coffee before the next wave of patients arrived.
The heat wave continued for weeks without respite, and residents began sleeping on rooftops in search of any cooler air.

restive.text: As the delayed train sat motionless for a third hour, the passengers grew restive, pacing the aisles and demanding answers from the conductor.
The horse became restive in its stall before the storm, stamping and tossing its head at every distant roll of thunder.
Years of rising prices made the urban workers increasingly restive, and the government feared that strikes would soon spread across the country.

resurgent.text: After decades in which the dialect seemed destined for extinction, it is now resurgent, taught in village schools and heard again on regional radio.
Economists who had written off the textile district were surprised by its resurgent factories, which, after years of closure, now hum with new orders.
Far from fading after the founder's death, the movement proved resurgent: membership doubled within two years as a younger generation revived its ideals.

reticent.text: Although the novelist's books are intensely confessional, she herself is famously reticent in interviews, deflecting personal questions with a polite shrug.
Colleagues were startled when the ordinarily reticent engineer spoke at length during the review; in five years he had hardly offered an opinion in a meeting.
Diplomats found the envoy reticent about his government's intentions, since he answered every probing question with brief, noncommittal remarks.

retiring.text: Although her novels are bold and outspoken, the author herself had a retiring disposition, rarely granting interviews and slipping away from parties early.
By temperament retiring, the young scholar let his colleagues present their joint findings, content to sit unnoticed at the back of the lecture hall.
Guests were surprised that the host, so retiring in everyday life, gave such a confident speech; normally he avoided even small talk with his neighbors.

retract.text: Faced with evidence that the data had been fabricated, the journal retracted the article and issued an apology to its readers.
Under intense pressure from the authorities, the astronomer publicly retracted his claim, though many suspected he privately held the same view.
When threatened, the snail retracts its soft body into its shell and remains there, motionless, until the danger has passed.

reverent.text: Visitors fell into a reverent hush as they entered the ancient library, lowering their voices as if the manuscripts themselves deserved deference.
Rather than mocking the old masters as some modernists did, the young painter adopted a reverent attitude toward them, copying their canvases with devout care.
Critics complained that the biography was too reverent to be useful: the author treated her subject as a saint and ignored every documented flaw.

ribald.text: The tavern songs were ribald, full of bawdy jokes that delighted the sailors but made the visiting clergyman blush.
The medieval collection mixes pious sermons with ribald tales of foolish husbands and scheming wives, a blend of the sacred and the crudely comic.
The comedian toned down his usually ribald routine for the charity luncheon, replacing his vulgar punch lines with gentler observations about family life.

rile.text: The umpire's questionable calls riled the home crowd, and by the ninth inning spectators were hurling insults at the field.
Few things rile the patient old professor more than students who check their phones while he is explaining a difficult proof.
Although the proposed fee was small, it riled local merchants, who saw it as one more petty annoyance imposed by a distant bureaucracy.

robust.text: Designed to survive rough seas, the research vessel was robust enough to withstand waves that would have capsized a lighter ship.
Despite his age, the farmer remained robust, lifting heavy sacks of grain and working from dawn until dusk without apparent fatigue.
Unlike the fragile economy of its neighbor, the country's economy proved robust, weathering the global downturn with only a mild slowdown.

row.text: The neighbors had a furious row over the fence line, shouting at each other across the hedge until the police were called.
A public row between the conductor and the lead soprano, carried on through angry letters to the newspaper, overshadowed the opera's premiere.
What began as a polite disagreement over the budget escalated into a bitter row, with ministers accusing each other of incompetence in front of reporters.

rudimentary.text: The prototype's navigation system is still rudimentary, able to detect large obstacles but not yet to plan a route around them.
Although she had only a rudimentary grasp of Portuguese, enough to order a meal and ask directions, she was unprepared for the technical vocabulary of the conference.
Early mammals possessed only rudimentary versions of the intricate inner ear that later species would develop over millions of years.

rustic.text: The architect rejected polished marble in favor of rough timber beams and stone floors, giving the lodge a deliberately rustic character suited to its mountain setting.
City visitors often found the villagers' customs charmingly rustic, though the villagers themselves resented being treated as quaint relics of farm life.
The composer drew on shepherds' dances and harvest festivals, and the resulting suite has a rustic simplicity that contrasts sharply with his ornate urban operas.

sagacious.text: The sagacious elder advised the villagers to plant drought-resistant crops, a recommendation that saved them when the rains failed the following year.
Although young, the judge was remarkably sagacious, weighing each argument carefully and delivering rulings that even veteran lawyers admired for their wisdom.
Investors who followed the sagacious fund manager avoided the crash, since she had recognized the bubble long before others and quietly sold her holdings.

sanctimonious.text: The minister's sanctimonious lectures on thrift rang hollow once reporters discovered his own lavish spending on private jets.
Readers find the narrator insufferably sanctimonious, forever congratulating himself on his virtue while condemning the moral failings of his neighbors.
Although she genuinely cared about the environment, Leah tried not to sound sanctimonious when discussing it, knowing that preaching tends to alienate listeners.

sanction-n.text: Players who leave the field without the referee's permission face stiff sanctions, including fines and suspension from future matches.
The regulatory agency warned that firms concealing their emissions data would incur sanctions severe enough to threaten their operating licenses.
Because the professional code carried no real sanction for violations, many practitioners ignored its provisions with impunity, knowing that nothing would happen to them.

sanction-v.text: Because the university had not formally sanctioned the experiment, the researchers were forced to suspend it until the ethics board granted its approval.
The league refused to sanction the exhibition match, so the players who took part could not count it toward their official records.
Although local custom seemed to sanction the hiring of relatives, the new charter explicitly prohibited the practice, citing concerns about fairness.

sangfroid.text: The pilot's sangfroid during the engine failure reassured the passengers; she announced the emergency landing as calmly as if she were describing the weather.
Even as the audience jeered and the lights failed, the pianist continued playing with remarkable sangfroid, never missing a note.
Negotiators prized her sangfroid, since no threat or insult across the table could provoke her into losing her composure.
