sanguine.text: Despite the poor early returns, the campaign manager remained sanguine, insisting that the late-reporting districts would swing the election in their favor.
Economists are less sanguine than the government about the recovery, warning that rising debt could halt growth within a year.
Having survived several previous crises, the veteran captain was sanguine about the storm, cheerfully assuring the passengers that they would reach port by morning.

sardonic.text: When the proposal was rejected yet again, the engineer gave a sardonic laugh and remarked that the committee's vision was truly breathtaking in its smallness.
The columnist's sardonic wit spared no one; she mocked politicians' pieties with a scornful irony that delighted readers and infuriated her targets.
Rather than offering sympathy, the older brother responded with a sardonic smile, as if the younger boy's misfortune merely confirmed his low opinion of him.

sartorial.text: The professor's sartorial choices, a rumpled tweed jacket and mismatched socks, suggested a man more concerned with ideas than with appearance.
The film's costume designer took great care with sartorial detail, ensuring that every cufflink and hat matched the fashions of the period.
Although he knew little about politics, the commentator had strong sartorial opinions and devoted most of his column to the candidates' suits and ties.

saturnine.text: The saturnine old librarian rarely smiled, and his gloomy silences made the reading room feel even more somber than it already was.
In contrast to his cheerful sister, Paul had a saturnine temperament, brooding for days over minor setbacks and expecting the worst from every venture.
The composer's late works reflect a saturnine mood, their slow, dark harmonies conveying a melancholy that his earlier, sunnier pieces never approached.

savvy-adj.text: Savvy travelers book their flights well in advance and avoid peak seasons, often paying half of what less informed passengers spend.
The museum's savvy curator anticipated which young artists would become famous and acquired their work while it was still inexpensive.
Though she had no formal training in politics, the mayor proved remarkably savvy, reading the mood of the council and timing her proposals perfectly.

savvy-n.text: The young director lacked experience but not savvy, and she quickly learned which producers could be trusted and which would undercut her.
It took real financial savvy to recognize that the struggling company's patents were worth far more than its share price suggested.
Although the candidate had impressive credentials, critics doubted that she possessed the media savvy needed to handle hostile interviewers.

savvy-v.text: The foreman rattled off the procedure in rapid slang and then asked, 'Savvy?', and the new hire nodded, though in truth he had understood almost nothing.
The trapper spoke little English, but he savvied enough of the traders' gestures and broken phrases to grasp that they wanted furs in exchange for rifles.
The jokes at the market turned on dialect puns, and the visiting reporter, who didn't savvy half of them, laughed a beat late to hide his confusion.

schadenfreude.text: Rivals watched the celebrated chef's restaurant fail with barely concealed schadenfreude, delighted that his arrogance had finally been punished.
Psychologists suggest that schadenfreude is strongest when the sufferer is envied, since another's misfortune can make us feel better about our own position.
Though she publicly expressed sympathy, the novelist admitted to a twinge of schadenfreude when the critic who had savaged her book was himself harshly reviewed.

scintillating.text: The host was a scintillating conversationalist, darting from art to astronomy to gossip with a wit that kept her guests enthralled until midnight.
Although his books are dry, the historian is scintillating in person, and students crowd his seminars for the sheer brilliance of his improvised arguments.
The dinner was expected to be dull, but a scintillating young physicist enlivened the evening with quick-witted, dazzling stories about her research.

screed.text: Instead of a reasoned review, the critic published a screed, three thousand words of invective against the novel, its publisher, and anyone who had enjoyed it.
The neighbor's letter to the editor was a rambling, angry screed about parking regulations that the newspaper printed only to fill space.
Far from offering a balanced history, the book is a screed, relentlessly attacking the author's rivals while ignoring any evidence that complicates her thesis.

scrupulous-adj1.text: The restorers were scrupulous in their work, cleaning each square inch of the fresco with a cotton swab and documenting every fleck of pigment they removed.
Her scrupulous attention to footnotes, comparing every citation against the original source, made her the journal's most valued copy editor.
Unlike his predecessor, whose data tables were riddled with transcription errors, the new analyst was scrupulous, confirming each figure twice before submitting a report.

scrupulous-adj2.text: A scrupulous official, she declined even the modest gifts that vendors customarily offered, lest anyone suspect that her decisions could be bought.
The dealer was scrupulous about disclosing every flaw in the paintings he sold, even when silence would have earned him a far higher price.
Though many of his rivals padded their expense claims, the scrupulous mayor reimbursed the treasury for a single personal phone call made on an official line.

sedulous.text: The sedulous researcher spent years combing through archives, checking every letter and ledger until she had reconstructed the merchant's entire trading network.
Thanks to the gardener's sedulous care, weeding daily and watering by hand, the neglected estate was transformed into a flourishing showpiece.
Unlike his careless predecessor, the new archivist was sedulous, cataloging each document meticulously and double-checking every entry.

semblance.text: The regime held elections to create a semblance of democracy, though the results were determined long before any ballots were cast.
Beneath a semblance of cooperation, the two firms were secretly working to undermine each other's bids.
The con artist maintained a semblance of wealth, renting a luxury car and an elegant office, while in fact he owed money to nearly everyone he knew.

sententious.text: The novel's narrator is insufferably sententious, pausing every few pages to deliver pompous moral lessons about the virtues of hard work and thrift.
Rather than offering practical advice, the retiring executive gave a sententious speech full of lofty maxims about integrity that he had rarely practiced himself.
Critics found the film sententious, complaining that its characters spoke in sanctimonious aphorisms rather than natural dialogue.

sentimental.text: The film's ending is shamelessly sentimental: swelling violins, a tearful reunion, and a dog racing across a meadow to greet its long-lost owner.
Unlike the sentimental verse popular in her day, which wallowed in tears and deathbed scenes, her poems treat grief with restraint and irony.
Critics dismissed the painter's portraits of wide-eyed orphans as sentimental, arguing that they manipulated viewers' emotions rather than revealing anything true.

serendipity.text: Many scientific breakthroughs owe as much to serendipity as to planning; a contaminated culture or a misread instrument can reveal something no one was looking for.
By sheer serendipity, the archivist searching for a tax record stumbled upon a lost letter from the city's founder tucked between its pages.
Some urban planners argue that cities should be designed for serendipity, with crowded sidewalks and mixed uses that invite unplanned but fruitful discoveries.

serene.text: Despite the chaos in the terminal around her, the elderly woman remained serene, knitting calmly as flight after flight was canceled.
The monastery's garden is serene, its raked gravel and still pond offering visitors a refuge from the clamor of the city.
In the portrait, the queen's expression is serene, betraying none of the anxiety that historians know she felt during that turbulent year.

simulacrum-n1.text: In the town square stands a bronze simulacrum of the founder, depicting him on horseback with one hand raised toward the harbor.
The wax museum's simulacrum of the old queen was so lifelike that visitors often paused before it, half expecting the figure to speak.
Ancient mourners placed a small clay simulacrum of the deceased in the tomb, believing that the likeness would house the spirit in the afterlife.

simulacrum-n2.text: The chain's so-called Italian restaurants offer only a simulacrum of Italian cooking, with bland sauces and frozen pasta that no cook in Rome would recognize.
Critics dismissed the reconstructed village as a hollow simulacrum, a theme-park version of history with plastic beams and costumed staff reciting scripts.
The dictator's parliament was a mere simulacrum of a legislature: it met rarely, debated nothing, and approved every decree unanimously.

sinecure.text: The title of honorary consul proved a sinecure: it paid a generous stipend but required nothing more than attending an annual reception.
Critics charged that the governor had created the post as a sinecure for his brother-in-law, who collected a salary without ever visiting the office.
Far from being the sinecure he had imagined, the chairmanship demanded long hours, constant travel, and difficult negotiations with unions.

slapdash.text: The report was so slapdash that it misspelled the client's name, repeated entire paragraphs, and cited figures from the wrong year.
Unlike the careful restoration of the east wing, the repairs to the west wing were slapdash, completed in a single weekend with mismatched bricks and sloppy mortar.
The editor rejected the article not for its argument but for its slapdash research, which relied on unverified sources and hastily copied quotations.

smattering.text: He had only a smattering of Latin, enough to recognize a few legal phrases but nowhere near enough to read the classical authors.
The lecture hall, which usually overflows, held only a smattering of students on the Friday before the holiday.
Though the novel's setting is exotic, the author displays little more than a smattering of knowledge about the region, relying on cliches rather than genuine research.

smug.text: Having predicted the market crash, the analyst wore a smug expression throughout the meeting, reminding colleagues at every turn that he had warned them.
The team's smug confidence after its early lead proved costly, as its players relaxed and allowed the underdogs to score three late goals.
Critics found the essay smug, its author so pleased with his own cleverness that he never seriously considered opposing views.

snide.text: Rather than criticizing the proposal openly, the manager made snide remarks about 'ambitious newcomers,' leaving everyone to guess whom he meant.
The reviewer's snide aside, praising the actor for 'remembering most of his lines,' hurt more than an outright attack would have.
Although the columnist claimed to admire her rival, her snide insinuations about the rival's sources suggested a very different attitude.

snub.text: The celebrated novelist snubbed the literary festival, declining its invitation without explanation and appearing at a rival event the same weekend.
At the reception, the ambassador pointedly snubbed his counterpart, turning his back when she offered her hand in greeting.
Although the academy snubbed the film, awarding it no prizes at all, audiences embraced it and it became the year's most popular release.

solecism.text: At the formal banquet, the young diplomat committed a solecism by addressing the ambassador by her first name, and an awkward hush fell over the table.
Arriving at a funeral in bright beach attire would be regarded as a grave solecism in almost any culture.
The etiquette manual catalogs every conceivable solecism, from using the wrong fork to interrupting one's host, so that anxious readers might avoid social embarrassment.

solicitous.text: The nurse was solicitous of her elderly patient, checking his pillows every hour and asking repeatedly whether he needed anything.
The hotel staff were almost too solicitous; within an hour of arrival, three different employees had called to ask whether the room was satisfactory.
Although his colleagues were solicitous about his recovery after surgery, offering meals and rides, he found their constant attention exhausting.

solicitude.text: Her mother's solicitude could be suffocating: she telephoned three times a day to ask whether her adult daughter was eating properly and dressing warmly.
The mayor's sudden solicitude for the neglected neighborhood, expressed only weeks before the election, struck residents as insincere.
Despite the doctors' assurances that the injury was minor, the coach's solicitude never wavered, and he insisted on examining the player's ankle before every practice.

soporific.text: The committee chair's soporific recitation of budget figures left half the audience nodding off before the first question was even asked.
Some antihistamines have a soporific side effect, so patients are warned not to drive or operate heavy machinery after taking them.
Far from the gripping thriller its publisher promised, the novel proved soporific: its long descriptive passages lulled even devoted readers into drowsiness.

sordid.text: The biography exposes the sordid dealings behind the tycoon's fortune: bribes, blackmail and the betrayal of his closest partners.
The detective's search led him to a sordid rooming house, its hallways reeking of mildew and its walls stained with years of grime.
Readers expecting a romantic tale of adventure were dismayed by the novel's sordid portrait of greed, in which every character acts from the basest motives.

spartan.text: The monks lived a spartan life, sleeping on wooden boards, eating a single plain meal each day, and owning nothing beyond a robe and a bowl.
The training camp was notoriously spartan: athletes woke before dawn, ran in freezing weather, and were denied any comforts that might soften their resolve.
Though the founder was a billionaire, his office was spartan, containing only a metal desk, a single chair, and no decoration whatever.

specious-adj1.text: The development's glossy brochure offered a specious vision of lakeside tranquility; the lake, buyers later discovered, was a drainage pond beside a highway.
Behind the specious charm of the courtier lay cold calculation, for his gracious manners were merely a mask for ruthless ambition.
The renovated storefronts gave the district a specious air of prosperity, since most of the attractive shops behind the fresh paint stood empty.

specious-adj2.text: The lawyer's reasoning seemed persuasive at first, but it proved specious once the jury realized that it rested on a misreading of the contract.
Students are taught to spot specious causal claims, such as the argument that ice cream sales cause drownings merely because both rise in summer.
Although the pamphlet's statistics sounded authoritative, they supported only a specious conclusion, since the sample had been chosen to favor the author's thesis.

spendthrift.text: Having inherited a vast fortune, the young spendthrift squandered it within a decade on racehorses, yachts, and lavish parties.
Critics called the council a spendthrift with public money, noting that it had bought marble fountains while the schools lacked textbooks.
Unlike her frugal sister, who saved every spare coin, Rosa was a spendthrift, buying whatever caught her eye and worrying about the bills later.

splenetic.text: The critic's columns grew increasingly splenetic in his old age, bristling at actors, sets, and even audiences as though every evening at the theater were a personal affront.
Chronic pain made the old sailor splenetic, and he would snap at anyone who asked him even the simplest question.
Unlike his patient predecessor, the new editor was splenetic, flying into a temper over minor typos and berating staff for trivial delays.

sporadic.text: Fighting along the border has been sporadic rather than continuous, with brief skirmishes erupting at unpredictable intervals over the past year.
Because her attendance at rehearsals was sporadic (she would appear one week and vanish for the next three), the director eventually gave her part to an understudy.
The survey team found only sporadic evidence of settlement in the valley: a hearth here, a few potsherds there, scattered across several centuries.

spurious.text: The historian dismissed the letter as spurious, noting that its paper and ink could not have been manufactured until decades after the supposed author's death.
Researchers warned that the apparent link between the two variables might be spurious, an artifact of a flawed sampling method rather than a genuine relationship.
Although the company promoted its supplement with impressive testimonials, regulators found the health claims spurious and ordered them removed from the label.

spurn.text: The proud artist spurned the wealthy patron's offer, declaring that he would rather starve than paint portraits to flatter the rich.
Spurned by the established journals, whose editors dismissed her as an untrained amateur, the young mathematician published her proof in an obscure newsletter, where it went unnoticed for years.
The union spurned management's final offer as insulting, and its members voted overwhelmingly to continue the strike indefinitely.

squander.text: The team squandered a ten-point lead in the final minutes, missing easy shots and turning the ball over repeatedly.
By squandering the windfall from oil exports on grand monuments, the government left nothing for schools or roads when prices collapsed.
Teachers lamented that the gifted student was squandering his talent, spending his evenings idly rather than practicing the violin he had once loved.

squelch.text: The authorities moved quickly to squelch the rumor of a bank failure, releasing audited statements before panic could spread among depositors.
A dismissive teacher can squelch a child's curiosity entirely, so that questions once eagerly asked are never voiced again.
The studio squelched the director's ambitious ending, replacing it with a conventional conclusion that test audiences found more comfortable.

staid.text: The staid old bank, with its marble columns and soft-spoken clerks, seemed an unlikely place for the daring investment strategy the new director proposed.
Readers accustomed to the staid tone of the previous editor were startled when the magazine's next issue appeared full of irreverent essays and bold graphics.
Although the professor was staid in the lecture hall, never raising his voice or departing from his notes, his friends knew him as a lively storyteller at dinner.

stalwart.text: Through decades of funding cuts, the librarian remained a stalwart defender of public access, never missing a council meeting where the budget was discussed.
The stalwart pioneers endured blizzards, failed harvests, and disease, yet they refused to abandon the homesteads they had built.
Although many donors withdrew after the scandal, a few stalwart supporters continued to fund the charity, confident that its mission remained worthy.

start.text: The deer started at the snap of a twig and bounded into the forest before the photographer could raise her camera.
Dozing over his books, the student started violently when the librarian tapped his shoulder, knocking his coffee across the table.
When the door slammed behind her, Mei started and dropped her keys, her heart pounding from the sudden noise.

staunch.text: Even when the rest of the board turned against the director, she remained a staunch ally, defending his decisions at every meeting.
For forty years the widow was the orchestra's most staunch patron, funding its seasons even when wealthier donors abandoned it during hard times.
The critic had been the playwright's staunchest defender through years of failed productions, which made his sudden condemnation of her latest work all the more startling.

steadfast.text: Through years of ridicule from his colleagues, the physician remained steadfast in his belief that handwashing could prevent infections.
The small nation's steadfast neutrality, maintained even when powerful neighbors pressured it to take sides, earned it respect as a mediator.
Her friends drifted away when her business failed, but her brother was steadfast, lending her money and visiting every week until she recovered.

stem.text: To stem the spread of the invasive beetle, officials banned the transport of untreated firewood across county lines.
The central bank raised interest rates sharply in an effort to stem inflation, which had been eroding workers' savings for months.
Nothing seemed able to stem the flood of complaints once customers learned that their personal data had been exposed.

stipend.text: Graduate students receive a modest stipend each month, enough to cover rent and groceries but little else besides.
The foundation awarded the young poet a yearly stipend so that she could devote herself to writing without taking a second job.
Although the volunteer position offered no salary, participants received a small weekly stipend to cover travel and meals.

stolid.text: The stolid guard stared straight ahead, his face betraying no reaction even as tourists shouted jokes and waved cameras inches from his nose.
The detective's stolid manner, unmoved by tears or threats alike, unnerved suspects who expected either sympathy or anger.
Although the townspeople seemed stolid to visitors, rarely laughing or showing surprise, they celebrated their harvest festival with remarkable exuberance.

stringent.text: Because the laboratory handles dangerous pathogens, it enforces stringent safety protocols: every visitor must shower, change clothing, and sign a detailed log.
The journal's review standards are notoriously stringent, and manuscripts with even minor methodological lapses are returned to their authors for revision.
Critics argued that the building code was too lax, while developers complained that its requirements were already so stringent that affordable construction had become impossible.

stultify.text: Years of filling out identical forms in the records office stultified the once-ambitious clerk, until he could no longer summon any interest in his work.
Critics argue that endless rote memorization can stultify young students, draining the curiosity and enthusiasm they bring to school.
The novelist found that the monotonous routine of her day job was stultifying her imagination, so she resigned in order to recover the energy she needed to write.

stymie.text: The investigation was stymied by missing records, and the auditors could not trace where the funds had gone.
A shortage of skilled workers has stymied the city's plan to rebuild its bridges, leaving several projects years behind schedule.
Every attempt to reform the tax code was stymied by lobbyists, who found ways to block the proposals before they reached a vote.

subsume-v1.text: When the two agencies merged, the smaller one was subsumed into the larger, and its staff, budget, and mission were folded into the new department.
The new curriculum subsumes the old courses on rhetoric and composition within a single writing sequence rather than eliminating them.
Over several centuries the independent duchy was gradually subsumed by its powerful neighbor until it existed only as a province within the kingdom.

subsume-v2.text: The philosopher argued that aesthetic judgments cannot be subsumed under general rules, since each work of art demands to be evaluated on its own terms.
Rather than treating the new disease as a unique phenomenon, the researchers subsumed it under a known class of autoimmune disorders that share the same mechanism.
A good legal theory should subsume particular rulings under broad principles, so that each verdict appears as an instance of a coherent doctrine.

subterfuge.text: Unable to get permission to enter the archive, the journalist resorted to subterfuge, posing as a visiting scholar to gain access to the files.
The company used an elaborate subterfuge to hide its losses, transferring debts to shell firms so that its balance sheet appeared healthy.
The general's victory depended on subterfuge: dummy tanks and false radio traffic convinced the enemy that the attack would come from the north.

subversive.text: The regime banned the poet's collections as subversive, fearing that their veiled allegories encouraged readers to question the authority of the state.
Under the military government, even a folk song about freedom could be deemed subversive, and its singers were arrested for threatening public order.
The pamphlets appeared innocuous (recipes and weather notes), yet their coded passages carried subversive instructions for organizing resistance against the occupying authorities.

sullen.text: Denied permission to join the expedition, the young apprentice spent the evening in sullen silence, refusing to eat and glaring at anyone who spoke to him.
The once cheerful workforce grew sullen after the layoffs, going about their tasks with resentful glances and muttered complaints.
Unlike her sunny older sister, the teenager was sullen at family gatherings, answering questions in monosyllables and moping in a corner.

summit-n1.text: From the summit, the climbers could see three countries spread out below them, their borders invisible from such a height.
The trail grows steeper and rockier near the summit, and many hikers turn back within sight of the top.
Snow lingered on the mountain's summit well into July, long after the valleys below had turned green and the lower slopes were covered in wildflowers.

summit-n2.text: Leaders of the neighboring nations met at a three-day summit to negotiate a treaty on sharing the river's water.
The summit ended without a joint statement, as the presidents could not agree on how to respond to the refugee crisis.
Ahead of the economic summit, finance ministers from each country met privately to draft proposals for their heads of state to sign.

supercilious.text: The supercilious waiter raised an eyebrow at the couple's choice of wine, as though their taste were beneath his notice.
Though brilliant, the professor alienated students with his supercilious manner, answering their questions with sighs and condescending remarks.
The aristocratic family treated the new neighbors with supercilious disdain, refusing to acknowledge them simply because their fortune came from trade.

superfluous-adj1.text: The editor struck out the ornate introductory paragraph as superfluous, since it contributed nothing to the argument that followed.
Engineers removed the superfluous buttons from the remote control after usage studies showed that several of them had never once been pressed.
Once the bridge opened, the ferry service was rendered superfluous, and its boats sat idle at the dock with no passengers left to carry.

superfluous-adj2.text: With three generators already able to power the entire hospital, a fourth struck the budget committee as superfluous, and the money went to hiring nurses instead.
The chef believed that a truly ripe tomato needs only a pinch of salt, and that any further seasoning is superfluous.
Having ordered five times the packing material it could use in a year, the warehouse stacked the superfluous cartons in its hallways.

supplant.text: Within a generation, the railroad had supplanted the canal as the region's chief means of transport, and the old waterways fell into disuse.
The ambitious deputy schemed for years to supplant her superior, courting the board members whose votes would decide who led the agency.
Linguists have documented how the colonial language gradually supplanted local tongues in commerce and schooling, until few children could speak their grandparents' dialect.

surfeit.text: The housing market suffered from a surfeit of apartments, and with far more units than buyers, prices fell sharply.
After a surfeit of rich holiday feasts, the family longed for simple meals of soup and bread.
Modern researchers face not a scarcity of information but a surfeit, so that the real challenge lies in filtering out what is irrelevant.

surly.text: The surly ferryman answered every question with a scowl and a growl, as if the passengers had personally insulted him.
After a sleepless night, the usually genial chef was surly, snapping at his assistants and slamming pots onto the stove.
The waiter's surly manner, all glares and muttered threats about the kitchen's closing time, drove customers to the restaurant across the street.

surreptitious.text: During the long lecture, several students cast surreptitious glances at their phones, hiding them beneath their desks whenever the professor looked their way.
The spy made surreptitious copies of the documents late at night, careful to return each file to its exact position before dawn.
Though the museum banned photography, one visitor took a surreptitious snapshot of the painting, concealing the camera inside his coat.

sybarite.text: A confirmed sybarite, the heir spent his days in silk robes, dining on delicacies and bathing in perfumed water while ignoring the family business.
The resort catered to the sybarite, offering champagne breakfasts, private masseuses, and suites with marble baths.
Friends were astonished that the former sybarite, who had once refused to travel without his wine cellar and silk sheets, had taken vows of poverty and moved to a remote monastery.

sycophant.text: Rather than offering honest counsel, the minister was a sycophant who praised every royal whim in hopes of securing a lucrative estate.
The director's films declined after she dismissed her frank collaborators and kept only a circle of sycophants who applauded every draft.
Colleagues regarded him as a sycophant: he laughed loudest at the dean's jokes and volunteered for every task that might earn her favor.

taciturn.text: The taciturn farmer answered the journalist's lengthy questions with a nod or a single word, leaving her with barely a paragraph of quotations.
Though his letters were expansive and witty, in person the poet was taciturn, sitting through entire dinner parties without offering a remark.
Negotiators found the delegation's leader taciturn and hard to read; unlike his talkative aides, he spoke only when directly addressed.

tact.text: Delivering bad news to patients requires great tact, since a single careless word can deepen a frightened family's anxiety and grief.
The diplomat's tact was legendary: she could refuse a request so gracefully that the other party left feeling flattered.
Lacking tact, the new manager told the team bluntly that their previous work had been worthless, and several employees resigned within the month.

tantamount.text: The judge ruled that the company's refusal to release the records was tantamount to contempt of court, since its effect was the same as open defiance of her order.
In that field, publishing without peer review is tantamount to professional self-sabotage: the work, however sound, will simply be ignored by other scholars.
The ambassador warned that massing troops along the border would be tantamount to a declaration of war, even if no shot were ever fired.

tarnish.text: Exposure to damp air had tarnished the silver candlesticks, and the housekeeper spent an afternoon polishing them back to a shine.
A single plagiarism scandal tarnished the historian's reputation, and even his earlier, scrupulously honest work came under suspicion.
The company's image, once synonymous with reliability, was tarnished by a series of embarrassing product recalls and lawsuits.

tawdry.text: The once elegant hotel had become tawdry, its lobby filled with plastic flowers, flickering neon, and cheap souvenir stands.
Critics dismissed the musical as a tawdry spectacle, all glitter and sequins with no genuine artistry beneath the surface.
Rather than the refined jewelry she had expected, the shop offered only tawdry trinkets that lost their shine within days.

taxing.text: Caring for a newborn while finishing her dissertation proved so taxing that Mariam slept barely four hours a night for months.
The final exam was less taxing than the students had feared; most finished within an hour and left the room relaxed.
Although the route is short, the climb is taxing, with steep switchbacks that leave even experienced hikers gasping for breath.

telling.text: The most telling detail in the letter is not what the general wrote but what he omitted: any mention of the soldiers he had lost.
It was telling that the company's founder sold all his shares a week before the scandal broke, and investigators took note.
Her hesitation before answering the question about her previous employer was telling, and the interviewers began to suspect she had been dismissed.

telltale.text: The telltale smell of smoke in the hallway alerted the tenants to the fire long before any alarm sounded.
Tree rings bear telltale marks of past droughts, allowing scientists to reconstruct centuries of climate history from a single trunk.
Although the forger was skillful, a telltale anachronism, a pigment not invented until decades after the painter's death, exposed the canvas as a fake.

temerity.text: The junior clerk had the temerity to contradict the chairman in front of the entire board, a boldness that astonished everyone present.
Few scholars had the temerity to challenge the eminent historian's thesis, but one young researcher published a rebuttal that dismantled it point by point.
It took considerable temerity for the explorers to cross the uncharted ice sheet with only a compass and a few weeks' provisions.

temperance.text: The philosopher praised temperance as the foundation of a good life, arguing that pleasures enjoyed in moderation outlast those pursued to excess.
Despite the lavish banquets that surrounded him, the emperor was known for his temperance, eating simple meals and rarely finishing a cup of wine.
Her financial success owed less to bold speculation than to temperance: she never borrowed beyond her means and resisted every fashionable spending spree.

tempered.text: After the accountant warned that costs had been badly underestimated, the committee's once exuberant support gave way to a far more tempered endorsement of the proposal.
Reviewers offered tempered praise for the debut album, admiring its ambition while noting that several tracks felt unfinished.
Years of failed reforms had left the minister with a tempered idealism; she still believed in change but no longer expected it to come quickly.

tempestuous.text: The composer's tempestuous temperament, swinging from rapture to fury within minutes, made him difficult to work with but gave his music its passion.
Their tempestuous friendship was marked by fierce loyalty and furious quarrels, followed by tearful reconciliations that never lasted long.
Historians describe the revolution's early years as tempestuous, with governments rising and falling in rapid succession amid violent swings of public feeling.

tenacious.text: The tenacious reporter filed requests for the documents for six years, refusing to abandon the story even after two editors told her to move on.
Invasive vines are notoriously tenacious, regrowing from tiny root fragments long after gardeners believe they have eradicated them.
Although the defending army was vastly outnumbered, its tenacious resistance held the mountain pass for weeks and upset the invaders' entire campaign.

tendentious.text: The documentary was criticized as tendentious, since it presented only the evidence that supported its thesis and omitted every dissenting expert.
Rather than an impartial history, the textbook offered a tendentious account that consistently portrayed one faction as heroes and the other as villains.
The reviewer warned readers that the author's tendentious summary of the research distorted the studies to favor his controversial theory of diet.

tender.text: Following the scandal, the minister tendered her resignation, though the premier persuaded her to stay until a successor was found.
The company tendered an offer to buy all outstanding shares at a premium, hoping to win control before rivals could organize.
At the close of the negotiations, the envoy tendered his government's apology, reading it aloud before the assembled delegates and then presenting a signed copy to their chair.

thoroughgoing.text: The new director ordered a thoroughgoing reform of the agency, replacing its leadership, rewriting its rules and closing half its regional offices.
Far from a superficial revision, the second edition is a thoroughgoing reworking of the text, with nearly every chapter rewritten from scratch.
A thoroughgoing skeptic, the philosopher doubted not only religious claims but also the reliability of his own senses and memory.

thrifty.text: Thrifty shoppers wait for end-of-season sales, buying winter coats in spring at a fraction of their original price.
Raised by thrifty parents who repaired everything rather than replacing it, Elena was appalled by her roommates' habit of throwing away barely worn clothes.
Although the town's budget was small, its thrifty council managed to build a new library by reusing materials from the old courthouse.

thwart.text: The engineers had designed the levee to withstand a century of storms, but an unforeseen shift in the riverbed thwarted their efforts within a decade.
Although the reformers enjoyed broad public support, a handful of entrenched committee chairs managed to thwart the bill by refusing even to schedule a hearing.
The detective's patient surveillance finally thwarted the forger's scheme: every counterfeit canvas was seized before it could reach the auction house.

timorous.text: The timorous deer bolted at the faintest snap of a twig, so the photographer had to wait motionless for hours to capture a single image.
Critics faulted the council's timorous response to the crisis, arguing that fear of offending anyone had kept it from taking decisive action.
Once a timorous student who dreaded speaking in class, she grew into a confident trial lawyer who relished cross-examination.

tirade.text: Rather than offering the measured critique the editors expected, the reviewer delivered a tirade, denouncing the novelist's prose as lazy, dishonest, and unworthy of print.
The coach's furious halftime tirade, in which he berated each player by name for a full ten minutes, left the team more rattled than motivated.
Though the professor usually answered objections with calm patience, a student's accusation of plagiarism provoked a furious tirade that silenced the seminar.

torpor.text: The long summer afternoons induced a pleasant torpor in the villagers, who dozed in the shade instead of tending their fields.
Economists warned that the market had sunk into a torpor, with investment stagnant and few firms willing to expand or hire.
Hibernating bears enter a state of torpor in which their heart rates slow dramatically and they barely move for months.

tortuous.text: The road to the monastery is tortuous, twisting through dozens of hairpin turns as it climbs the side of the gorge.
The bill's tortuous passage through the legislature, with its endless amendments, reversals, and procedural detours, left even its sponsors unsure what it finally contained.
Rather than stating his conclusion plainly, the author led readers through a tortuous chain of qualifications and digressions before revealing his point.

tout.text: The pharmaceutical firm touted its new drug as a breakthrough, yet the published trials showed only a marginal improvement over existing treatments.
Real estate brochures routinely tout a property's 'charming character,' praising as a virtue what often turns out to be cramped rooms and aging plumbing.
Eager to attract investors, the startup's founders touted every modest milestone in glowing press releases, as if each were a triumph of engineering.

tractable.text: The new foreman found the crew surprisingly tractable, willing to adopt his revised procedures without the complaints he had been warned to expect.
Unlike the stubborn ponies of the northern highlands, this breed is notably tractable, which makes it popular for teaching children to ride.
Once it was broken into smaller components, the problem proved far more tractable than the committee had feared, and a solution emerged within weeks.

transient.text: The drug's side effects are usually transient, fading within a few hours of the first dose and rarely recurring.
Tourists drawn by the festival lend the town a transient prosperity; once they depart in September, the shops close and the streets fall quiet.
The poet dwelt on the transient beauty of cherry blossoms, which fall from the branches only days after they open.

transitory.text: The economist cautioned that the spike in consumer spending was transitory, driven by a one-time tax rebate rather than by any lasting rise in wages.
Unlike the cathedral's stone, which has endured for centuries, the sand mandala is deliberately transitory: the monks sweep it away soon after completing it.
Critics dismissed the fashion for minimalist interiors as transitory, predicting that ornament would return as soon as the novelty wore off.

transmute.text: The poet had a gift for transmuting ordinary experiences, such as washing dishes or waiting for a bus, into moments of luminous significance.
Over the centuries, the folk tale was transmuted from a grim cautionary story into a gentle fable for children.
In a nuclear reactor, certain elements can be transmuted into others as their atoms absorb neutrons and change their fundamental nature.

travail.text: The biography chronicles the composer's travails in exile: poverty, illness, and years of rejection by publishers who had once courted him.
After months of travail in the archives, deciphering faded ledgers line by line, the historian finally reconstructed the merchant's trading network.
Far from the effortless genius of legend, the painter's letters reveal constant travail, with each canvas reworked dozens of times before she was satisfied.

travesty.text: The defendant's lawyers called the trial a travesty of justice, since the judge had excluded their key witnesses and admitted hearsay from the prosecution.
The film adaptation was a travesty of the novel, reducing its subtle meditation on grief to a series of car chases and cheap gags.
Purists regarded the modernized opera production as a travesty, arguing that its garish costumes and rewritten libretto mocked the composer's intentions.

treacherous-adj1.text: The king trusted his chancellor completely, never suspecting that this treacherous adviser was secretly passing state secrets to a foreign court.
Once a loyal partner, he proved treacherous in the end, abandoning the firm and taking its largest clients with him to a rival.
In the epic, the hero's downfall comes not from his enemies but from a treacherous companion who opens the city gates at night to the invading army.

treacherous-adj2.text: After the thaw, the ice on the lake was treacherous: solid in some places, it was thin enough elsewhere to give way beneath a single skater.
Sailors dreaded the treacherous strait, whose shifting sandbars, hidden rocks, and sudden squalls had wrecked countless vessels over the centuries.
The mountain path, though pleasant in summer, grows treacherous after rain, when loose scree can send a careless hiker sliding toward the cliff edge.

trenchant.text: The critic's trenchant review cut through the film's lavish spectacle to expose the emptiness of its plot.
Although most commentators offered vague praise, one economist delivered a trenchant analysis that pinpointed exactly why the policy would fail.
Her trenchant wit made her a formidable debater; opponents found that a single incisive remark from her could demolish their entire argument.

tribulation.text: The memoir recounts the tribulations of a family of immigrant farmers: failed harvests, crushing debt, and a flood that swept away their only barn.
Despite the many tribulations of the expedition, including frostbite and a lost supply cache, the team completed its survey of the glacier.
Every generation of settlers on the frontier faced some fresh tribulation, so the town's founders came to regard hardship as the ordinary condition of life.

trite.text: The judges faulted the essay's trite conclusion, which ended with the stale reminder that every cloud has a silver lining.
Although the melody is pleasant, its chord progression is so trite that listeners feel they have heard the song a hundred times before.
Critics dismissed the novel's romance as trite, a recycling of the same star-crossed formula that countless earlier books had exhausted.

truculence.text: The prisoner's truculence, glaring at the guards and shoving anyone who approached, earned him extra days in solitary confinement.
Diplomats were alarmed by the envoy's truculence; instead of negotiating, he pounded the table and threatened war over the smallest concession.
The coach hoped the player's truculence would fade with maturity, but he continued to challenge referees and pick fights with his teammates.

truculent.text: The truculent warlord ruled through terror, ordering brutal raids on any village that resisted his demands.
Visitors were warned to stay clear of the truculent guard dogs, which snarled and lunged at anyone who approached the gate.
Despite his genial public image, the tycoon was truculent in negotiations, attacking rivals with a ferocity that left them shaken.

truncate.text: Because the broadcast ran over its allotted time, the network truncated the final interview, cutting it off after only two questions.
The editor asked the author to truncate the sprawling third chapter, trimming it to half its length so that the narrative would move faster.
His career as a concert pianist was truncated by an injury to his wrist, which forced him to retire in his early thirties.

tumult.text: When the verdict was announced, the courtroom erupted into tumult, with reporters shouting questions and spectators pushing toward the doors.
The composer deliberately follows the movement's opening tumult, all clashing brass and pounding drums, with a passage of almost unbearable stillness.
Amid the tumult of the trading floor, where hundreds of brokers were shouting orders at once, the young clerk could barely hear his own thoughts.

turgid.text: The committee's report was so turgid that few members read beyond the first page, where a single inflated sentence took forty words to announce that the budget was late.
Students dreaded the textbook's turgid prose, which buried simple ideas beneath inflated phrases and interminable sentences.
Although his early essays were lively and direct, the philosopher's later writing grew turgid, swollen with grandiose terminology and tiresome repetition.

turpitude.text: The lawyer was disbarred for moral turpitude after it emerged that he had defrauded elderly clients of their life savings.
The historian catalogs the tyrant's turpitude, from bribery and extortion to the betrayal of allies who had trusted him.
Novels of the period often contrast the virtue of rural life with the turpitude of the city, depicting urban society as a sink of corruption.

tyro.text: Though a tyro in the kitchen, the new cook learned quickly, and within a few months he was preparing dishes that impressed even veteran chefs.
The seasoned investor warned tyros not to trade on margin until they had gained enough experience to understand the risks.
As a tyro in politics, the candidate made mistakes that a more experienced campaigner would have avoided, such as answering hypothetical questions with reckless candor.

umbrage.text: The senior partner took umbrage at being left off the invitation list, interpreting the oversight as a deliberate insult.
Though the reviewer intended her comments as constructive, the author took umbrage, firing back an angry letter to the editor.
The delegates took umbrage when the host remarked that their country's cuisine was bland, and they left the banquet early in protest.

unassailable.text: With a twenty-point lead and only two games left, the team's position at the top of the league was unassailable.
The prosecution's case seemed unassailable, resting on DNA evidence, security footage, and three independent eyewitnesses.
Perched on a sheer cliff with a single narrow approach, the fortress was considered unassailable, and no army had ever captured it.

uncanny.text: The forger possessed an uncanny talent for mimicry; even the museum's experts could not distinguish his copies from the originals.
Visitors to the abandoned lighthouse often report an uncanny sense of being watched, though no one has lived there for decades.
The novelist has an uncanny ability to anticipate social trends: themes she explored years ago now seem to describe the present with eerie precision.

uncompromising.text: An uncompromising architect, she refused every request from the developers to cheapen the materials, even when it meant losing the commission.
Rather than softening his findings to placate the funding agency, the scientist published an uncompromising report that confirmed every alarming result.
Negotiations collapsed because both delegations remained uncompromising: neither would yield an inch on the disputed water rights.

unconscionable.text: Consumer advocates argued that the lender's interest rates were unconscionable, since borrowers could end up repaying several times what they had borrowed.
The judge voided the contract as unconscionable, noting that it stripped the tenant of nearly every right while imposing no obligations on the landlord.
Delaying the vaccine shipment merely to raise its price struck even the company's own board as unconscionable, and the executive responsible was dismissed.

undermine.text: Repeated revelations of fabricated data have undermined public confidence in the institute, and even its sound studies are now greeted with suspicion.
The manager's habit of reversing her team's decisions without explanation undermined their morale, and within months several key members had resigned.
Critics argued that the treaty's vague enforcement provisions would undermine its purpose, allowing signatories to ignore their obligations without penalty.

underscore.text: The minister's surprise visit to the flooded district underscored the government's claim that recovery was its highest priority.
In her closing remarks, the professor underscored the central point of the lecture: correlation, however striking, is not proof of causation.
The rising number of hospital admissions underscores the need for better air quality monitoring, lending weight to warnings that had previously been dismissed.

underwrite.text: A consortium of local banks agreed to underwrite the restoration of the old opera house, covering costs that the city could no longer afford.
Because a wealthy patron underwrote the expedition, the archaeologists could spend an entire season excavating without worrying about their budget.
The foundation declined to underwrite the documentary, so the filmmakers had to finance it themselves through years of freelance work.

unequivocal.text: Unlike the evasive statements of her predecessors, the chancellor's answer was unequivocal: the program would be ended, and no exceptions would be granted.
The trial results were unequivocal; every reviewer, regardless of prior skepticism, reached the same conclusion about the vaccine's effectiveness.
The union demanded an unequivocal commitment to job security, having learned that vaguely worded promises could be reinterpreted whenever management found it convenient.

unflappable.text: The unflappable air traffic controller calmly guided the damaged plane to the runway while alarms blared around her.
Reporters tried to provoke the spokesperson with hostile questions, but she remained unflappable, answering each one in the same even tone.
Even when the power failed during the operation, the surgeon was unflappable, instructing staff to switch to backup lights as if nothing unusual had occurred.

unforthcoming.text: When pressed about the missing funds, the treasurer was unforthcoming, offering only vague answers and refusing to show investigators the ledgers.
The witness proved unforthcoming, declining to name the other people present and claiming not to remember anything useful.
Although the company publicized its successes eagerly, it was unforthcoming about the safety tests that its new product had failed.

unimpeachable.text: The source of the report was unimpeachable, a respected scientist whose data had never once been called into question.
Because the judge's integrity was unimpeachable, even the losing party accepted her ruling as fair.
The historian's credentials were unimpeachable, yet her controversial thesis still met resistance from colleagues who disliked its conclusions.

unnerve.text: The candidate had rehearsed every answer, yet the interviewer's long, unblinking silences unnerved her so much that she began to stammer.
Seasoned climbers are rarely unnerved by heights, but the sudden crack of the ice shelf beneath them left even the guide visibly shaken.
Nothing seemed to unnerve the veteran diplomat: while his aides panicked over the leaked memo, he calmly drafted a reply.

unprecedented.text: The drought was unprecedented in the region's recorded history; not even the oldest farmers could remember the river running completely dry.
When the museum allowed visitors to handle the original manuscripts, curators elsewhere called the decision unprecedented and, in some cases, reckless.
The treaty granted the small nation an unprecedented degree of autonomy, a privilege that no colonial territory had ever before received.

unprepossessing.text: The restaurant's unprepossessing exterior, a peeling sign above a cramped doorway, gave no hint of the exceptional food served inside.
Though the candidate seemed unprepossessing at first, with his rumpled suit and halting speech, his sharp answers soon won over the committee.
Collectors overlooked the unprepossessing little painting, dark with grime and hung in a corner, until restoration revealed it as a lost masterpiece.

unpropitious.text: The timing was unpropitious for launching a luxury brand, since the economy had just entered a recession and consumers were cutting back.
Despite unpropitious beginnings, including a leaking roof, no funding, and only two students, the school eventually became one of the finest in the region.
The weather looked unpropitious for the outdoor concert, with dark clouds gathering and forecasters predicting heavy rain by evening.

unruly.text: The substitute teacher, faced with an unruly class that ignored every instruction, finally abandoned the lesson plan and sent for the principal.
Although the crowd began peacefully, it grew unruly as the evening wore on, and stewards had to remove spectators who were throwing bottles onto the field.
Early parliaments were often unruly assemblies in which members shouted down speakers and openly defied the chair's calls for order.

unscrupulous.text: Unscrupulous landlords exploited the housing shortage by charging illegal fees and ignoring repairs, confident that desperate tenants would not complain.
The collector was defrauded by an unscrupulous dealer who sold him forged prints accompanied by fabricated certificates of authenticity.
Though her methods were effective, her unscrupulous willingness to deceive rivals and break promises eventually left her without a single ally.

unseemly.text: Mourners found it unseemly that the heirs began arguing over the estate before the funeral service had even ended.
The official's eagerness to accept lavish gifts from contractors struck many observers as unseemly, even though no law had technically been broken.
In the rigidly formal court, it was considered unseemly for a courtier to laugh aloud or to turn his back on the king.

unstinting.text: The volunteers' unstinting efforts, working through nights and weekends without pay, allowed the shelter to open ahead of schedule.
In her memoir, the scientist expresses gratitude for her mentor's unstinting support, which included countless hours of advice and even personal loans.
Critics are rarely unanimous, but their praise for the young pianist was unstinting, with every reviewer lavishing superlatives on her performance.

untenable.text: Once new fossils showed that the two species had coexisted rather than one evolving from the other, the old theory became untenable.
The minister's position grew untenable after documents contradicted his denials, and he resigned within the week.
Critics argued that the author's claim, which rested on a single ambiguous letter, was untenable in the face of so much contrary evidence.

untoward.text: The expedition met with untoward circumstances almost at once: unseasonable storms closed the mountain passes, and supplies ran short within weeks.
Unless something untoward occurs, such as a strike or a supply shortage, the bridge should be completed on schedule next spring.
The negotiators feared that any untoward publicity before the agreement was signed might cause one side to withdraw.

untrammeled.text: Freed from the constraints of her former employer, the designer enjoyed untrammeled creativity, pursuing whatever projects interested her.
The frontier offered settlers an untrammeled existence, far from the laws and customs that had governed their lives in the crowded cities of the east.
Critics warned that untrammeled development along the coast, with no zoning or environmental review, would destroy the wetlands.

unviable.text: Without a reliable water supply, the proposed settlement was unviable, and planners abandoned it after the preliminary survey.
Rising fuel costs made the airline's discount routes unviable, forcing it to cancel flights that could no longer cover their expenses.
The seeds proved unviable, failing to sprout despite the botanists' careful attention to soil, light, and moisture.

upbraid.text: The conductor upbraided the brass section in front of the entire orchestra for arriving late and unprepared for the dress rehearsal.
Rather than praising the junior analyst for spotting the error, the director upbraided her for failing to notice it sooner.
The editorial upbraided city officials for their negligence, listing in stinging detail the years of warnings they had ignored about the aging dam.

urbane.text: Unlike his provincial cousins, who were awkward at formal dinners, the diplomat was urbane, gliding effortlessly between conversations in four languages.
The essayist's urbane wit, polished through years in the salons of several capitals, made even his harshest criticisms sound gracious.
Though raised on a remote farm, she had become thoroughly urbane after decades abroad, as comfortable discussing opera as negotiating a contract.

vacillate.text: The committee vacillated for months between renovating the old theater and building a new one, and by the time it decided, construction costs had doubled.
Historians attribute the defeat partly to the general's tendency to vacillate: he ordered an advance, rescinded it, and then ordered it again, squandering the element of surprise.
Her opinion of the novel vacillated as she read it, swinging from admiration in one chapter to exasperation in the next.

vacuous.text: The advertisement's vacuous slogans promised 'excellence' and 'innovation' without saying a single concrete thing about the product.
Critics praised the lead actor's performance but found the script vacuous, a series of glossy scenes with no discernible ideas beneath them.
The student's vacuous answers, which merely repeated each question in slightly different words, convinced the examiners that he had not read the assigned texts.

vanquish.text: The underdog chess player vanquished the reigning champion in only twenty moves, stunning commentators who had predicted an easy defeat for her.
Although the rebel army was vastly outnumbered, it vanquished the imperial forces by luring them into a narrow mountain pass.
Having vanquished every rival bidder, the company now controlled the only railway line through the valley.

variance.text: Researchers were surprised by the variance in patients' responses to the drug: some recovered within days, while others showed no improvement at all.
Because the vineyard's soil changes so markedly from one row of vines to the next, there is considerable variance in the flavor of grapes picked only yards apart.
Critics of standardized curricula warn that eliminating variance among schools would also eliminate the experimentation that produces better teaching methods.

vaunted.text: The team's vaunted defense collapsed in the final, conceding four goals in the first half and leaving columnists to wonder how they had ever called it the league's best.
The much vaunted reforms, which the government had trumpeted for months, turned out to change very little in practice.
Diners expecting the vaunted cuisine of the famous restaurant were disappointed to find the dishes bland and overpriced.

vehement.text: The proposal to close the rural clinic drew vehement opposition from residents, who packed the hearing and shouted down the officials who defended it.
Though he is mild in conversation, the critic is vehement in print, denouncing films he dislikes with a ferocity that startles his readers.
Her vehement denial of the rumor, delivered with a fist pounding the lectern, convinced some listeners and made others suspect she protested too much.

venality.text: If our legal system becomes plagued with venality, then the very notion of justice is imperiled.
Reformers blamed the port's decline on the venality of its customs officials, who routinely waved through smuggled cargo in exchange for cash.
The novel exposes the venality of a city council whose members, one by one, accept payments from a developer in return for favorable zoning votes.
Judges were given generous salaries and lifetime appointments precisely to guard against venality, since poorly paid magistrates had often sold their verdicts.

veneer.text: Beneath the firm's veneer of prosperity, with its marble lobby and lavish parties, lay a mountain of unpaid debt.
The diplomat's courtesy was only a veneer; in private negotiations he proved ruthless and contemptuous of his counterparts.
The novel exposes the thin veneer of civility in a small town, where polite greetings conceal decades of feuds and resentments.

venerate.text: In many cultures, elders are venerated as keepers of wisdom, and their counsel is sought before any important communal decision.
Though ignored during her lifetime, the painter is now venerated by younger artists, who make pilgrimages to her studio and study her every brushstroke.
The monks venerate the ancient relic, bowing before it each morning and permitting no one to touch it without elaborate rites of purification.

venial.text: The teacher treated forgetting homework as a venial offense, deserving a gentle reminder, but regarded plagiarism as a serious breach requiring formal discipline.
Compared with the embezzlement uncovered later, the manager's habit of taking home extra office supplies seemed a venial lapse.
Readers forgive the narrator's venial faults, such as vanity and occasional laziness, because his deeper loyalty and kindness are never in doubt.

veracious.text: Historians consider the diarist a veracious witness, since the details she recorded have been confirmed repeatedly by independent archives.
A veracious account of the expedition would have admitted its failures, but the leader's memoir exaggerated every triumph and omitted every blunder.
The court valued the witness precisely because he was veracious to a fault, admitting even details that damaged his own reputation.

verisimilitude.text: To lend the historical novel verisimilitude, the author studied period diaries and letters so that every detail of daily life would ring true.
The forger's work possessed such verisimilitude that experts examined the painting for months before detecting the modern pigments.
Although the film is pure fantasy, its careful attention to the physics of flight gives the dragon scenes a surprising verisimilitude.

veritable.text: The attic proved a veritable treasure trove, containing rare first editions, antique maps, and letters from long-forgotten statesmen.
When the dam burst, the quiet stream became a veritable torrent, sweeping away bridges and flooding the valley within minutes.
Her office, stacked floor to ceiling with papers and books, was a veritable labyrinth that visitors could scarcely navigate.

vicarious.text: Unable to travel because of her illness, she took vicarious pleasure in her grandson's letters from abroad, savoring every description of the places he visited.
Some psychologists argue that sports fans derive a vicarious sense of achievement from their team's victories, as if they themselves had been on the field.
Parents who push their children into careers they themselves abandoned may be seeking vicarious fulfillment rather than serving the child's interests.

vicissitude.text: The biography follows the family through the vicissitudes of three generations, from prosperity to bankruptcy and exile.
Farmers learn to accept the vicissitudes of weather, knowing that a single hailstorm can destroy a season's work.
Despite the vicissitudes of her career, including two bankruptcies and a bitter lawsuit, the entrepreneur never lost her optimism.

vie.text: Three architectural firms vied for the commission to design the new library, each submitting elaborate models to the city council.
In the crowded market for electric cars, dozens of startups now vie with established manufacturers for the attention of cautious buyers.
As the aging king's health declined, his nephews began to vie for the loyalty of the nobles, each hoping to secure the throne.

vilify.text: The reformer was vilified in the tabloid press, which portrayed her as a reckless schemer bent on destroying the city's institutions.
Rather than engaging with his critics' arguments, the author chose to vilify them, spreading rumors about their motives and their private lives.
Although later historians have rehabilitated his reputation, the engineer was widely vilified in his own time as the man responsible for the bridge's collapse.

vindicate.text: The scientist's once ridiculed hypothesis was vindicated when new telescopes detected precisely the faint signal she had predicted decades earlier.
The audit vindicated the treasurer, showing that the missing funds had been misplaced through a clerical error rather than stolen.
Accused of plagiarism, the student produced early drafts and notes that vindicated her, proving that the ideas had been her own from the start.

vindictive.text: Rather than forgiving the critic who had panned her debut, the novelist grew vindictive, mocking him by name in every book she published afterward.
The deposed minister's vindictive campaign against his former colleagues, whom he blamed for his downfall, eventually alienated even his supporters.
Historians note that the victors' terms were vindictive rather than prudent: designed to punish the defeated nation, they instead bred lasting resentment.

virago.text: In the play, the landlady is portrayed as a virago who berates her tenants at the slightest provocation and once hurls a teapot at a lodger.
Contemporary pamphlets caricatured the outspoken duchess as a virago, exaggerating her occasional sharp words into a reputation for constant rage.
The villagers avoided the miller's wife, a notorious virago whose furious outbursts could be heard across the square.

vitriol.text: The online forum was filled with vitriol, as anonymous users hurled insults and threats at anyone who disagreed with them.
The candidate's speech, full of vitriol toward his opponents, alarmed moderates who had hoped for a more civil campaign.
Years of rivalry had left the two scholars with nothing but vitriol for each other, and their reviews of each other's books were venomous attacks.

vitriolic.text: The critic's vitriolic review, which called the novel a monument to incompetence, devastated the young author.
Although the debate began courteously, it soon became vitriolic, with each speaker harshly attacking the other's character.
Unlike his measured public statements, the senator's private letters were vitriolic, full of caustic remarks about colleagues he despised.

vituperate.text: The coach would vituperate his players after every loss, berating them in the locker room for mistakes both large and small.
Rather than offering constructive criticism, the reviewer vituperated the playwright, and even readers who disliked the play found the abuse out of proportion to its faults.
For months the pamphleteers vituperated the governor, denouncing him in the harshest language as corrupt and incompetent.

vociferous.text: The plan to pave over the park drew vociferous protests, with hundreds of residents chanting outside city hall late into the night.
A small but vociferous minority of the audience booed and jeered throughout the premiere, drowning out the singers during the final act.
The professor welcomed disagreement but not the vociferous interruptions of one student, who shouted objections before others could finish speaking.

volubility.text: The host's volubility was an asset on the radio, where she could fill an hour of airtime without a pause, but it exhausted guests who hoped to speak.
Readers of her letters are struck by their volubility: she could write twenty pages about a single afternoon and still apologize for leaving things out.
In contrast to his quiet brother, Paulo was the family's spokesman, and his volubility allowed him to chat with strangers for hours without running out of words.

voracious.text: A voracious collector, the banker filled three warehouses with paintings, manuscripts, and antique instruments, yet was always hunting for more.
After the long winter, the bears emerged voracious, stripping berry bushes and raiding campsites in their search for food.
Her appetite for languages was voracious: by the time she finished graduate school, she had learned Greek, Arabic, Persian, and Russian.

wanting.text: The candidate's credentials were impressive, but in the interview her knowledge of the field was found wanting, and the committee chose someone else.
Though the translation is fluent, it is wanting in precision; several technical terms are rendered so loosely that the original meaning is lost.
Critics praised the building's facade but judged its interior wanting, with cramped rooms and too little natural light for its intended use as a gallery.

wanton.text: The invading soldiers engaged in wanton destruction, burning libraries and smashing statues that had no military value whatsoever.
The court condemned the factory owners' wanton disregard for safety, noting that they had ignored repeated warnings about the crumbling walls.
Moralists of the period denounced the courtier's wanton extravagance, since he indulged every appetite while the peasants on his estates went hungry.

wax.text: As the campaign against the tax wore on, public anger only waxed, and by autumn the protests had spread to every major city.
The composer's reputation waned after his death but waxed again a century later, when conductors rediscovered his forgotten symphonies.
Interest in the obscure philosopher has been waxing steadily among graduate students, whose dissertations now cite him more often than ever.

whimsical.text: The dictator's whimsical decrees, issued without consultation and often reversed within days, left his ministers unable to plan anything.
Rather than follow a systematic research agenda, the eccentric chemist pursued whimsical lines of inquiry, abandoning each one the moment a new idea struck him.
The garden's layout appears whimsical, with paths that wander aimlessly, but the designer insists that every curve was carefully calculated.

winsome.text: The toddler's winsome grin disarmed even the grumpiest passengers, who found themselves waving back at her across the aisle.
The film's heroine is winsome rather than glamorous; audiences who would never envy her find themselves won over by her artless curiosity and her delight in small things.
Though the illustrations are winsome (all round faces and wide, innocent eyes), the story they accompany is surprisingly dark.

zeitgeist.text: The zeitgeist of the 2000's was a curious admixture of fear and frivolity; when we were not anxious over the state of the economy and the world, we escaped into reality T.V. shows, either those on popular networks or the ones we would create ourselves on YouTube.
The novel captured the zeitgeist of the postwar years, its restless characters embodying a generation's disillusionment and hunger for change.
Fashion designers try to anticipate the zeitgeist, sensing the moods and values that will define a season before consumers can articulate them.
Historians argue that the architecture of the era reflects its zeitgeist, since the soaring glass towers expressed an optimistic faith in technology and progress.

zenith.text: At the zenith of its power, the trading city controlled nearly every port along the coast; within a century, however, it had faded into obscurity.
Critics regard the late quartets as the zenith of the composer's achievement, the culmination of decades of experimentation.
The company reached its zenith in the year it bought out its largest rival; after that, a series of poor decisions sent it into steady decline.
